`ArtAttack/Save.cpp:112-135` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

`save/save_data.json` is `{"resolution":{"x":1920,"y":1080},"fullscreen":false}` and the three level JSONs have top-level keys `level_name, sound, spawn_locations, level_bounds, collision_objects, non_collision_objects` (verified across all three). Neither format carries a version.

Consequences, concretely:
- Old save read by new code: any field added later is simply absent, so `d["new_field"]` takes the unguarded-access path above — garbage in Release, assert in Debug. There is no migration hook.
- New save read by old code: `convert_ivec_to_resolution` (Save.cpp:112-135) matches four hardcoded pairs and `else return screen_resolution::S_1280_720;` — an unrecognised resolution is silently downgraded, and the very next `set_full_screen_and_save` writes 1280x720 back over the user's setting. Silent data loss with no way to detect it.
- `Save::write_save_file` also serialises the resolution as x/y integers while the in-memory type is the closed enum `screen_resolution` (screen_resolution.h:4-11), so the file format promises more than the code accepts.

Also still tracked next to it: `ArtAttack/save/save_data.txt` containing `1920x1080\nfalse` — a dead legacy save format with no reader anywhere in the codebase.

**Fix:** Add a `"version"` integer to both formats, check it on load, and fail loudly (or migrate explicitly) on mismatch. Preserve unknown values rather than silently rewriting them. Delete save_data.txt.

#### 10. C-era file handling: NULL, fopen-as-existence-check, unchecked fclose, duplicated 65536 literal, FILE* leaks on throw

`ArtAttack/Save.cpp:33-42, 58-83` — **low** · `robustness`

Merged from 3 candidates.

    bool Save::check_if_save_file_exists() {
        FILE* fp = fopen(SAVE_FILE_PATH.c_str(), "rb");
        if (fp == NULL) { return false; }
        fclose(fp); return true;
    }

`NULL` instead of `nullptr` (the only occurrence in this module — line 61 correctly uses nullptr), and opening-then-closing a file to test existence.

In `write_save_file` (58-83): `65536` is written twice as a bare literal (lines 66 and 67) — the exact setup that produced the read-path bug where the buffer size and the allocation already disagree — to serialise a 52-byte document. `fclose`'s return is discarded, and rapidjson's `FileWriteStream::Flush` deliberately ignores short-write failures, so `fclose` is the last place a full-disk error could be caught; `write_save_file` returns `true` regardless and `save_to_file` prints "Save was successful" for a save that did not happen.

No `FILE*` in this module is RAII-owned, so `Document` operations that can throw `bad_alloc` between fopen and fclose leak the handle in all five loaders. Also `FileWriteStream os` still references `fp` after `fclose(fp)` at line 81 — harmless only because rapidjson's Writer flushes at the end of the top-level value and FileWriteStream has no destructor, which is a property of the vendored library, not something this code establishes.

**Fix:** `std::filesystem::exists(...)` and `nullptr`. `constexpr size_t WRITE_BUFFER_SIZE = 4096;` used in both places. Call `os.Flush()` explicitly then `return fclose(fp) == 0;`. Wrap every handle: `std::unique_ptr<FILE, int(*)(FILE*)> fp(fopen(p, "rb"), &fclose);`.

## `ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp`

_7 findings: 1 critical, 2 high, 1 medium, 3 low_

#### 1. rapidjson read buffer is a 1-byte allocation sized with sizeof(unique_ptr) — heap overrun on every JSON load, then leaked

`ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:152-161` — **critical** · `memory-safety`

Merged from 4 near-identical candidates. Verbatim at SoundBank.cpp:152-161:

    FILE* fp = fopen(json_path, "rb");
    auto read_buffer = std::make_unique<char>();
    FileReadStream is(fp, read_buffer.get(), sizeof(read_buffer));
    ...
    fclose(fp);
    read_buffer.release();

Three compounded defects, all verified:
1. `std::make_unique<char>()` allocates exactly ONE char. `std::make_unique<char[]>(N)` was intended.
2. `sizeof(read_buffer)` is `sizeof(std::unique_ptr<char>)` == 8 on x64 (4 on Win32), not the buffer size. I read external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/filereadstream.h: the ctor asserts `bufferSize >= 4` (line 46, passes), then `Read()` does `readCount_ = std::fread(buffer_, 1, bufferSize_, fp_)` (line 71) — 8 bytes into a 1-byte heap block, repeatedly for the whole file — and on the final short read also writes `buffer_[readCount_] = '\0'` (line 76), index up to 7. Heap corruption on every asset load.
3. `read_buffer.release()` relinquishes ownership WITHOUT deleting, so the block leaks. The author likely meant `reset()`, or nothing at all.

All four sites verified line by line: ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:152-161, ArtAttack/Save.cpp:14-23, ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.cpp:72-81, ArtAttack/LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:96-110 (the last uses the name `readBuffer`). Secondary effect: the file is consumed 8 bytes at a time, so a 22 KB level JSON costs ~2,700 fread calls.

**Fix:** Delete all four copies and write ONE helper — `rapidjson::Document parse_json_file(const char* path)` — that opens with a checked/RAII FILE*, uses `char buf[65536]` (or `std::vector<char>`) with its real size, and returns the document. Drop every `.release()`.

#### 2. A wave name typo in sound_bank_1.json stores a null SoundEffectInstance that crashes later at play time

`ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:110-141` — **high** · `robustness` · confidence: likely

```cpp
try { sound_effect_instances[name] = this->_wave_bank->CreateInstance(wave.c_str()); }
catch (const std::out_of_range& e) { throw std::out_of_range("Wave with name " + wave + " not found"); }
```

DirectXTK's `WaveBank::CreateInstance(const char* name, ...)` (packages/directxtk_desktop_2019.2023.10.31.1/include/Audio.h:338) returns a `unique_ptr` that is **null** when the name isn't in the wave bank — it deliberately does not throw, because titles commonly ignore missing assets. So the catch is dead code, a null instance is stored under a valid key, `get_sound_effect_instance` (:78, using `.at()`) reports success, and `play_effect` (:33-37) null-derefs on `sei->SetVolume(volume)` the first time that sound is triggered mid-gameplay.

The same dead `catch (const std::out_of_range& e)` wraps `_wave_bank->Play()` at :19-26 and appears again at :80-83 and :137-140; in all four the bound `e` is unused (a /W4 C4101 warning that nobody sees because `TreatWarningAsError` is not set).

This matters because sounds/sound_bank_1.json:2-28 is a hand-maintained list of 24 wave names duplicating the XWBTool command line in sounds/sound_bank_1/cmd.txt — two sources of truth for the same list, with nothing checking they agree.

**Fix:** Null-check the result of `CreateInstance` and throw naming the wave, the bank and the JSON path, at load time. Delete the four dead `catch (std::out_of_range)` blocks. Better: derive the wave name list from the wave bank itself (`WaveBank::Find`) rather than duplicating it in JSON.

#### 3. fopen result unchecked and ParseStream result never inspected — a missing or malformed asset is UB in Release, not an error

`ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:150-172` — **high** · `robustness`

Merged from 4 candidates. `FILE* fp = fopen(json_path, "rb");` is passed straight into `FileReadStream` with no null test. `FileReadStream`'s only guard is `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(fp_ != 0)` (filereadstream.h:45), which is plain assert. I confirmed ArtAttack.vcxproj lines 138 and 164 define NDEBUG for both Release configs, so in Release a missing file gives `fread(buf, 1, 8, nullptr)` then `fclose(nullptr)`.

`d.ParseStream(is)` returns a ParseResult that is discarded everywhere; a grep of the first-party tree finds zero uses of `HasParseError`/`GetParseError`. The subsequent member lookups are also unguarded: SoundBank.cpp:163-166 `d["waves"]`, `d["sound_effect_instances"]`, `d["create_effect_instance_for_each_wave"].GetBool()`; SoundBank.cpp:125-126 `effect["name"]`, `effect["wave"]`; Save.cpp:25-26 `d["resolution"]["x"].GetInt()`, `d["fullscreen"].GetBool()`. rapidjson's `operator[](const Ch*)` on a missing member asserts (compiled out) and returns a shared static NullValue, on which `.GetInt()`/`.GetBool()` assert again and read garbage.

Save.cpp is the worst case because save/save_data.json is the one file here that is genuinely untrusted: `write_save_file` opens it with "wb" (Save.cpp:60), truncating immediately, so a crash mid-write leaves a zero-length file that `check_if_save_file_exists()` happily reports as present.

Same at SpriteSheet.cpp:72-88 and LevelLoadedInfo.cpp:96-110.

**Fix:** In the shared loader from the previous finding: check `fp != nullptr` and throw naming the path; check `d.ParseStream(is).IsError()` and report `GetParseErrorCode()` + `GetErrorOffset()`; guard each member with `HasMember` + the matching type predicate. For Save specifically, any failure should fall back to `SaveData{}` defaults and rewrite the file rather than propagate.

#### 4. WaveBank::CreateInstance returns nullptr for an unknown wave; the catch(out_of_range) never fires and the null is stored under a valid key

`ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:99-148` — **medium** · `robustness`

Merged from 3 candidates.

    try { sound_effect_instances[name] = this->_wave_bank->CreateInstance(wave.c_str()); }
    catch (const std::out_of_range& e) { throw std::out_of_range("Wave with name " + wave + " not found"); }

I verified in packages/directxtk_desktop_2019.2023.10.31.1/include/Audio.h that `CreateInstance` (lines 336-339) returns `std::unique_ptr<SoundEffectInstance>` and that `WaveBank::Find(const char*)` returns `int` (line 362) — the name-resolution path. DirectXTK returns nullptr on a miss rather than throwing `std::out_of_range`. So both catch blocks here (116-119 and 137-140) are dead code, and a typo in sounds/sound_bank_1.json stores a live map key with a null value.

That null survives every downstream guard: `get_sound_effect_instance` (74-84) uses `.at()`, which SUCCEEDS because the key exists, and returns `.get()` == nullptr. Every caller dereferences it unchecked — `play_effect` lines 33-37 does `sei->SetVolume(...)`, and `stop_effect`/`pause_effect`/`resume_effect`/`set_effect_*`/`get_effect_state`/`is_effect_looping` (39-73) are all one-line `get_sound_effect_instance(x)->Method()`.

Same dead-catch shape at play_wave (19-26) — `WaveBank::Play(const char*, float, float, float)` returns `void` (Audio.h:334) and cannot throw out_of_range — so a misspelled wave name is a permanent SILENT no-op in Release. I checked the current data and every name used in code does exist in sound_bank_1.json, so nothing is broken today; but nothing would tell you if it were.

Downgraded from high: it takes a data-authoring error to trigger.

**Fix:** `auto inst = _wave_bank->CreateInstance(wave.c_str()); if (!inst) throw std::runtime_error("wave '" + wave + "' not in wave bank"); sound_effect_instances.try_emplace(name, std::move(inst));`. Delete the dead catches. Have `get_sound_effect_instance` throw on a null mapped value so failure surfaces at the lookup. For play_wave, resolve via `Find()` and fail loudly on -1.

#### 5. Four catch blocks bind an exception name they never use and discard the original what()

`ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:23, 80, 116, 137` — **low** · `modern-cpp`

`catch (const std::out_of_range& e)` at SoundBank.cpp:23, 80, 116 and 137 — `e` is unreferenced in all four, which is /W4 noise, and every block throws a freshly-constructed `out_of_range` that discards `e.what()`. Three of the four are also unreachable dead code per the earlier findings; only the one at line 80 (wrapping `.at()`) can actually fire, and that one is the one that throws away the real message.

In the same function (99-148): `std::string name = wave;` at line 109 is a full copy of `wave` used only as a map key, and `sound_effect_instances[name] = ...` default-constructs then move-assigns where `try_emplace` would construct once. `decode_wave_names_json` (89-97) `push_back`s into an unreserved vector when `json.Size()` is known up front.

**Fix:** Drop the unused `e` names, or append `e.what()` to the new message. Use `sound_effect_instances.try_emplace(wave, _wave_bank->CreateInstance(wave.c_str()))` and delete the `name` copy; add `wave_names.reserve(json.Size())`.

#### 6. A name collision in the sound bank JSON aborts startup rather than being reported as a data error

`ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:123-146` — **low** · `robustness`

if (sound_effect_instances.find(name) == sound_effect_instances.end()) { ...create... }
    else { throw std::runtime_error("SoundEffectInstance with name " + name + " already exists"); }

With `create_effect_instance_for_each_wave: true` (verified at sounds/sound_bank_1.json:29), every one of the 24 wave names is pre-registered as an instance name first. So if anyone adds an entry to `sound_effect_instances` named after a wave — e.g. `{"name": "LaserGun", "wave": "LaserGun"}` — the whole game fails to start during `Game::initialize`. The message does not even include the JSON path, so the offending file is not named. A content-authoring mistake is escalated to a fatal error with no breadcrumb.

**Fix:** Treat the collision as a warning (skip the duplicate, log the file and entry name) or make the two name spaces explicitly distinct. Include `json_path` in every message this loader produces.

#### 7. clamp_levels mutates three out-parameters, and the valid ranges are re-stated in four places

`ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:174-179` — **low** · `api-quality`

void SoundBank::clamp_levels(float& volume, float& pitch, float& pan)
    { volume = clamp(volume, 0.0f, 1.0f); pitch = clamp(pitch, -1.0f, 1.0f); pan = clamp(pan, -1.0f, 1.0f); }

Called only to overwrite the caller's own by-value parameters (SoundBank.cpp:18 and :32). Then `set_effect_volume`/`set_effect_pitch`/`set_effect_pan` (51-65) re-implement the same three clamps inline, so the range knowledge lives in four places.

Related in the same signatures: `play_effect(name, bool loop, float volume, float pitch, float pan)` gives call sites like `play_effect("roller_a0", true, 0.5f, 0.0f, 0.0f)` where nothing says what `true` means, and pitch and pan share the same [-1,1] range so transposing them compiles and silently misbehaves. Every one of these signatures exists twice — once in SoundBank, once as a SoundBankObject forwarder — so any change is a two-file edit.

`clamp` here is `MattMath::clamp`, a hand-rolled `std::clamp` the project cannot use because no LanguageStandard is set (see the build-config finding).

**Fix:** `struct SoundParams { float volume = 1.0f, pitch = 0.0f, pan = 0.0f; SoundParams clamped() const; };` with the ranges declared once as constexpr, plus `enum class loop_mode { once, loop };` and `enum class stop_mode { fade, immediate };`. `play_effect(name, loop_mode::loop, {0.5f})` is self-documenting and un-transposable.

## `ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.cpp`

_7 findings: 2 critical, 2 high, 3 medium_

#### 1. load_from_json freads into a 1-byte allocation using sizeof(unique_ptr) as the buffer size, leaks it, and never checks fopen

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.cpp:70-90` — **critical** · `memory-safety`

Merged from four independent reports; all four describe the same six lines and all four are correct.

```cpp
FILE* fp = fopen(json_path, "rb");            // 72: result never checked
auto read_buffer = std::make_unique<char>();  // 74: allocates exactly ONE char
FileReadStream is(fp, read_buffer.get(), sizeof(read_buffer)); // 75: sizeof(unique_ptr<char>) == 8
Document d; d.ParseStream(is);
fclose(fp);
read_buffer.release();                        // 81: drops ownership without deleting
```
I read the vendored stream to confirm the consequence. external/rapidjson/include/rapidjson/filereadstream.h:66-81 `Read()` does `readCount_ = std::fread(buffer_, 1, bufferSize_, fp_);` and then, when `readCount_ < bufferSize_`, `buffer_[readCount_] = '\0';`. With bufferSize_==8 and a 1-byte allocation that is a 7-byte heap overflow on every refill, repeated for the whole file. It also forces the parser to refill 8 bytes at a time.

`release()` abandons the allocation (author meant `reset()`, which was itself unnecessary). `fopen` is unchecked and rapidjson's `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT(fp_ != 0)` compiles out under NDEBUG, so a missing file gives `fread(nullptr)` then `fclose(nullptr)`.

The identical five lines exist verbatim in ArtAttack/SoundBank.cpp:150-161 (I read it; same `make_unique<char>()` + `sizeof(read_buffer)` + `release()`), so this is two sites, not one. Live at startup via ResourceLoader.

**Fix:** Use a real buffer and its real size, check the open, RAII the handle:
```cpp
std::vector<char> read_buffer(64 * 1024);
FILE* fp = nullptr;
if (fopen_s(&fp, json_path, "rb") != 0 || !fp)
    throw std::runtime_error(std::string("cannot open ") + json_path);
std::unique_ptr<FILE, decltype(&fclose)> guard(fp, &fclose);
rapidjson::FileReadStream is(fp, read_buffer.data(), read_buffer.size());
rapidjson::Document d;
if (d.ParseStream(is).HasParseError()) throw std::runtime_error(...);
```
Fix SoundBank.cpp:150-161 the same way. For a 14KB file, `Document::Parse` on a slurped string is simpler than streaming at all. Grep the tree for `sizeof(` applied to any smart pointer.

#### 2. SpriteSheet::draw calls std::map::operator[] on a shared sheet from up to 16 worker threads

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.cpp:92-132` — **critical** · `concurrency` · confidence: certain

Two of the four `SpriteSheet::draw` overloads are non-const and index the frame map with `operator[]`:

```cpp
void SpriteSheet::draw(SpriteBatch* sprite_batch, const std::string& frame_name, ...)  // :92, no trailing const
{
    sprite_batch->Draw(this->_texture, position.get_xm_vector(),
        this->_sprite_frames[frame_name].get_source_rectangle(),   // :105
        ...);
}
// identical at :114-132, line :126
```

`_sprite_frames` is `std::map<std::string, SpriteFrame>` (SpriteSheet.h:61) and `std::map::operator[]` **default-constructs and inserts** when the key is absent — a tree mutation. `SpriteSheet` objects are owned once by `ResourceManager` and handed out as raw pointers to every `SpriteSheetObject`, so a single sheet is shared by every player, projectile and tile.

Those objects' `draw()` calls all funnel into this from inside the thread-pool tasks submitted at Level.cpp:388 and MenuPage.cpp:142. Concurrent `operator[]` on one `std::map` from N threads is undefined behaviour even when every key already exists (it is a non-const member function on shared state), and a genuine red-black-tree corruption the first time any lookup misses — e.g. a typo'd frame name in a JSON sheet, which today silently inserts an empty `SpriteFrame` instead of failing.

Note the other two overloads (:134, :156) are correctly `const` and take a pre-resolved `RECT*`, which proves the const version is achievable.

**Fix:** Make both string-keyed overloads `const` and replace `_sprite_frames[frame_name]` with `auto it = _sprite_frames.find(frame_name); if (it == _sprite_frames.end()) throw/log;`. That removes the mutation, makes the missing-frame case loud instead of silent, and is a prerequisite for any multithreaded draw. Longer term, resolve frame names to indices/handles once at load time so the render path does no string lookups at all.

#### 3. Both name-keyed draw overloads look frames up with map::operator[], so a typo draws nothing silently and the overloads cannot be const

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.cpp:92-132` — **high** · `correctness`

`this->_sprite_frames[frame_name].get_source_rectangle()` at SpriteSheet.cpp:105 and :126.

`operator[]` default-constructs on a miss. `SpriteFrame`'s default `_source_rectangle` is `{0,0,0,0}` (SpriteFrame.h:21), so a misspelled frame name in code or level JSON produces an invisible sprite with no error, no assert and no log, plus a permanent junk entry in the atlas. Contrast `get_animation_strip` (SpriteSheet.cpp:17) on the same class, which uses `.at()` and throws — two lookups, opposite failure semantics.

Because `operator[]` is non-const these two overloads cannot be `const`, while the two `const RECT*` overloads directly below them (SpriteSheet.cpp:134-174) are. That single choice is what forces the entire chain above — `TextureObject::draw`, `SpriteSheetObject::get_sprite_sheet`, `DrawObject::get_resource_manager` — to hand out non-const pointers out of const methods.

On severity I am downgrading the reviewers' "heap corruption today" framing. `draw_player_view_level` genuinely runs on N thread-pool workers sharing one `SpriteSheet` (see the concurrency finding), but every frame name actually used at runtime exists in sprite_sheet_1.json (I checked "pixel" at line 209 and "health_box" at line 378), so `operator[]` is not currently restructuring the tree. The race is latent behind a content typo, not active.

I also reject one sub-claim attached to this by two reviewers: `SpriteFrame::get_source_rectangle()` returning `&_source_rectangle` is not a live hazard — DirectXTK's `SpriteBatch::Draw` copies the source rect into its own sprite record, and `_sprite_frames` is only reassigned wholesale in `load_from_json`, which does not run concurrently with drawing.

**Fix:** `find()` + throw naming the missing frame, or `.at()`. Mark both overloads `const`. Best: resolve frame names to an index/handle once at load so the render path never touches a string or a map, which removes the mutability and the per-draw lookup together.

#### 4. A misspelled frame_name in level JSON silently draws a 0x0 sprite instead of failing

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.cpp:105` — **high** · `robustness` · confidence: certain

```cpp
sprite_batch->Draw(this->_texture, position.get_xm_vector(),
    this->_sprite_frames[frame_name].get_source_rectangle(), ...);
```

`operator[]` inserts a default-constructed `SpriteFrame`, whose `RECT _source_rectangle = { 0, 0, 0, 0 }` (SpriteFrame.h:21). The result is an invisible zero-area sprite, silently, every frame, forever — with the bogus entry now permanently cached in the map. The 91 `frame_name` strings across the three level JSONs and the ~40 hardcoded `"sprite_sheet_1"`/frame-name literals scattered through MainMenu.cpp, PauseMenu.cpp, EndMenu.cpp, InterfaceGameplay.cpp and player_consts.h are all validated only by this silent-failure path.

Note the inconsistency: `SpriteSheet::get_animation_strip` (SpriteSheet.cpp:17) uses `.at()` and throws for the same class of error. Two lookups in the same class, two opposite failure modes.

Second site: SpriteSheet.cpp:126 (the RectangleI destination overload).

**Fix:** Use `.at()` (or `find()` with a descriptive throw naming both the sheet and the frame). Given every frame name is fixed at load time, prefer resolving names to indices/pointers once during load so a bad name fails at startup, not silently at draw time.

#### 5. Sprite sheet JSON is parsed with zero validation, so a malformed file is undefined behaviour in Release

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.cpp:20-90` — **medium** · `robustness`

`load_from_json` does `d.ParseStream(is)` and never calls `d.HasParseError()`. It then does `Value& sprite_frames = d["sprite_frames"];` and `d["animation_strips"]` with no `HasMember` check.

`decode_sprite_frames_json` (:20-47) indexes `frame["name"]`, `frame["position"]["x"]`, `frame["size"]["w"]` and calls `GetString`/`GetInt`/`GetFloat` with no type checks. `decode_animation_strips_json` (:49-68) does the same for `first_frame`/`frame_count`/`frame_time`/`looping`. RapidJSON guards all of these with `RAPIDJSON_ASSERT`, which is a no-op under NDEBUG — and Release defines NDEBUG. So a truncated or hand-edited sheet does not produce an error message, it reads past `MemberEnd()`.

`frame_count` and `frame_time` are also never range-checked before being handed to `AnimationStrip`, which is the upstream cause of two other findings here (zero frame_time poisoning the animation accumulator, and an unvalidated `frame_count` driving an unreserved allocation loop).

**Fix:** After `ParseStream`, `if (d.HasParseError()) throw` with `GetParseError_En(d.GetParseError())` and `GetErrorOffset()`. Add a `require_member(v, "name")` helper that checks `HasMember` plus the expected `Is*()` and throws a message naming the file, the frame and the field. Validate `frame_count > 0` and `frame_time > 0` before constructing `AnimationStrip`.

#### 6. Unknown frame name silently draws a 0×0 sprite and mutates a shared map from render threads

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.cpp:92-132` — **medium** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

Both `SpriteSheet::draw` overloads look the frame up with `std::map::operator[]`:

    this->_sprite_frames[frame_name].get_source_rectangle()

`operator[]` default-constructs and inserts on a miss. `SpriteFrame`'s default source rect is `RECT _source_rectangle = { 0, 0, 0, 0 }` (ArtAttack/SpriteFrame.h:21), so a misspelled frame name produces a silent degenerate draw with no error — in sharp contrast to `get_animation_strip` (SpriteSheet.cpp:15-18) which uses `.at()` and throws.

The shipped data proves the failure mode is real, not hypothetical: ArtAttack/levels/unused/test_1.json:159 and ArtAttack/levels/unused/structure_test_old.json:261 both contain `"frame_name": "grsquare_white_4ass"` — a botched find-and-replace of `grass` → `square_white_4`. That frame does not exist in ArtAttack/textures/sprite_sheet_1.json, and nothing would have told the author.

Second, sharper problem: these overloads are non-const and mutate `_sprite_frames`, and they are called from the multi-threaded draw path. `Level::draw_active_level` dispatches `draw_player_view_level` (Level.cpp:491-593) as ThreadPool tasks, each recording into its own deferred context but all going through the *same* `SpriteSheet*` handed out by `ResourceManager`. A single missing frame name therefore causes a concurrent `std::map` insert while up to three other threads are reading it — undefined behaviour, and a heisenbug that only appears when content is wrong.

**Fix:** Make both `draw` overloads `const` and use `_sprite_frames.at(frame_name)`, or a `find()` that throws a message naming the frame and the sheet. Validate all frame/strip names once at load time against the atlas rather than at draw time.

#### 7. Const draw path mutates shared std::maps from 4 render threads (std::map::operator[]), reached thousands of times per frame by paint tiles

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.cpp:114-132` — **medium** · `memory-safety` · confidence: likely

`SpriteSheet::draw` is non-const and indexes with `this->_sprite_frames[frame_name]` (line 126) - `std::map::operator[]`, which default-constructs and inserts on a miss. It is called from `TextureObject::draw(...) const` (ArtAttack/TextureObject.cpp:26-33), which `PaintTile::draw` invokes at PaintTile.cpp:52/72. The sheet itself is fetched through `ResourceManager::get_sprite_sheet`, which is also `_sprite_sheets[name]` with `operator[]` (ArtAttack/ResourceManager.cpp:46-58) - and whose `catch (const std::out_of_range&)` at line 53 is dead, because `operator[]` never throws that; a typo'd sheet name silently inserts a null `unique_ptr` and the caller dereferences nullptr.
`Level::draw_active_level` dispatches these draws onto up to 4 ThreadPool tasks over the same `ResourceManager`/`SpriteSheet` instances (ArtAttack/Level.cpp:388-397), so four threads concurrently invoke non-const members on the same containers - formally a data race per [res.on.data.races], and a real one (RB-tree rebalance under concurrent readers) the moment any key is missing. Paint tiles make this the single hottest path in the renderer: 5,574 tiles x 4 viewports x 5 map lookups = 111,480 concurrent map accesses per frame on turbulence.

**Fix:** Make both lookups const and non-mutating: `SpriteSheet::draw(...) const` using `_sprite_frames.at(frame_name)`, and `ResourceManager::get_sprite_sheet(...) const` using `find()` with an explicit throw on miss. Then resolve `SpriteSheet*` and the `SpriteFrame*`/`AnimationStrip*` once at object construction and cache the pointers, so the render threads do pure reads of immutable data.

## `ArtAttack/SpriteSheetObject.cpp`

_2 findings: 1 critical, 1 high_

#### 1. Resource lookup mutates shared std::maps and is called per-draw from thread-pool worker threads

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheetObject.cpp:31-35` — **critical** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

`Level::draw_active_level` (Level.cpp:386-399) dispatches `draw_player_view_level` onto `ThreadPool` workers, one per player partition, each recording into its own deferred context. Those tasks call `object->draw(...)` on shared game objects, which reaches:

```cpp
SpriteSheet* SpriteSheetObject::get_sprite_sheet() const {
    return this->get_resource_manager()->get_sprite_sheet(this->get_sprite_sheet_name());
}
```

`ResourceManager::get_sprite_sheet` is `_sprite_sheets[name]` (ResourceManager.cpp:51) — a **non-const, potentially-inserting** `std::map` operation on an object shared by all worker threads. The draw then calls `SpriteSheet::draw`, whose body is `this->_sprite_frames[frame_name].get_source_rectangle()` (SpriteSheet.cpp:105 and :126) — a second mutating `operator[]` on a second shared map, from N threads at once.

Even when no insertion occurs, concurrent invocation of a non-const `std::map` member from multiple threads is a data race by [res.on.data.races]. When an insertion *does* occur (any unknown sheet or frame name) the red-black tree is rebalanced under other threads' iterators. `ResourceManager::get_sprite_font` (:31) and `get_sound_bank` (:95) have the same shape and are reached from the same draw path (TextObject.cpp:30,50; DebugText.cpp:106).

**Fix:** Make every ResourceManager and SpriteSheet lookup `const` and non-mutating (`.at()` / `find()`), which removes the race entirely for read-only lookups. Better still for a per-frame hot path: resolve the `SpriteSheet*` and the `SpriteFrame` once at object construction and store them, instead of doing two string-keyed map lookups per sprite per frame.

#### 2. Renderables store resource names, so every draw costs 2-3 string-keyed std::map lookups through a chain of virtual getters

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheetObject.cpp:31-35` — **high** · `performance`

```cpp
SpriteSheet* SpriteSheetObject::get_sprite_sheet() const {
    return this->get_resource_manager()->get_sprite_sheet(this->get_sprite_sheet_name());
}
```
Each call is an O(log n) red-black-tree walk with full `std::string` compares. `TextureObject::draw` then passes `get_element_name()` into `SpriteSheet::draw`, which does a second string map lookup on `_sprite_frames`.

`AnimationObject` is worse: `get_animation_strip()` (AnimationObject.cpp:24-28) is sheet lookup + strip lookup = two map lookups, and it is called from `get_source_rectangle()` (:139-143) on every draw, from `update()` (:87), from `set_frame_index` (:129) and from `set_frame_time_to_default` (:158). `TextObject::draw` does a font map lookup per string per frame (TextObject.cpp:29-30, 49-50).

Every hop is a virtual call — DrawObject.h:20-25 and SpriteSheetObject.h:19-23 make all the trivial accessors `virtual` — so none of it inlines. Amplification is severe: `draw_player_view_level` redraws every object once per player viewport, and `StructurePaintable::draw` draws its whole `PaintTile` grid, each tile doing a `TextureObject::draw` plus a `PaintTileSplash` `AnimationObject::draw`.

The irony: the dead `AnimatedSprite` class already caches `SpriteSheet*` and `const AnimationStrip*` at construction and never looks a name up again.

**Fix:** Names are load-time data. Have `ResourceManager` issue opaque handles (indices into contiguous arrays) at load, and have renderables store the handle plus a resolved `const AnimationStrip*`, invalidated only in `set_animation_strip_and_reset`. Resolution happens once, in the builder/loader layer that can report a missing asset usefully. This also makes the render path const and thread-safe for free.

## `ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp`

_16 findings: 2 critical, 3 high, 10 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. Paintable face selection maps edge indices to the wrong faces — 3 of 4 faces paint on the wrong side

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:188-213` — **critical** · `correctness`

generate_paint_tiles() recovers which faces are paintable by matching `this->get_shape()->get_edges()` against `_paintable_edges` and mapping the positional index: `if (i==0) top_edge=true; else if (i==1) right_edge=true; else if (i==2) bottom_edge=true; else if (i==3) left_edge=true;`.

MattMath.cpp:808-818 returns `{ get_top_edge(), get_bottom_edge(), get_left_edge(), get_right_edge() }` — top, bottom, left, right. So the actual mapping is: JSON top→top (correct), JSON bottom→right face, JSON left→bottom face, JSON right→left face.

I verified this against the shipped level data (all three files parsed). Live consequences:
- king_of_the_hill.json `castle_ceiling` (1650x25, bottom only): should get ~412 tiles on its underside, actually gets ~6 on its right end. The castle ceiling is unpaintable.
- `castle_wall_left` (25x750, right only) and `castle_wall_right` (25x750, left only): tiles land on the opposite face, i.e. the outside of the castle instead of the inside.
- `castle_floor_left` (top+right) → generates top+left; `castle_floor_right` (left+top) → generates bottom+top.
- close_quarters.json `lower_paint` (3000x50, top+bottom) → generates top+right, losing ~738 tiles.
- turbulence.json `central_divider_ledge_paint` (left+top+right) → generates bottom+top+left.
All-four-face structures (mountain_platform_left/right, upper_top_paint, etc.) are unaffected because the set is symmetric — which is why this has gone unnoticed.

The root cause is the round trip itself: LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:107-130 encodes four JSON booleans as `Segment`s, and this code decodes them back into booleans via an undocumented positional ordering. Candidates 1, 43, 57 and 76 all report this; merged here.

**Fix:** Delete the encode/decode entirely. Pass the four booleans (or a `paintable_faces` bitmask) straight from LevelObjectBuilder into StructurePaintable — the commented-out `PaintableFaces` struct at StructurePaintable.h:17-23 and LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:101-105 already did exactly this. If edge matching must stay, compare against the named accessors (`rect.get_top_edge()` etc.) rather than positional indices, and add a unit test pinning `RectangleF::get_edges()` ordering.

#### 2. Paintable-face index map is wrong for 3 of 4 faces; JSON faces paint on the wrong side of the structure

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:188-213` — **critical** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

`generate_paint_tiles()` maps edge indices to faces as `i==0 -> top_edge`, `i==1 -> right_edge`, `i==2 -> bottom_edge`, `i==3 -> left_edge` (lines 195-210). But `RectangleF::get_edges()` (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:808-818) returns `{ top, bottom, left, right }`. The correct map is 0->top, 1->bottom, 2->left, 3->right. So only `top` is right; the other three are permuted:
  JSON `bottom:true` -> matches at i==1 -> generates a RIGHT band
  JSON `left:true`   -> matches at i==2 -> generates a BOTTOM band
  JSON `right:true`  -> matches at i==3 -> generates a LEFT band
Because top/bottom bands use `num_paint_tiles_x` and left/right bands use `num_paint_tiles_y`, the permutation also changes the tile count, so the paintable surface area of the map is wrong, not just mirrored. Worked out against the shipped JSON:
  king_of_the_hill.json `castle_ceiling` (1650x25, `bottom:true`): intended 412 tiles across the 1650-wide underside (area 19,800); actually generates 6 tiles as a 12-wide strip on the right end (area 300) - a 66x loss, and the castle ceiling is effectively unpaintable.
  king_of_the_hill.json `castle_wall_right` (25x750, `left:true`): intended 187 tiles down the inner face (area 9,000); actually 6 tiles along the bottom (area 300).
  king_of_the_hill.json `castle_floor_right` (700x25, `left`+`top`): intended 181 tiles; actually 350 - the designer-disabled underside gets a full 700-wide band while the intended left face gets nothing.
  close_quarters.json `lower_paint` (3000x50, `top`+`bottom`): intended 1,500 tiles (area 72,000); actually 762 (area 36,600). The main arena platform's underside cannot be painted at all; instead a 12x50 sliver appears on its right end.
Level totals, actual vs intended: king_of_the_hill 3,348 vs 4,116; close_quarters 1,160 vs 1,898; turbulence 5,574 vs 5,230. Note `castle_wall_left` and `castle_floor_left` in king_of_the_hill happen to keep the same tile count but paint the opposite physical face.

**Fix:** Stop matching by index entirely - it couples StructurePaintable to the ordering of an unrelated function. Either have `LevelObjectBuilder` pass a `PaintableFaces { bool left, top, right, bottom; }` struct straight through (the struct is already written and commented out at StructurePaintable.h:17-23 and LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:101-105), or compare the matched segment against `rect.get_top_edge()/get_bottom_edge()/get_left_edge()/get_right_edge()` by value instead of by position in `get_edges()`. If index matching is kept, add a static assertion / unit test pinning `get_edges()` order.

#### 3. Paint tiles are never viewport-culled — thousands of sprites submitted per viewport per frame

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:45-52` — **high** · `performance`

```cpp
void StructurePaintable::draw(SpriteBatch* sprite_batch, const Camera& camera)
{
    Structure::draw(sprite_batch, camera);
    for (auto& paint_tile : this->_paint_tiles)
        paint_tile.draw(sprite_batch, camera);   // no visibility test
}
```
`Level::draw_player_view_level` culls at the *structure* level (`object->is_visible_in_viewport(camera_view)`, Level.cpp:527), which for a StructurePaintable tests only the parent sprite rectangle (Structure.cpp:39-42). Once one pixel of the parent is on screen, all tiles are submitted. `PaintTile::is_visible_in_viewport` exists (PaintTile.cpp:149-152) and is never called by anything.

The scale is real: I parsed the shipped levels. `boundary_floor` in both king_of_the_hill.json and turbulence.json is a single 6000x1000 StructurePaintable with `top: true`, which at WIDTH=4.0f generates **1,500 tiles** on one object that spans the whole map and is therefore always "visible". Every painted tile issues two sprites (splash + tile), and each sprite does a string-keyed `std::map` lookup in `SpriteSheet::draw` (SpriteSheet.cpp:105/126) plus another for the sheet itself. Multiply by up to 4 viewports per frame.

**Fix:** Cull per tile — pass `camera_view` down and `if (!paint_tile.is_visible_in_viewport(camera_view)) continue;`. Better, exploit the regular grid: compute the visible index range with two divisions and draw only that slice. Resolve the sheet pointer and source RECT once per structure rather than once per tile per frame.

#### 4. Paint tiles are never viewport-culled: whole structures' tile lists are drawn per viewport, PaintTile::is_visible_in_viewport is dead code

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:45-62` — **high** · `performance` · confidence: certain

`StructurePaintable::draw` unconditionally iterates `_paint_tiles` (lines 48-51 and 57-60). `Level::draw_player_view_level` only culls at the structure level (ArtAttack/Level.cpp:525-531 `object->is_visible_in_viewport(camera_view)`), and `PaintTile::is_visible_in_viewport` (ArtAttack/PaintTile.cpp:149-152) is never called by anything - the only call sites in the codebase are Level.cpp:518/527/536 over `_non_collision_objects`/`_collision_objects`/`_player_objects`, and PaintTiles are in none of those lists.
Numbers for a 4-player split screen (ViewportManager.cpp:208-216 gives 960x540 quadrants; Camera scale is 1.0, MattMath.h:1010, and CameraTools never changes it, so a viewport shows 960x540 world units):
  - turbulence.json generates 5,574 tiles. Fully painted, that is 5,574 x 4 viewports = 22,296 PaintTile::draw calls per frame, each painted tile emitting 2 SpriteBatch::Draw (splash + tile) = 44,592 sprite submissions per frame = 2.68M/sec at 60Hz.
  - `boundary_floor` in turbulence is 6000 wide with 1,500 tiles; a 960-wide viewport can see at most 16% of it, so >=1,260 of its 1,500 tiles are processed off-screen per viewport, 5,040 off-screen tiles per frame across 4 viewports.
  - Each painted tile's draw performs 5 string-keyed `std::map` lookups (SpriteSheetObject.cpp:31-35 -> ResourceManager.cpp:46-58 for the sheet, x3 via the splash path in AnimationObject.cpp:33/141, plus `_sprite_frames[frame_name]` in SpriteSheet.cpp:126): 5,574 x 4 x 5 = 111,480 map lookups per frame.

**Fix:** Cull per tile against `camera_view` inside `StructurePaintable::draw` using the already-written `PaintTile::is_visible_in_viewport` (that needs the camera view passed down, so change the IGameObject draw signature to carry it, or precompute the visible index range from the band geometry - the tiles are a regular grid, so the visible span is two integer divisions, not a scan). Longer term this should not be thousands of sprite objects at all: a paintable face is a 1-D array of team ids and should be rendered as a handful of merged quads or a dynamic texture.

#### 5. Paintable-face flags are permuted: edge index map disagrees with RectangleF::get_edges() ordering

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:188-213` — **high** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

`RectangleF::get_edges()` (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:808-818) returns edges in the order **top, bottom, left, right**:

    std::vector<Segment> edges = { get_top_edge(), get_bottom_edge(), get_left_edge(), get_right_edge() };

`StructurePaintable::generate_paint_tiles()` matches the JSON-derived `_paintable_edges` against that vector and then decodes the index as **top, right, bottom, left**:

    if (i == 0) top_edge = true;
    else if (i == 1) right_edge = true;    // edges[1] is the BOTTOM edge
    else if (i == 2) bottom_edge = true;   // edges[2] is the LEFT edge
    else if (i == 3) left_edge = true;     // edges[3] is the RIGHT edge

So three of the four faces authored in the level JSON are wired to the wrong face. Only `top` is correct. `LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:108-126` reads `paintable_faces.left/top/right/bottom` faithfully, so the data is fine; the decode is not.

I simulated this against the shipped levels. Concrete misbehaviour in ArtAttack/levels/king_of_the_hill.json:
- `castle_ceiling` (json:525-545, rect 1650×25, faces `bottom:true` at json:537-543) → produces 6 tiles down its RIGHT edge instead of 412 tiles along its bottom. The castle ceiling is effectively unpaintable.
- `castle_wall_right` (json:503-523, rect 25×750, `left:true`) → 6 tiles along its BOTTOM instead of 187 down its left face.
- `castle_wall_left` (json:459-479, `right:true`) → tiles on its LEFT face (buried inside the facade) instead of the right face that lines the castle interior.
- `castle_floor_left` (json:437-457, `top,right`) → top + LEFT instead of top + right.
- `castle_floor_right` (json:481-501, `left,top`) → top + BOTTOM (350 tiles) instead of top + left (181).
- `castle_room_floor_left`/`_right` (json:658-700, `top,bottom`) → top + RIGHT instead of top + bottom.
Same in ArtAttack/levels/close_quarters.json `lower_paint` (json:246, `top,bottom` → top+right) and ArtAttack/levels/turbulence.json `central_divider_ledge_paint` (json:297, `left,top,right` → bottom,left,top).

Because King-of-the-Hill scoring sums paint-tile areas (`StructurePaintable::get_paint_total`, lines 300-319), this silently changes the win condition: e.g. castle_floor_right contributes 350 tiles of score surface where the designer asked for 181, and castle_ceiling contributes 6 where 412 was intended. Objects that declare all four faces true are unaffected, which is why the bug survived.

**Fix:** Delete the index-decoding entirely — the builder already knows which faces are wanted. Pass a `PaintableFaces{left,top,right,bottom}` struct (the commented-out struct at StructurePaintable.h:17-23 and LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:101-105 is exactly this) instead of round-tripping booleans through geometric `Segment` equality. If the segment matching must stay, drive it off named accessors (`edge == rect.get_top_edge()`) rather than a positional index into `get_edges()`.

#### 6. StructurePaintable is a second, hand-rolled mini-level: hidden object list, own broadphase, own draw loop, own audio

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:33-102` — **medium** · `design`

`StructurePaintable` generates a grid of `PaintTile` objects in its **constructor** (`_paint_tiles = generate_paint_tiles()`, :33) and then re-implements the level's own responsibilities for them: update loop (:37-43), draw loop duplicated across both overloads (:45-62), a linear-scan broadphase in `on_collision` (:89-101), audio via its own `SoundBank*` looked up from the hardcoded literal `"sound_bank_1"` playing `"WaterSplashing"` (StructurePaintable.h:12-14, .cpp:34, :97), and scoring (:300-319).

The tiles are full `ICollisionGameObject`s (PaintTile.h:51) that the level never sees, so they get none of the level's culling, partitioning or parallel draw — which is exactly why the never-culled-tiles and linear-scan-per-hit performance findings exist. `PaintTile` implements `is_colliding`/`get_for_deletion`/`get_collision_object_type` purely so its parent can call them by hand; the interface is being used as a "give me collision helpers" mixin.

Doing 195 lines of grid generation in a constructor also means construction can throw or divide by zero (see that finding) with no recovery point.

**Fix:** Make the paint surface a component, not an object graph: a `PaintSurface` holding a flat `std::vector<uint8_t> team_per_cell` plus origin and cell size, with O(1) world-position→cell indexing. Rendering becomes one batched pass; scoring becomes a counter updated on write. Audio belongs to an event the level's audio system reacts to, not a `SoundBank*` looked up by a string literal inside a wall.

#### 7. Every paint tile's animation is ticked every frame, and all N splashes start unpaused so the whole level animates for the first 0.25s

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:37-43` — **medium** · `performance` · confidence: certain

`StructurePaintable::update` iterates all `_paint_tiles` and calls `PaintTile::update` -> `_splash.update()` (ArtAttack/PaintTile.cpp:30-33) once per fixed update for every tile in the level, painted or not. `AnimationObject::_paused` defaults to **false** (ArtAttack/AnimationObject.h:51) and nothing pauses a freshly built `PaintTileSplash`, so at level start every tile's splash is playing from frame 0. `AnimationObject::update` (AnimationObject.cpp:81-107) calls `get_animation_strip()`, which is two string-keyed `std::map` lookups (SpriteSheetObject.cpp:31-35 -> ResourceManager.cpp:46-58, then SpriteSheet.cpp:15-18).
turbulence: 5,574 tiles x 2 map lookups = 11,148 lookups per update tick for the first 15 ticks (5 frames x 0.05s), on the single game thread, right at level start where the frame budget is already spent on load. After that the splashes pause and `update` early-returns, but the 5,574-element loop still runs every tick forever.

**Fix:** Construct `PaintTileSplash` paused (call `stop()` in the PaintTile ctor, or default `_paused = true`), and keep an active-splash list on the structure so `update` touches only the handful of tiles actually animating instead of all 5,574. Resolving the sprite sheet once at construction into a cached pointer would remove the per-frame map lookups entirely.

#### 8. Every projectile hit linear-scans all of a structure's paint tiles, and the splash sound fires once per projectile

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:86-101` — **medium** · `performance`

```cpp
bool tile_painted = false;
for (auto& paint_tile : this->_paint_tiles)
{
    if (paint_tile.is_colliding(other))
    {
        paint_tile.on_collision(other);
        if (!tile_painted) this->_sound_bank->play_wave(SOUND_NAME, SOUND_VOLUME);
        tile_painted = true;
    }
}
```
The tiles sit on a strictly regular grid (generated at StructurePaintable.cpp:221-296 as `get_left() + paint_tile_width * i`), so the small set a projectile can overlap is computable in O(1) from its AABB — yet this scans all of them. For `boundary_floor` (1,500 tiles, confirmed from the shipped JSON) that is 1,500 `PaintTile::is_colliding` calls per projectile hit, each doing a virtual `get_shape()`, two by-value `get_bounding_box()` calls, and possibly a `Shape::intersects` dynamic_cast chain.

The `tile_painted` flag only dedupes *within one* `on_collision` call, and `on_collision` fires once per colliding projectile, so N projectiles hitting the floor in one frame issue N one-shot voices.

**Fix:** Store tiles as an explicit grid (origin, tile size, counts, `std::vector<player_team>`) and convert the projectile AABB to an index range — a handful of integer ops with no virtual calls. Add a per-structure per-frame flag or short cooldown before `play_wave`.

#### 9. Every projectile hit linear-scans the structure's entire tile list; ~6,000 tile tests per frame on the shipped levels

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:89-101` — **medium** · `performance` · confidence: certain

`on_collision` walks all of `_paint_tiles` calling `paint_tile.is_colliding(other)` for every tile (lines 89-91). Each of those is a virtual `get_shape()` plus `Shape::AABB_intersects` plus possibly a narrow-phase `intersects` (ArtAttack/PaintTile.cpp:84-109). The tiles are a regular grid whose index could be computed in O(1) from the projectile's AABB.
Sizing it with the shipped data: turbulence's `boundary_floor` holds 1,500 tiles, `left_lower_paint` and `right_lower_paint` 774 each. The sprayer has `shoot_interval = 0.0f` (ArtAttack/weapon_consts.h:41) and `Weapon::check_if_shooting_and_ammo_update` gates on `shoot_timer > shoot_interval` (Weapon.cpp:202), so it emits one projectile per 60Hz fixed update per player - roughly one landing per player per frame in sustained fire. With 4 players spraying the floor that is ~4 x 1,500 = 6,000 tile intersection tests per frame; a burst of 8 projectiles contacting paintables in one frame is ~12,000. Each hit also re-enters from `Level::update_level_logic`'s O(n^2) pair loop (ArtAttack/Level.cpp:277-292).

**Fix:** Store the tiles per face in index order with the band origin and pitch, and on a hit convert the projectile AABB to a `[first, last]` index range - a couple of divisions instead of a scan. The tile grid is uniform by construction (`num * tile_size == extent`), so this is exact.

#### 10. Shipped levels generate 3,348-5,574 PaintTile objects, each updated every frame and scanned linearly per projectile hit

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:104-116` — **medium** · `performance` · confidence: certain

`generate_paint_tiles()` tiles a face at `paint_tile_consts::WIDTH = HEIGHT = 4.0f` (ArtAttack/PaintTile.h:12-13). Applying that to the shipped level data gives:
- king_of_the_hill.json: 3,348 PaintTiles across 13 StructurePaintables, of which `boundary_floor` (json:229-250, 6000×1000, top face) alone is 1,500.
- turbulence.json: 5,574 PaintTiles across 9 objects.
- close_quarters.json: 1,160 across 2.

Each `PaintTile` is a `TextureObject` + `ICollisionGameObject` that also owns a `PaintTileSplash` (an `AnimationObject`, PaintTile.h:83), so level load constructs ~5,600 polymorphic objects and does ~11,000 sprite-sheet/resource-manager lookups. `StructurePaintable::update()` (lines 37-43) then calls `paint_tile.update()` on every tile unconditionally every frame — ~5,600 virtual calls per frame doing nothing for tiles that were never painted.

Worse, `StructurePaintable::on_collision` (lines 64-102) does a linear `is_colliding` scan over all of that object's tiles for *each* colliding projectile. A single spray projectile landing on `boundary_floor` costs 1,500 AABB tests, and `Level::update_level_logic` (Level.cpp:180-322) already tests each pair twice per frame in its player×object and object×object loops. With a sprayer firing at ~1 projectile/frame this is the dominant cost in the whole simulation.

There is also no per-tile visibility culling: `StructurePaintable::draw` (lines 45-52) draws every tile once the parent structure passes `is_visible_in_viewport` in Level.cpp:527. Unpainted tiles bail out early in `PaintTile::draw` (PaintTile.cpp:35-47, `default: return;`), so this is mostly wasted call overhead rather than wasted draws — but it scales with tile count, not screen area.

**Fix:** Store paint coverage as a flat bitmap/grid per structure (one `std::vector<uint8_t>` of team ids) rather than a vector of full game objects, index it arithmetically from the impact point instead of scanning, and drop `update()` on tiles entirely — the splash animation only needs to tick for the handful of recently-painted tiles.

#### 11. Tile-count division has no zero guard and fabs is applied to the quotient instead of the divisor

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:104-116` — **medium** · `robustness` · confidence: certain

```
const int num_paint_tiles_x = static_cast<int>(std::fabs(get_rectangle().get_width() / WIDTH));
const float paint_tile_width = get_rectangle().get_width() / num_paint_tiles_x;
```
Two defects:
1. `num_paint_tiles_x` is zero for any structure narrower than `WIDTH` (4.0), and the very next line divides by it. Float division by an int-converted zero yields +/-inf under the default masked FP environment (and /fp:fast is on in all four ArtAttack configs), so it does not crash - the face silently produces no tiles and `paint_tile_width` is inf. Same for `num_paint_tiles_y` / `HEIGHT`.
2. The `fabs` is on the quotient, not on the divisor. A negative extent therefore gives a POSITIVE tile count and a NEGATIVE tile size: `width = -100` -> `num = 25`, `paint_tile_width = -4`. Those tiles get negative `RectangleF::get_area()` (MattMath.cpp:819-822), so they subtract from the team's score in `get_paint_total`, and `get_rectangle_i()/get_win_rect()` produce inverted RECTs for SpriteBatch.
Proof that nothing shipped triggers either today: the smallest paintable dimension across all three levels is 25 (king_of_the_hill `castle_wall_left`/`castle_wall_right` 25 wide, `castle_floor_left`/`castle_floor_right`/`castle_ceiling` 25 tall; turbulence `central_divider_ledge_paint` 25 tall), giving `num >= 6`, and every paintable uses the `"rectangle"` form with positive width/height - `grep -c rectangle_tlbr levels/*.json` returns 0 for all three. But the negative path is reachable from data: `LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:88-95` accepts `rectangle_tlbr` and `RectangleF::from_top_left_bottom_right` (MattMath.cpp:1122-1128) does not normalise, so a JSON file with `right < left` produces a negative-width paintable with no diagnostic.

**Fix:** Validate the rectangle where it is built (LevelObjectBuilder) - reject non-positive width/height with a message naming the object - and in `generate_paint_tiles` compute `num = std::max(1, static_cast<int>(width / WIDTH))` on an already-positive width. Better still, normalise in `RectangleF::from_top_left_bottom_right` itself.

#### 12. Tile size divides by a truncated tile count that can legitimately be zero, and fabs is applied to the count but not the divisor

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:108-116` — **medium** · `robustness`

```cpp
const int num_paint_tiles_x = static_cast<int>(std::fabs(this->get_rectangle().get_width() / WIDTH));
const float paint_tile_width = this->get_rectangle().get_width() / num_paint_tiles_x;
const int num_paint_tiles_y = static_cast<int>(std::fabs(this->get_rectangle().get_height() / HEIGHT));
const float paint_tile_height = this->get_rectangle().get_height() / num_paint_tiles_y;
```
`WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` are 4.0f (PaintTile.h:12-13). Any paintable structure narrower or shorter than 4 units truncates the count to 0 and the next line divides by it. `FloatingPointModel` is `Fast` in all four configurations (ArtAttack.vcxproj:94, 116, 139, 165) and no FP exceptions are enabled, so this silently yields ±inf or NaN rather than trapping. The guarded loops then don't run, so the observable failure is that the structure silently gets no paint surface at all with no diagnostic.

Secondly, `std::fabs` is applied to the *count* but not the *tile size*, so a rectangle with negative width (which `RectangleF::from_top_left_bottom_right`, used at LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:51/94, will happily produce from mis-ordered `rectangle_tlbr` values) yields a positive count and a negative tile width — tiles with negative `get_area()` that subtract from a team's score.

Nothing between the JSON and this code validates width/height (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:80-99 accepts any float). Latent today — every shipped structure is ≥ 25 units — but it is an unguarded divide on externally supplied data.

**Fix:** Normalise the rectangle first, then `if (num_x < 1 || num_y < 1) throw` with a message naming the offending object, or clamp to 1 if that is the intended behaviour. Validate width/height > 0 at parse time in LevelObjectBuilder.

#### 13. Paintable faces are matched by exact float equality on Segment endpoints under /fp:fast

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:189-194` — **medium** · `correctness`

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < edges.size(); i++)
    for (int j = 0; j < this->_paintable_edges.size(); j++)
        if (edges[i] == this->_paintable_edges[j])
```
`Segment::operator==` (MattMath.cpp:4045-4049) forwards to `Vector2F::operator==` (MattMath.cpp:1574-1577), which is bare `this->x == other.x && this->y == other.y` on floats.

This works today only because LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:107-125 derives `paintable_edges` from the *same* `RectangleF` value that is also passed as the collision shape (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:135-136), so the bit patterns are identical. The moment the collision shape differs from the sprite rectangle by one ULP — a rotated shape, a shrunk collision box, anything built via subtraction — *zero* edges match and the structure silently generates no paint tiles. There is no diagnostic for the all-unmatched case, and the loops don't break out once a match is found.

The loops are also `int i < edges.size()`, a signed/unsigned comparison (C4018 under /W4).

This is the same root cause as the face-index bug: geometry is being used to smuggle four booleans.

**Fix:** Delete `_paintable_edges` and carry the booleans through from JSON. If edge matching must stay, compare with an epsilon and assert that at least one edge matched when `_paintable_edges` is non-empty.

#### 14. Adjacent paintable faces overlap at every corner, so the same physical area is scored twice

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:217-296` — **medium** · `correctness`

The top/bottom loops emit tiles spanning the structure's full width (`get_left() + paint_tile_width * i`, height THICKNESS=12) and the left/right loops emit tiles spanning the full height (`get_top() + paint_tile_height * i`, width THICKNESS). Nothing excludes the corners, so for any structure with two adjacent faces enabled the 12x12 corner square is covered by tiles from both faces.

`get_paint_total` (StructurePaintable.cpp:300-319) sums `paint_tile.get_area()` over all tiles, so that area is counted twice. Worse, the overlapping tiles are independent: team A can own the top corner tile while team B owns the left corner tile at the same screen position, and both are added to their team's score. Both are also drawn, one over the other.

I verified the arithmetic against turbulence.json `upper_top_paint` (1200x50, all four faces): top and bottom contribute 300 tiles each of 4x12 = 14,400 units each; left and right contribute 12 tiles each of 12x4.167 = 600 each; total 30,000. The four double-counted corners are 4 × 144 = 576, about 1.9% of that structure's scoreable area. Every all-four-face structure in every level has this.

**Fix:** Inset the horizontal runs by THICKNESS on each end when the corresponding vertical face is enabled (adjusting the tile count), or generate the border ring as a single grid and de-duplicate, so each unit of surface belongs to exactly one tile.

#### 15. Adjacent face bands overlap by exactly THICKNESS^2 at each corner, double-counting area and paying ~2x score for corner hits

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:219-296` — **medium** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

The top band spans `x in [left, left+width] , y in [top, top+12]` (lines 223-227); the left band spans `x in [left, left+12] , y in [top, top+height]` (lines 264-268). Their intersection is exactly `THICKNESS x THICKNESS = 144` square units, and the same holds at all four corners. Within a band the tiles tile exactly (`num_tiles * tile_size == width`), so the only overlap is at corners.
Concrete: close_quarters.json `upper_paint` (750x50, all four faces enabled) generates 187 top + 187 bottom + 12 left + 12 right = 398 tiles with total tile area 19,200, but the union of the four bands is 19,200 - 4*144 = 18,624. `StructurePaintable::get_paint_total` (lines 300-318) sums `paint_tile.get_area()` with no de-duplication, so the score over-reports this structure's surface by 576 units (3.09%).
The gameplay-visible half is worse than the aggregate: a single projectile landing in a corner is matched against BOTH the ~3 top tiles and the ~3 left tiles that occupy the same 12x12 square, so it scores roughly twice what the identical shot scores mid-face (a 15x15 spray AABB mid-face claims ~4 tiles x 48 = 192; the same shot in a corner claims ~4 top tiles x 48 plus ~4 left tiles x 50 = ~392).
A second latent case: the top and bottom bands are `2 * THICKNESS = 24` thick combined, and the thinnest shipped paintable is 25 units (`castle_floor_left`, `castle_ceiling`, `central_divider_ledge_paint` are all 25 tall; `castle_wall_left/right` are 25 wide) - a 1-unit margin. Any 23-unit-thick paintable would have its two opposite bands overlap along their entire length.

**Fix:** Generate the tile grid from the shape's perimeter once rather than per-face, mitring the corners (start the left/right bands at `top + THICKNESS` and stop at `bottom - THICKNESS`), and assert at construction that `min(width, height) > 2 * THICKNESS`. That fixes both the double-count and the corner scoring exploit.

#### 16. Tile vector is built with push_back(const&) and no reserve: ~25k PaintTile constructions and 151 reallocations to produce 5,574 tiles

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.cpp:106-298` — **low** · `efficiency` · confidence: certain

`auto paint_tiles = std::vector<PaintTile>();` (line 106) is never reserved, and each band does `auto paint_tile = PaintTile(...); paint_tiles.push_back(paint_tile);` (lines 228-233, 249-254, 269-274, 289-294) - a named local copied in, not moved or emplaced. So each tile costs one construction plus one copy, on top of MSVC's 1.5x growth moves.
Measured against the shipped data (sizeof(PaintTile) ~= 376 bytes on MSVC x64 release: DrawObject 56 + two std::strings 64 = TextureObject 120, + ICollisionGameObject vptr 8 + RectangleF 24 (Shape is polymorphic, MattMath.h:68-89, so the rect carries a vptr) + player_team 4 + TeamColour 32 + const float* 8 + PaintTileSplash 176):
  king_of_the_hill 3,348 tiles = 1.20 MiB, 169 vector reallocations, 7,835 move-constructions, 14,531 PaintTile constructions total
  close_quarters   1,160 tiles = 0.42 MiB,  34 reallocations,  3,089 moves,  5,409 constructions
  turbulence       5,574 tiles = 2.00 MiB, 151 reallocations, 13,505 moves, 24,653 constructions
Each of the 5,574 real constructions also builds a `PaintTileSplash`, whose ctor does two string-keyed map lookups (AnimationObject.cpp:21) = 11,148 map lookups at load. And 128 of every tile's 376 bytes are four `std::string` members holding just two distinct literals ("sprite_sheet_1", "pixel", "sprite_sheet_1", "splash_1") - they fit SSO so there is no extra heap traffic, but that is 713 KiB of duplicated string storage on turbulence.

**Fix:** `paint_tiles.reserve(2 * num_paint_tiles_x + 2 * num_paint_tiles_y)` up front and `emplace_back(...)` in place. That removes every copy and every reallocation. Replacing the four per-tile `std::string`s with a shared, resolved `SpriteSheet*` + `const RECT*` would cut ~34% of the per-tile footprint and every one of the per-frame map lookups at the same time.

## `ArtAttack/ThreadPool.cpp`

_10 findings: 1 critical, 3 high, 5 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. No exception barrier in the thread-pool callback — any task exception terminates the process and leaks the task

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.cpp:60-65` — **critical** · `robustness` · confidence: certain

```cpp
void CALLBACK ThreadPool::work_callback(PTP_CALLBACK_INSTANCE instance, PVOID parameter, PTP_WORK work)
{
    std::function<void()>* task = static_cast<std::function<void()>*>(parameter);
    (*task)();
    delete task;
}
```

There is no try/catch. An exception escaping a Win32 thread-pool callback is unhandled: the process is terminated, `delete task` never runs, and the caller in `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` has no way to observe the failure (there are no futures, no error channel, `add_task` returns void).

The tasks *do* throw, on ordinary paths:
- `Level::draw_player_view_level` — `throw std::exception("Deferred context not created")` (Level.cpp:500) and `throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list")` (Level.cpp:590).
- `Level::draw_zoom_out_level_component` — Level.cpp:616, 649.
- `MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports` — MenuPage.cpp:96, 120.
- Every `->at(i)` in those functions (Level.cpp:498, 503-506, 587; MenuPage.cpp:176) throws `std::out_of_range`.
- `SpriteSheet::get_animation_strip` uses `_animation_strips.at(name)` (SpriteSheet.cpp:17) — a missing animation name in a JSON asset crashes the process from a worker with no diagnostic.

Also note `instance` and `work` are unnamed-unused parameters under /W4 (C4100).

**Fix:** Wrap the invocation: `try { (*task)(); } catch (...) { /* capture into a per-task std::exception_ptr */ }` and store the `std::unique_ptr<std::function<void()>>` so the delete is exception-safe. Change `add_task` to return a handle (or `std::future<void>`) and have `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` rethrow the first captured exception on the calling thread.

#### 2. add_task is not exception-safe and there is no RAII drain, so a mid-loop throw abandons tasks pointing at the caller's stack

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.cpp:38-58` — **high** · `robustness` · confidence: certain

```cpp
void ThreadPool::add_task(std::function<void()> task)
{
    PTP_WORK work = CreateThreadpoolWork(work_callback,
        new std::function<void()>(task), &_callback_environment);   // :40-41
    if (!work)
    {
        throw std::runtime_error("Failed to create thread pool work object.");  // :44  leaks the new'd std::function
    }
    _work_items.push_back(work);   // :46  can throw bad_alloc -> `work` leaked, never closed
    SubmitThreadpoolWork(work);    // :47
}
```

(The submit/push_back ordering itself is fine — push happens first, so `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` cannot miss a submitted handle. The problem is what happens when the loop around it unwinds.)

All three call sites submit in a loop and only wait *after* the loop, with nothing between them but ordinary code:

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < partitioned_players.size(); i++)
    this->_thread_pool->add_task([...]{...});   // Level.cpp:388
this->_thread_pool->wait_for_tasks_to_complete();  // Level.cpp:399  — NOT in a destructor
```

If `add_task` throws on iteration 2 of 4, the two tasks already submitted keep running while the stack unwinds straight past line 399. What they are pointing at is the caller's stack:

- **MenuPage.cpp:142-143** captures two locals **by reference**: `&partitioned_mobjects` (local at :134) and `&command_lists` (local at :128). It also captures `mobjects`, a pointer to the *caller's* local (e.g. `std::vector<...> mobjects;` at MainMenu.cpp:38, ResultsMenu.cpp:204, MainMenu.cpp:1775 — nine such sites).
- **Level.cpp:388-389** captures `command_lists`, a pointer to `GameLevel::draw`'s local `std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*> command_lists(...)` (GameStates.cpp:313).
- **Level.cpp:601** captures the same `command_lists` pointer.

So on the throw path, live background threads write `command_list` out-params and read the partition vector through references to frames that no longer exist. The `PTP_WORK` handles are also leaked (never `CloseThreadpoolWork`d) and `_work_items` is left holding stale entries for the next batch to trip over.

This is entirely unguarded: no `try`/`catch`, and `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` is a plain statement rather than a destructor, at all three sites (Level.cpp:399, Level.cpp:606, MenuPage.cpp:150).

**Fix:** Introduce a scoped batch handle — `class TaskBatch { ~TaskBatch() { pool.wait(); } }` — obtained before the submit loop, so the drain happens on every exit path including unwinding. Inside `add_task`, own the closure with `auto payload = std::make_unique<std::function<void()>>(std::move(task));` and only `payload.release()` after `CreateThreadpoolWork` succeeds *and* `push_back` succeeds; reserve the vector up front so `push_back` cannot throw. Separately, stop capturing stack locals by reference into tasks — the by-value capture used at Level.cpp:388 is the right pattern, and MenuPage should match it.

#### 3. work_callback invokes the task with no exception handling — an escaping throw terminates the process and leaks the task

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.cpp:60-65` — **high** · `robustness`

Merged from 4 candidates.

    void CALLBACK ThreadPool::work_callback(PTP_CALLBACK_INSTANCE instance, PVOID parameter, PTP_WORK work)
    {
        std::function<void()>* task = static_cast<std::function<void()>*>(parameter);
        (*task)();
        delete task;
    }

An exception escaping `(*task)()` unwinds out of a Win32 thread-pool callback — undefined behaviour, in practice `std::terminate` on a worker thread mid-frame with no diagnostic — and `delete task` is skipped, so the payload leaks.

This is reachable, not hypothetical. I verified the submitted tasks throw: `Level::draw_zoom_out_level` submits a task at Level.cpp:601 whose body reaches `throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list")` at Level.cpp:590; `MenuPage::draw_mobjects_in_viewports` submits at MenuPage.cpp:142 and its body throws the same at MenuPage.cpp:120. Add the `std::out_of_range` throws in ResourceManager/SoundBank that also run on that path.

`instance` and `work` are both unused named parameters — C4100 at /W4.

**Fix:** Adopt ownership first, then catch at the boundary:

    std::unique_ptr<std::function<void()>> owner(static_cast<std::function<void()>*>(parameter));
    try { (*owner)(); } catch (...) { /* store exception_ptr on the pool */ }

and rethrow the first captured exception from `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` so the failure lands on the submitting thread with its message intact.

#### 4. No exception barrier in work_callback: every draw body throws, so one bad frame terminates the process and leaks the closure

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.cpp:60-65` — **high** · `robustness` · confidence: certain

```cpp
void CALLBACK ThreadPool::work_callback(PTP_CALLBACK_INSTANCE instance, PVOID parameter, PTP_WORK work)
{
    std::function<void()>* task = static_cast<std::function<void()>*>(parameter);
    (*task)();      // :63  no try/catch
    delete task;    // :64  skipped if (*task)() throws
}
```

The bodies this invokes throw as a matter of routine:
- `Level::draw_player_view_level`: `throw std::exception("Deferred context not created")` (Level.cpp:500) and `throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list")` (Level.cpp:590)
- `Level::draw_zoom_out_level_component`: Level.cpp:616 and :649
- `MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports`: MenuPage.cpp:96 and :120
- plus every `->at(i)` in those functions (Level.cpp:498, 503, 506, 587; MenuPage.cpp:176) can throw `std::out_of_range`
- and `DeviceResources::get_deferred_context` (MenuPage.cpp:175) throws too — see the separate `noexcept` finding.

A C++ exception unwinding out of a Win32 thread-pool callback finds no handler on the worker thread's stack; the result is an unhandled-exception process termination, not a caught error. Consequences, in order: (a) the process dies with no diagnostic tying it back to the draw code, (b) `delete task` never runs so the heap `std::function` leaks (moot at that point, but it is the same missing-cleanup bug that bites if cancellation is ever added), (c) `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` at Level.cpp:399 / :606 / MenuPage.cpp:150 is never reached, so the `PTP_WORK` handles are never closed either.

There is no `try`/`catch` anywhere on the path either — `Game::tick` (Game.cpp:75-84) and the message loop (Main.cpp:213-224) have none, so even a main-thread throw is an unhandled crash.

**Fix:** Wrap the invocation: `try { (*task)(); } catch (...) { /* record to an atomic failure flag or a per-batch exception_ptr */ }` and put the `delete` in a `std::unique_ptr<std::function<void()>> owner{static_cast<...>(parameter)};` so it is released on every path. Then have `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` rethrow the captured `exception_ptr` on the calling thread (the standard `std::async`/`packaged_task` contract) so failures surface where they can be handled. Separately, stop using exceptions as the reporting channel for per-frame conditions like "context is not deferred" — that is an assertion about program structure, not a runtime error.

#### 5. Thread counts unvalidated and cast to DWORD; SetThreadpoolThreadMinimum's BOOL discarded; _work_items unsynchronised

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.cpp:4-28` — **medium** · `robustness`

Merged from 3 candidates.

    SetThreadpoolThreadMaximum(_pool, static_cast<DWORD>(max_num_threads));
    SetThreadpoolThreadMinimum(_pool, static_cast<DWORD>(min_num_threads));

1. No validation that `min > 0`, `max > 0`, or `min <= max`. The members are `int` defaulted to `-1` in the header (ThreadPool.h:25-26); a negative value casts to a ~4-billion DWORD. Win32 requires min <= max. The two adjacent same-typed int parameters are also trivially transposable at the call site.
2. `SetThreadpoolThreadMinimum` returns BOOL and is the one call here that can genuinely fail (it must create persistent threads immediately). The result is discarded, so the pool can silently come up under-provisioned while `get_max_num_threads()` — used at Level.cpp:379 and MenuPage.cpp:131 to size partitions and index `sprite_batches`/`deferred_contexts` — keeps reporting the requested value.
3. `_work_items` (ThreadPool.h:27) is a bare `std::vector` mutated by `add_task` and cleared by `wait_for_tasks_to_complete` with no mutex and no documented threading contract. Safe today only because both are called from the main thread.

Currently saved only by the call site passing NUM_THREADS_MIN=1, NUM_THREADS_MAX=16 (Game.h:13-14, verified).

**Fix:** Take the counts as `unsigned` (or a `ThreadPoolConfig { unsigned min, max; }` so they cannot be transposed), assert `0 < min <= max` and throw otherwise, and check the BOOL: `if (!SetThreadpoolThreadMinimum(...)) { CloseThreadpool(_pool); throw ...; }`. Document in the header that add/wait are main-thread-only.

#### 6. ~ThreadPool silently blocks the main thread on all outstanding callbacks, and the cancel path (if ever used) leaks every closure

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.cpp:30-36` — **medium** · `robustness` · confidence: certain

```cpp
ThreadPool::~ThreadPool()
{
    CloseThreadpoolCleanupGroupMembers(_cleanup_group, FALSE, nullptr);   // :32
    CloseThreadpoolCleanupGroup(_cleanup_group);
    CloseThreadpool(_pool);
    DestroyThreadpoolEnvironment(&_callback_environment);
}
```

`fCancelPendingCallbacks = FALSE` means *do not cancel* — the call blocks until every submitted callback, including ones that have not started, has run to completion. Two consequences:

1. The destructor is a hidden unbounded block on whatever thread destroys the pool. Since the pool is destroyed from `create_device_dependent_resources` (Game.cpp:236, reached via `OnDeviceRestored`) and from `~Game` (Main.cpp:226), that is always the main/UI thread. There is no comment saying so, and no `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` call before either destruction — the blocking behaviour of this one line is the *only* thing standing between the codebase and a use-after-free on a worker.

2. `FALSE` is load-bearing for a reason the code does not state: the closure is a raw `new std::function<void()>` (ThreadPool.cpp:41) whose only `delete` is inside the callback body (ThreadPool.cpp:64). Change that flag to `TRUE` — the natural thing for anyone trying to make shutdown responsive — and every cancelled work item leaks its closure with no way to recover it, because `SetThreadpoolCallbackCleanupGroup(&_callback_environment, _cleanup_group, nullptr)` (ThreadPool.cpp:27) passes `nullptr` for the cleanup-group cancel callback, which is the exact hook that exists to free per-work-item state on cancellation.

Also note `_work_items` is not cleared or closed here; if a draw ever unwound without waiting, the vector's stale handles are released by the cleanup group as a side effect, which happens to be correct but is not obvious and is not what the code appears to intend.

**Fix:** Call `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` explicitly as the first statement of `~ThreadPool` so the drain is visible in the source rather than buried in a Win32 flag, and add a comment stating that the destructor blocks. Then remove the raw `new`/`delete` entirely: pass a `std::unique_ptr<std::function<void()>>::release()`d pointer and reclaim it with a `unique_ptr` at the top of `work_callback`, and register a cleanup-group cancel callback (the third argument at ThreadPool.cpp:27) that deletes the closure, so cancellation becomes a supported option instead of a leak.

#### 7. add_task leaks the heap-allocated std::function when CreateThreadpoolWork fails, and copies the task twice

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.cpp:38-48` — **medium** · `memory-safety`

Merged from 4 candidates.

    PTP_WORK work = CreateThreadpoolWork(work_callback,
        new std::function<void()>(task), &_callback_environment);
    if (!work) { throw std::runtime_error("Failed to create thread pool work object."); }
    _work_items.push_back(work);
    SubmitThreadpoolWork(work);

The `new`'d function is unowned between the allocation and the eventual callback. On the `!work` path the throw orphans it permanently — nothing will run `work_callback` to delete it. If `_work_items.push_back` throws `bad_alloc`, the work object is never submitted and never closed either.

Separately the task is copied twice: `std::function<void()> task` is a by-value parameter (copy 1), then copy-constructed into the heap object because `task` is named rather than moved (copy 2). The Level.cpp:388 lambda captures a whole `std::vector<std::pair<int,int>>` by value, so this is not free.

I graded medium rather than high: the leak needs an allocation failure, whereas the callback finding above fires on ordinary draw errors.

**Fix:** auto payload = std::make_unique<std::function<void()>>(std::move(task));
    PTP_WORK work = CreateThreadpoolWork(work_callback, payload.get(), &_callback_environment);
    if (!work) throw std::runtime_error("...");
    _work_items.push_back(work);   // may throw; still owned
    SubmitThreadpoolWork(work);
    payload.release();             // ownership transfers only now

#### 8. add_task is not thread-safe, leaks the task closure on failure, and copies the std::function twice

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.cpp:38-58` — **medium** · `concurrency` · confidence: certain

```cpp
void ThreadPool::add_task(std::function<void()> task)
{
    PTP_WORK work = CreateThreadpoolWork(work_callback, new std::function<void()>(task), &_callback_environment);
    if (!work) { throw std::runtime_error("Failed to create thread pool work object."); }
    _work_items.push_back(work);
```
