#### 5. The engine colour palette ships this game's team colours, and every drawable includes it

`ArtAttack/Colour.h:309-313 (reached from DrawObject.h:4)` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

`Colour.h` is a 469-line engine-level palette (149 HTML colour name strings plus 153 `MattMath::Colour` constants). Lines 309-313 append this game's content:
```
const MattMath::Colour TEAM_BLUE   = { 6, 52, 204, 255 };
const MattMath::Colour TEAM_YELLOW = { 255, 255, 0, 255 };
const MattMath::Colour TEAM_ORANGE = { 255, 127, 0, 255 };
const MattMath::Colour TEAM_PINK   = { 255, 0, 127, 255 };
const MattMath::Colour TEAM_GREEN  = { 0, 255, 0, 255 };
```
These exist only to feed `TeamColour.h:27-42` (`team_colour_consts::BLUE_ORANGE/PINK_GREEN/BLUE_YELLOW`). Because `DrawObject.h:4` includes `Colour.h`, *every* drawable in the engine — and via `MattMathTests` every test TU — transitively compiles the game's team palette. (Secondary cost: these are namespace-scope non-inline `const` objects in a header, so each of ~81 TUs gets its own copy with dynamic initialisation.)

**Fix:** Delete the `TEAM_*` block from `Colour.h` and define those five colours in game/paint/team_colours.h next to `TeamColour`. While there, make the palette `constexpr`/`inline constexpr` so it costs nothing per TU, and stop including the full palette from `DrawObject.h` (forward-declare `Colour` or include a minimal `colour_type.h`).

#### 6. Colour.h is a 469-line header-only blob of internal-linkage objects reaching most of the codebase, of which 130 of 153 colours are unused

`ArtAttack/Colour.h:6-466` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

`Colour.h` declares 153 namespace-scope `const std::string` HTML codes (`:10-467` inside `namespace html`, closing at `:158`), then 153 namespace-scope `const MattMath::Colour` objects built from them (`:160-313`), then a 152-line `static MattMath::Colour colour_from_name(const std::string& name)` (`:315-466`) that is a flat chain of 153 `if (name == "ALICE_BLUE") return colour_consts::ALICE_BLUE;` lines. Namespace-scope `const` in C++ has internal linkage, so **every TU that includes this header gets its own copy of all 306 objects plus its own copy of `colour_from_name`**, and pays a dynamic-initialisation pass at startup for 153 `std::string` constructions plus 153 hex-parsing `Colour` constructions. It reaches most of the codebase because `DrawObject.h:4` includes it, and DrawObject is the base of every drawable. Actual demand: only 23 distinct `colour_consts::X` names appear anywhere outside Colour.h itself, and the three shipped level JSONs between them use exactly 7 colour names (SADDLE_BROWN, TAN, GREY, WHITE, LIGHT_SKY_BLUE, DARK_GREY, DARK_SLATE_GREY). Because `colour_from_name` is `static` in a header, any TU that includes Colour.h without calling it also emits /W4 C4505.

**Fix:** Move the table into Colour.cpp behind a single `const Colour& colour_from_name(std::string_view)` that looks up a `static const std::unordered_map`, and make the handful of genuinely-referenced colours `inline constexpr` (C++17) so there is one object, not one per TU. The full 153-colour HTML table is a library concern, not something to paste into an engine header.

#### 7. Colour.h maintains the same 149 colour names as three parallel hand-written tables (~450 lines)

`ArtAttack/Colour.h:8-352` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

The one list of HTML colour names is written out three times:

1. `colour_consts::html` (Colour.h:8-158): 149 `const std::string NAME = "rrggbb";`
2. `colour_consts` (Colour.h:160-308): 149 `const MattMath::Colour NAME = { html::NAME };`
3. `colour_consts::colour_from_name` (Colour.h:315-352 and preceding): a 149-branch `if (name == "NAME") return colour_consts::NAME;` chain, linear-scanned on every JSON colour lookup in `LevelObjectBuilder`.

Adding or renaming a colour means three coordinated edits, and a typo in table 3 silently falls through to `return colour_consts::WHITE;`. These are also namespace-scope non-inline `const std::string`/`const Colour` objects in a header included nearly everywhere — ~300 dynamically-initialised objects per translation unit.

**Fix:** Write the list once as an X-macro or a `constexpr std::array<std::pair<std::string_view, uint32_t>, N>` and generate the named constants plus the lookup from it. Make the lookup a `std::unordered_map`/binary search over the sorted table instead of a 149-branch chain, and mark the constants `constexpr`/`inline`.

#### 8. ~300 dynamically-initialised namespace-scope objects plus a 150-branch static function, duplicated into every TU

`ArtAttack/Colour.h:160-467` — **medium** · `performance` · confidence: certain

`Colour.h` is included transitively by almost every source file and contains, at namespace scope:

- 149 `const std::string` hex literals (Colour.h:10-158)
- 153 `const MattMath::Colour X = { html::X };` (Colour.h:160-312)

`Colour`'s constructor takes a `std::string` and parses hex at runtime, and `Vector2F`/`Colour` constructors are non-constexpr out-of-line functions (MattMath.h:407-413 shows the same pattern for `Vector2F`). `const` at namespace scope gives internal linkage, so **every one of the ~81 translation units gets its own private copy** of all 302 objects, each with its own dynamic initialiser. That is roughly 12,000 `std::string` constructions and 12,000 hex parses executed before `wWinMain`, plus the corresponding `.bss`/init-array bloat.

Worse, Colour.h:315-467 defines

```cpp
static MattMath::Colour colour_from_name(const std::string& name)
{
    if (name == "ALICE_BLUE") return colour_consts::ALICE_BLUE;
    ... ~150 more string comparisons ...
}
```

A 150-branch string-comparison chain compiled into every TU that includes the header, and O(n) at runtime.

The same header-constant idiom is repeated in `player_consts.h:20-63`, `interface_consts` (InterfaceGameplay.h:15-34), `viewport_consts` (ViewportManager.h:12-15), `MainMenu.h`, `Level.h:35-51` — with inconsistent spellings (`const` vs `const static`) that make no difference here but signal the author wasn't sure.

**Fix:** Give `Colour` a `constexpr` constructor over `uint8_t` channels and declare the constants `inline constexpr` (requires C++17 — the vcxproj sets no `<LanguageStandard>` so it is on the C++14 default; bumping to /std:c++20 is safe, there are zero C++17 idioms in the tree today). Move `colour_from_name` into a .cpp behind a single static lookup table. Delete the 149 hex strings entirely once colours are numeric.

#### 9. colour_from_name silently returns WHITE for unknown names, omits the TEAM_* colours, and is `static` in a header

`ArtAttack/Colour.h:315-466` — **medium** · `robustness`

Verified. A 150-line if-chain of `if (name == "ALICE_BLUE") return colour_consts::ALICE_BLUE;` ending in `return colour_consts::WHITE;` at line 465.

1. Silent fallback on external data. This is the sole colour path for level content — LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:65, 142, 176, 196 all pass `json["colour"].GetString()` straight in, and none of them checks HasMember/IsString first. A typo produces a white object with no exception and no log, while every other JSON field in that file throws (`"Invalid collision type"` at :34, `"Invalid rectangle type"` at :55, `"Invalid paintable edges"` at :128). Colour is the one field that fails silently.
2. Incomplete table, verified: the five TEAM_* colours defined immediately above at Colour.h:309-313 have no entries in the ladder. A level author writing `"colour": "TEAM_BLUE"` — the obvious guess — gets white.
3. `static` at namespace scope in a header means every including TU compiles its own copy of the ~150-branch function and discards it in all but the one TU that calls it.

**Fix:** Return `bool try_colour_from_name(std::string_view, Colour& out)` or std::optional so the caller must handle the miss, add the TEAM_* entries, back it with one function-local `static const std::unordered_map`, and move the definition into a .cpp. Have LevelObjectBuilder throw with the offending file, object and colour string.

#### 10. colour_from_name is a 150-branch string if-chain in a header that silently returns WHITE for unknown names

`ArtAttack/Colour.h:315-466` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

```cpp
static MattMath::Colour colour_from_name(const std::string& name) {
    if (name == "ALICE_BLUE") return colour_consts::ALICE_BLUE;
    ... 148 more ...
    return colour_consts::WHITE;   // :465
}
```

This is the sole validation point for the `"colour"` field on all 91 objects in the three level JSONs (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:65, 142, 176, 196). A typo — `"DARK_GERY"`, or a colour name that exists in the HTML set but not in the if-chain — silently produces white geometry with no error, which is indistinguishable from an intentionally white object.

The implementation is also expensive and duplicated: `static` at namespace scope in a header gives it internal linkage, so all 150 string comparisons are compiled into each of the 81 TUs that include Colour.h, alongside the 153 namespace-scope `const MattMath::Colour` objects and 149 `const std::string`s in the same header, each of which gets a per-TU copy with dynamic initialisation.

The level data uses a small fraction of these; a grep of the level JSONs would confirm well under 20 distinct colour names are actually referenced.

**Fix:** Replace with a single `const std::unordered_map<std::string, Colour>` defined in a .cpp, and return `bool try_colour_from_name(name, out)` or throw naming the unknown value so bad level data fails at load. Move the colour constant tables out of the header (`inline constexpr` or a .cpp with `extern` declarations).

## `ArtAttack/DebugText.h`

_5 findings: 1 high, 3 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. DebugText, an engine-level overlay, includes Player.h and hardcodes knowledge of ~18 game-specific fields

`ArtAttack/DebugText.h:4-33` — **high** · `engine-separation`

`DebugText.h:7` is `#include "Player.h"` and the sole API is `draw_debug_info(SpriteBatch*, const Player* player, int num_projectiles) const`.

DebugText.cpp:21-102 reaches into `Player` for `get_input()`, `get_rectangle()`, `get_center()`, `get_velocity()`, `get_camera()`, `get_viewport()`, `get_input_x_movement()`, `get_input_shoot_direction()`, `input.shoot_angle`, `input.left_analog_stick`, `input.right_analog_stick`, `get_input_primary_shoot()`, `get_input_jump_pressed()`, `get_input_jump_held()`, `get_move_state()`, `get_state()`, `get_player_move_state_string()`, and switches on `player_state::ALIVE/DEAD` at :93-101. It also takes `num_projectiles`, a level-wide statistic, as a parameter.

The dependency points the wrong way: the debug renderer knows the game object instead of the game object describing itself. Adding one debug field means editing the renderer. And because `DebugText.h` is pulled in by `Level.h`, every TU that reaches `Level.h` compiles the whole `Player` hierarchy.

DebugText.cpp:113-131 also hand-rolls drop-shadow text (draw at `pos + offset` in black, then at `pos` in grey) — precisely what `TextDropShadow` already does. `DEBUG_FONT = "courier_new_bold_16"` hardcodes an asset name into an engine header.

**Fix:** `class DebugOverlay { void add_line(std::string); void draw(SpriteBatch*, const TextStyle&) const; void clear(); }` with zero knowledge of `Player` — it renders a `vector<string>`. Give game objects `void append_debug_lines(DebugOverlay&) const` so `Player` formats its own fields and `Level` supplies the projectile count. Font/colour/spacing arrive as a `TextStyle` value. Reuse the shared text-draw path instead of re-implementing the shadow. The header only needs `class Player;` regardless.

#### 2. Wrong-case include of Colour.h, plus heavy headers included where forward declarations suffice

`ArtAttack/DebugText.h:4-8` — **medium** · `header-hygiene`

`InterfaceGameplay.h:7` is `#include "colour.h"` but the file on disk is `Colour.h` (I listed the directory to confirm — only `Colour.h`, `TeamColour.h`, `TeamColour.cpp`). This resolves only because NTFS is case-insensitive; it is a hard build break on any case-sensitive filesystem, which for a project whose stated goal is a reusable engine is a portability failure hiding in one character. Every other TU spells it correctly (`DrawObject.h:4`, `SpriteSheet.h:5`). It is also redundant — line 6 already pulls `ResourceManager.h` → `SpriteSheet.h` → `Colour.h` — as are `MattMath.h` (line 8, already via `Drawer.h:7`) and `ResourceManager.h` (already via `Drawer.h:5`).

`DebugText.h` has the same shape: line 7 includes the full `Player.h` where the only use is `const Player*` in a declaration, so `class Player;` would do; line 5 includes `ResolutionManager.h` for a `const ResolutionManager*` member; line 6's `MattMath.h` is already provided by `Drawer.h:7`. As written, every TU reaching `DebugText.h` via `Level.h:11` compiles the whole `Player` hierarchy and rebuilds when any of it changes.

**Fix:** Fix `"colour.h"` → `"Colour.h"` or delete it as redundant. In `DebugText.h`, replace the `Player.h` and `ResolutionManager.h` includes with forward declarations and move the real includes into the .cpp. Drop the redundant `MattMath.h`/`ResourceManager.h` from both headers, and `player_team.h` once `InterfaceDraw` is dealt with.

#### 3. The engine's debug overlay is compiled against `Player` and a projectile count

`ArtAttack/DebugText.h:7, 29 (impl DebugText.cpp:18-102)` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

An on-screen dev overlay is a canonical engine feature, but `DebugText.h` does `#include "Player.h"` (:7) and its only public method is `void draw_debug_info(SpriteBatch*, const Player* player, int num_projectiles) const;` (:29). The body (DebugText.cpp:21-102) reads `player->get_input()`, `get_input_shoot_direction()`, `get_input_primary_shoot()`, `get_input_jump_pressed()`, `get_move_state()`, `get_player_state()` and switches on `player_state::ALIVE/DEAD`. `Level.h:11` includes it and `Level.h:144` owns one.

So the engine's diagnostic facility cannot display anything about a game that has no `Player`, no jump, and no projectiles — and `Player.h` (with its weapons, teams and animation states) is dragged into the engine include graph by a debug widget. The generic 40% of it (`dt`, `fps`, camera, resolution, viewport) is unusable independently.

**Fix:** Reduce `DebugText` to an engine `DebugOverlay` with `add_line(const std::string&)` / `add_line(const char* label, float value)` and a `draw(SpriteBatch*)` that renders whatever was pushed this frame. Keep dt/fps/camera/resolution as engine-supplied lines. The game pushes its own player/projectile lines from `PaintBattleScene`. Drop the `Player.h` include.

#### 4. Cross-TU static initialisation order dependency on MattMath's dynamically-initialised class statics

`ArtAttack/DebugText.h:14` — **medium** · `correctness` · confidence: likely

```cpp
const static MattMath::Vector2F DEBUG_POSITION = MattMath::Vector2F::ZERO;
```

`Vector2F::ZERO` is a class static declared at MattMath.h:488 and **defined in a different translation unit**, MattMath.cpp:1907: `const Vector2F Vector2F::ZERO = { 0.0f, 0.0f };`. Because `Vector2F` has user-provided, non-`constexpr`, out-of-line constructors (MattMath.h:407-413, defined in MattMath.cpp), it is not an aggregate and that definition is *dynamically* initialised, not constant-initialised.

So `DEBUG_POSITION` — an internal-linkage object created afresh in every TU that includes DebugText.h — has a dynamic initialiser that reads a dynamically-initialised object from another TU, with no ordering guarantee. It currently "works" only because zero-initialisation happens first and the intended value is also zero; the bug is invisible until someone writes `const static Vector2F FOO = Vector2F::ONE;` (MattMath.cpp:1908) or similar with a non-zero value.

The same class-static-with-dynamic-init pattern covers `RectangleF::ZERO` (MattMath.cpp:1134), `Vector2I::ZERO` (:1495), `Vector2F::ONE` (:1908), `RectangleI::ZERO` (:2138), `Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA` (:4180 — itself initialised from `Vector2F::ZERO`, safe only because it is later in the same file).

**Fix:** Make `Vector2F`, `RectangleF`, `Colour` etc. literal types with `constexpr` constructors and declare the well-known values `static constexpr` in-class. Then all of these become constant-initialised and the ordering question disappears. As an interim fix, replace `DEBUG_POSITION = MattMath::Vector2F::ZERO` with `{ 0.0f, 0.0f }`.

#### 5. en-GB `Colour` type with en-US `color` parameters throughout, and two `COLOR` constants among ~200 `COLOUR` ones

`ArtAttack/DebugText.h:15-16` — **low** · `naming` · confidence: certain

The type is `MattMath::Colour`, the namespace is `colour_consts`, members are `_colour`, setters are `set_colour` - but nearly every constructor parameter that takes one is spelled `color`. Representative: `DrawObject.h:13 const MattMath::Colour& color = colour_consts::WHITE` assigned at `DrawObject.cpp:14 _colour(color)`. Same in `AnimatedSprite.h:15,23`, `AnimationObject.h:15`, `TextureObject.h:84`, `TextObject.h:120`, `Visual.h:16,26`, `SpriteSheet.h:22,33,43,54`, `Mh.h:83,121,147-148` (where `MTexture` takes `color` at :83 and declares `set_colour` at :99), `Player.cpp`, `PaintTile.cpp:14,159`. In constants the split is 2 vs ~200: `DebugText.h:15-16` `DEBUG_COLOR` / `DEBUG_SHADOW_COLOR` against `COUNTDOWN_COLOUR`, `TITLE_TEXT_COLOUR`, `HEALTH_COLOUR`, `TIMER_COLOUR`, `DIVIDER_COLOUR` and the whole of `colour_consts`. `MattMath.h:641 get_sm_colour()` returns a `DirectX::SimpleMath::Color`, so one expression carries both spellings.

**Fix:** Pick en-GB (the type already is) and rename every `color` parameter to `colour`, plus `DEBUG_COLOR` -> `DEBUG_COLOUR` and `DEBUG_SHADOW_COLOR` -> `DEBUG_SHADOW_COLOUR`. The DirectX-facing spellings (`SimpleMath::Color`, `Colors::Black`) stay as they are - they are not yours.

## `ArtAttack/DeviceResources.cpp`

_7 findings: 5 high, 2 medium_

#### 1. HandleDeviceLost never touches the deferred-context pool, so restore builds SpriteBatches on contexts of a destroyed device

`ArtAttack/DeviceResources.cpp:418-453, 716-730` — **high** · `correctness`

`HandleDeviceLost` (DeviceResources.cpp:418-453) resets the RTV/DSV, swap chain, `m_d3dContext`, `m_d3dAnnotation`, `m_d3dDevice` and `m_dxgiFactory`, recreates the device, then calls `OnDeviceRestored()`. `_deferred_contexts` is not in that list, and `create_deferred_contexts` is called from exactly one place — `Game::initialize` (Game.cpp:52). So after a device-removed event the vector still holds 16 contexts owned by the destroyed device, and `Game::OnDeviceRestored` → `create_device_dependent_resources` immediately does `std::make_unique<SpriteBatch>(this->_device_resources->get_deferred_context(i))` (Game.cpp:229) on them. `Game::clear()` (Game.cpp:136-149) then calls `OMSetRenderTargets`/`RSSetViewports` on the same stale contexts every frame. The reset list predates the author's deferred-context addition and was never updated.

**Fix:** Clear the pool at the top of `HandleDeviceLost` (before `m_d3dDevice.Reset()`) and recreate it at the end of `CreateDeviceResources()` from a remembered count, so the pool's lifetime is structurally tied to the device rather than to one call in `Game::initialize`.

#### 2. HandleDeviceLost destroys the D3D device but never recreates the deferred contexts; SpriteBatches are then built on dead contexts

`ArtAttack/DeviceResources.cpp:418-453` — **high** · `memory-safety` · confidence: certain

`HandleDeviceLost` resets everything and recreates the device:

```cpp
m_d3dContext.Reset();  // :430
m_d3dDevice.Reset();   // :443
CreateDeviceResources();
CreateWindowSizeDependentResources();
if (m_deviceNotify) m_deviceNotify->OnDeviceRestored();   // :451
```

It never calls `create_deferred_contexts` (DeviceResources.cpp:716-730), which is invoked exactly once, from `Game::initialize` (Game.cpp:52). So `_deferred_contexts` still holds the 16 `ID3D11DeviceContext*` created from the **destroyed** device.

Then `OnDeviceRestored` → `create_device_dependent_resources` immediately builds new SpriteBatches on those dead contexts:
```cpp
this->_sprite_batches[i] = std::move(std::make_unique<SpriteBatch>(
    this->_device_resources->get_deferred_context(i)));   // Game.cpp:229
```
DirectXTK's `SpriteBatch` constructor calls `GetDevice` on that context, so this is a call through a dangling COM pointer. And every draw task dereferences the same dead pointers — `deferred_contexts->at(i)->GetType()` (Level.cpp:498), `FinishCommandList` (Level.cpp:587).

Compounding it, those contexts are raw `ID3D11DeviceContext*` in `std::unique_ptr<std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>>` (DeviceResources.h:128) and are **never `Release()`d** — `~DeviceResources() = default` (DeviceResources.h:32), and `create_deferred_contexts` starts with `this->_deferred_contexts = std::make_unique<std::vector<...>>();` (:718), which drops the old vector without releasing its contents. So the 16 contexts leak at every exit, and 16 more would leak on every re-call.

**Fix:** Store deferred contexts as `std::vector<Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11DeviceContext>>` so they are released deterministically, and call `create_deferred_contexts(NUM_THREADS_MAX)` from inside `CreateDeviceResources()` (or at the top of `Game::OnDeviceRestored`, before `create_device_dependent_resources`) so the context pool is always rebuilt with the device it belongs to. Everything downstream that caches a context pointer must then be rebuilt too — which is the same stale-snapshot problem as the ThreadPool/CommonStates finding.

#### 3. Deferred contexts are raw AddRef'd COM pointers that are never released — 16 leaked contexts, rule-of-5 violation on vendor code

`ArtAttack/DeviceResources.cpp:716-745` — **high** · `resource-lifetime`

`create_deferred_contexts` (DeviceResources.cpp:716-730) puts raw `ID3D11DeviceContext*` (refcount 1 from `CreateDeferredContext`) into `std::unique_ptr<std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>> _deferred_contexts` (DeviceResources.h:128). A grep for `->Release()` across ArtAttack/ finds only GameStates.cpp:329 and MenuPage.cpp:162 (both command lists) plus a commented-out line in Main.cpp:55 — the contexts are never released. `~DeviceResources() = default` (DeviceResources.h:32) destroys a vector of raw pointers and nothing else, so all 16 leak and pin the D3D device for the process lifetime.

Every other COM object in this class is a `ComPtr` (DeviceResources.h:95-105); these are the sole exception. This is an owning resource grafted onto vendor code that still has `= default` destructor and `= default` move operations (:34-35). Two secondary leaks in the same function: `make_unique` at :718 replaces the old vector unconditionally, so a second call leaks the previous batch; and the `throw std::runtime_error` at :726 abandons the contexts already created in the loop.

**Fix:** `std::vector<Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11DeviceContext>> m_deferredContexts;` (drop the pointless unique_ptr<vector<>> indirection), pass `ReleaseAndGetAddressOf()`, `clear()` first, and use `ThrowIfFailed` for consistency with the rest of the file. Then the defaulted destructor is correct again. Better still, move the pool out of the vendored file entirely so DeviceResources.h/.cpp stay upstream-updatable.

#### 4. 16 deferred contexts are raw COM pointers: never Released, never recreated on device loss

`ArtAttack/DeviceResources.cpp:716-745` — **high** · `memory-safety` · confidence: certain

```cpp
void DeviceResources::create_deferred_contexts(int num)
{
    this->_deferred_contexts = std::make_unique<std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>>();
    for (int i = 0; i < num; i++) {
        ID3D11DeviceContext* deferred_context = nullptr;
        HRESULT hr = m_d3dDevice->CreateDeferredContext(0, &deferred_context);
        ...
        this->_deferred_contexts->push_back(deferred_context);
    }
}
```

The member is `std::unique_ptr<std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>>` (DeviceResources.h:128) — raw interface pointers in a heap vector. Three defects:
1. **Leak on re-entry**: assigning a fresh vector drops the previous 16 contexts with no `Release()`. Every other COM object in this file uses `ComPtr`.
2. **Leak at shutdown**: `~DeviceResources` never releases them either.
3. **Use of contexts from a dead device**: `HandleDeviceLost()` (DeviceResources.cpp:418-453) resets `m_d3dContext`, `m_d3dDevice` and calls `CreateDeviceResources()` — but *never* calls `create_deferred_contexts` again. It then calls `OnDeviceRestored()`, and `Game::create_device_dependent_resources` (Game.cpp:226-232) builds 16 brand-new `SpriteBatch`es on `get_deferred_context(i)` — contexts that belong to the destroyed device.

The 16 contexts are also unconditional (`NUM_THREADS_MAX`, Game.h:14) regardless of how many are ever used.

**Fix:** Store them as `std::vector<Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11DeviceContext>>` (drop the pointless `unique_ptr<vector<...>>` indirection), clear the vector at the top of `create_deferred_contexts`, and call `create_deferred_contexts` from `HandleDeviceLost` after `CreateDeviceResources()` — or make it part of `CreateDeviceResources` itself.

#### 5. get_deferred_context is declared noexcept but throws std::out_of_range — the bounds check is a guaranteed std::terminate

`ArtAttack/DeviceResources.cpp:737-745` — **high** · `correctness`

```
ID3D11DeviceContext*
DeviceResources::get_deferred_context(int index) const noexcept
{
    if (index < 0 || index >= this->_deferred_contexts->size())
    {
        throw std::out_of_range("Invalid index.");
    }
    return this->_deferred_contexts->at(index);
}
```
Declaration at DeviceResources.h:88 is also `noexcept`. Throwing from `noexcept` calls `std::terminate` — no unwinding, no message, the one defensive path in the function hard-kills the process. Three more defects in the same three lines: (a) `index >= ...->size()` compares `int` to `size_type` (C4018 at /W4, and `TreatWarningAsError` is not set anywhere in the vcxproj); (b) `_deferred_contexts` is dereferenced to call `size()` before any null check, so it is a null deref if called before `create_deferred_contexts`; (c) `at()` re-does the bounds check that was just done by hand, so the manual check buys nothing but the terminate.

It is reachable: `MenuPage::draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:172-177) indexes the pool by **menu-object index**, not thread index — `get_deferred_context(i)` and `command_lists->at(i)` where `i` runs over the mobject list, while `command_lists` is sized to `deferred_contexts->size()` (MenuPage.cpp:128). Any menu page with more than 16 drawable widgets terminates the process here.

**Fix:** Drop `noexcept`, take `std::size_t index`, null-check the container, and delete the redundant manual check in favour of `at()`. Separately fix MenuPage.cpp:175-176 to index by partition/thread rather than by object.

#### 6. 16 deferred contexts are raw, never Released, and get_deferred_context is noexcept yet throws

`ArtAttack/DeviceResources.cpp:716-745` — **medium** · `memory-safety` · confidence: certain

void DeviceResources::create_deferred_contexts(int num)
    {
        this->_deferred_contexts = std::make_unique<std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>>();
        for (int i = 0; i < num; i++) {
            ID3D11DeviceContext* deferred_context = nullptr;
            HRESULT hr = m_d3dDevice->CreateDeferredContext(0, &deferred_context);
            ...
            this->_deferred_contexts->push_back(deferred_context);
        }
    }

`CreateDeferredContext` returns an AddRef'd interface. It is stored as a raw pointer in a `unique_ptr<vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>>` (DeviceResources.h:128), `~DeviceResources() = default` (DeviceResources.h:32), and there is no `Release()` call anywhere in the file. Sixteen deferred contexts leak on every shutdown, and another sixteen on every device-loss cycle — and because a deferred context holds a reference to its device, the leaked contexts keep the removed ID3D11Device alive too, which is why the mismatch in the OnDeviceRestored finding manifests as garbage rendering rather than an immediate access violation. In `_DEBUG`, `ReportLiveDeviceObjects` at DeviceResources.cpp:436-439 will dump all of them.

Separately, `get_deferred_context` (lines 737-745) is declared `noexcept` in both the header (DeviceResources.h:88) and the definition, yet its body throws `std::out_of_range("Invalid index.")` — that is an unconditional `std::terminate`, not an exception. `MenuPage::draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:172-177) indexes it by *object* index rather than partition index, so any menu page with more than 16 MObjects would terminate the process rather than throw.

**Fix:** Store `Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11DeviceContext>`; drop the `unique_ptr<vector<...>>` indirection; remove `noexcept` from `get_deferred_context` (or make it return nullptr / assert); and fix MenuPage to index by partition, not by object.

#### 7. get_deferred_context is declared noexcept but throws — guaranteed std::terminate on a bad index

`ArtAttack/DeviceResources.cpp:737-745` — **medium** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

Declared `ID3D11DeviceContext* get_deferred_context(int index) const noexcept;` (DeviceResources.h:88), defined as:

```cpp
ID3D11DeviceContext* DeviceResources::get_deferred_context(int index) const noexcept
{
    if (index < 0 || index >= this->_deferred_contexts->size())
        throw std::out_of_range("Invalid index.");
    return this->_deferred_contexts->at(index);
}
```

Throwing from a `noexcept` function calls `std::terminate` — the bounds check converts a recoverable programming error into an unconditional process kill with no unwinding. It is called from a worker thread in `MenuPage::draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:175), where even a normal exception would already be fatal (see the thread-pool exception-barrier finding).

Secondary: `index >= this->_deferred_contexts->size()` compares `int` to `size_t` (/W4 C4018), and `_deferred_contexts` is dereferenced without a null check although it is `nullptr` until `create_deferred_contexts` runs.

**Fix:** Drop the `noexcept` (and let it throw), or keep `noexcept` and return `nullptr` on a bad index. Cast the size: `index >= static_cast<int>(...->size())`. Add a null check on `_deferred_contexts`.

## `ArtAttack/DeviceResources.h`

_2 findings: 2 high_

#### 1. Raw D3D11 contexts and command lists are the public draw API, and the record/execute/Release protocol is copy-pasted

`ArtAttack/DeviceResources.h:86-88` — **high** · `design`

Because `DeviceResources` exposes `std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>* get_deferred_contexts()` (line 87), every drawing entry point in the game speaks raw D3D11: `Level::draw` and friends take `std::vector<ID3D11DeviceContext*>*, std::vector<ID3D11CommandList*>*, std::vector<SpriteBatch*>*` (Level.h:83-85). The same protocol — fetch contexts, allocate `vector<ID3D11CommandList*>(n, nullptr)`, hand the raw pointers down, then loop `ExecuteCommandList` + `->Release()` skipping nulls — is written twice verbatim at GameStates.cpp:311-330 and MenuPage.cpp:127-163, with the leaf `FinishCommandList` calls scattered at Level.cpp:587, Level.cpp:646 and MenuPage.cpp:117, each guarded by its own `throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list")`. Command lists are released by raw `->Release()`, so any early return or exception between `FinishCommandList` and the loop leaks them — and Level.cpp:590 throws from inside a thread-pool worker, which is `std::terminate` on its own.

A game object should never see `ID3D11` anything if the engine is to be reusable or ever ported.

**Fix:** Introduce a `Renderer` facade owning the context pool and command lists: `renderer.record(view_index, [&](DrawList&){ ... })` plus one `renderer.flush()` that executes and releases (via ComPtr) in a single place. Level and MenuPage then take a `Renderer&` and D3D11 stays behind the platform boundary.

#### 2. get_deferred_context is declared noexcept but throws — guaranteed std::terminate, called from a worker thread

`ArtAttack/DeviceResources.h:88` — **high** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

Declaration:
```cpp
ID3D11DeviceContext* get_deferred_context(int index) const noexcept;   // DeviceResources.h:88
```

Definition:
```cpp
ID3D11DeviceContext* DeviceResources::get_deferred_context(int index) const noexcept
{
    if (index < 0 || index >= this->_deferred_contexts->size())
    {
        throw std::out_of_range("Invalid index.");   // DeviceResources.cpp:742
    }
    return this->_deferred_contexts->at(index);      // :744  .at() can throw too
}
```

Throwing out of a `noexcept` function calls `std::terminate` immediately — no unwinding, no catch site, no chance for any handler. This is not a theoretical path: it is called from inside a thread-pool task at `MenuPage::draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:175) with `i` being an index into the caller's `mobjects` vector, while the guard is against the number of deferred contexts (16). Any menu page that pushes more than 16 `MObject`s into its `mobjects` vector — see the pattern at MainMenu.cpp:38-45, PauseMenu.cpp:205, ResultsMenu.cpp:204-211, all currently 2 — terminates the process from a background thread.

Secondary: `index >= this->_deferred_contexts->size()` compares `int` against `size_t` (C4018 under /W4, which is enabled but not treated as an error), and `_deferred_contexts` is dereferenced without a null check even though it is `nullptr` until `create_deferred_contexts` runs.

**Fix:** Drop `noexcept` from both the declaration and the definition (or, better, keep `noexcept` and change the contract: return `nullptr`, or assert on the precondition, since an out-of-range context index is a programming error not a runtime condition). Then fix the real bug behind it: `draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports` should index the context/command-list/sprite-batch arrays by *task* index, not by mobject index, so the number of drawable widgets is decoupled from the number of deferred contexts.

## `ArtAttack/GameData.h`

_4 findings: 1 high, 3 medium_

#### 1. GameData is a 13-pointer service locator that is also inherited as a base by five game-specific data bags, with no virtual destructor

`ArtAttack/GameData.h:13-62` — **high** · `design`

Merged from 3 candidates. `GameData` holds raw non-owning pointers to `Save`, `ResolutionManager`, `HWND`, `float* _dt`, `ResourceLoader`, `ResourceManager`, `GamePad`, `DeviceResources`, `ViewportManager`, `CommonStates`, `std::vector<SpriteBatch*>*`, `ThreadPool` and `const Partitioner*` — 13 members, every engine service in one struct, handed to essentially everything. Any class that needs frame time also gets the D3D device and the gamepad, so nothing here can be unit-tested or reused in isolation.

(Two candidates said "12 pointers"; the actual count is 13 members, one of which is an HWND handle.)

Then it is INHERITED: `class MenuData : public GameData` (MenuData.h:7), which adds `MenuInput* _input`, which is in turn the base of MainMenuData/PauseMenuData/ResultsMenuData/EndMenuData. `GameData` has no destructor at all, hence a public non-virtual one; deletion through a `GameData*` is UB, and `GameData::get_game_data()` even hands out a `GameData*` to `this`.

Construction goes through `explicit GameData(const GameData* game_data)` (GameData.cpp:4-20), a hand-written field-by-field copy calling 13 getters. That is exactly what the implicit copy constructor already does, and it must be edited every time a service is added — forgetting silently drops a pointer. Its pointer parameter also makes slicing invisible: `MenuData::MenuData(const GameData*)` passes a derived pointer and the derived state is dropped with no diagnostic. And it means each menu holds a SNAPSHOT of the pointers, not a view, which is what makes the device-restore finding above fatal.

**Fix:** Add `protected: ~GameData() = default;` so base-pointer deletion cannot compile. Replace the pointer-taking ctor with the implicit copy ctor. Strategically: split into narrow interfaces (`IAssetRegistry`, `IJobSystem`, `IAudioSystem`, `Clock`) injected per-class, and make `MenuData` HOLD services rather than BE them.

#### 2. GameData.h drags in 8 concrete headers for 13 members that are all raw pointers

`ArtAttack/GameData.h:4-11,49-61` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

GameData.h:4-11 includes ResolutionManager.h, Save.h, ResourceLoader.h, ResourceManager.h, DeviceResources.h, ViewportManager.h, ThreadPool.h and Partitioner.h. Every one of its 13 data members (lines 49-61) is a pointer - `Save* _save`, `ResolutionManager* _resolution_manager`, `HWND _window`, `float* _dt`, `ResourceLoader*`, `ResourceManager*`, `DirectX::GamePad*`, `DX::DeviceResources*`, `ViewportManager*`, `DirectX::CommonStates*`, `std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>*`, `ThreadPool*`, `const Partitioner*` - and every accessor returns or takes a pointer. Not one of these includes is required by the header; all eight could be forward declarations. Because ResourceManager.h is in that list, GameData.h transitively pulls in rapidjson/document.h, DirectXTK's <Audio.h>, and <iostream> (via Save.h:4). This is the service-locator hub of the whole program, so it lands in Game.h, GameStates.h, LevelBuilder.h, Level.h, Weapon.h and Player.h.

**Fix:** Replace all 8 includes with forward declarations (`class Save; class ResourceManager; namespace DX { class DeviceResources; } namespace DirectX { class GamePad; class CommonStates; class SpriteBatch; }`) plus <vector> and <windows.h> for HWND. Longer term the pointer-bag itself should be replaced by explicit constructor dependencies, but the include cleanup is a zero-risk first step.

#### 3. GameData is a public base of five menu data classes but has no virtual destructor and is freely copyable and sliceable

`ArtAttack/GameData.h:13-62` — **medium** · `design`

`GameData` (GameData.h:13-62) is a concrete bag of thirteen raw pointers with no `virtual ~GameData()`, no protected destructor and no copy/move control, yet it is publicly inherited by `MenuData` (MenuData.h:7), `MainMenuData`, `PauseMenuData`, `EndMenuData` and `ResultsMenuData`. It actively hands out upcasts: `GameData* GameData::get_game_data()` returns `this` (GameData.cpp:122) and `MenuData* MenuData::get_menu_data()` returns `this` (MenuData.cpp:26-28) — both of which a grep shows are called from **nowhere** in the codebase. Nothing deletes through a `GameData*` today (GameStates.h holds `unique_ptr<MainMenuData>` etc.), but the API invites it, and one `unique_ptr<GameData>` is undefined behaviour that leaks `PauseMenuData::_action` and `ResultsMenuData::_level_end_info`. The implicit copy constructor is equally live and is already used deliberately by `MenuData::MenuData(const GameData*)`. The ctor const-qualification also drifted for no reason: `MenuData(const GameData*)` and `ResultsMenuData(const GameData*, ...)` vs `MainMenuData(GameData*)`, `PauseMenuData(GameData*, ...)`, `EndMenuData(GameData*, ...)`.

**Fix:** Make the base non-polymorphic and non-inheritable (`final`, held by composition in the *MenuData classes — the right fix anyway), or give it `virtual ~GameData() = default;` plus deleted copy/move. Do not leave it in the middle. Settle on one const-qualification across the four ctors and delete the dead `get_game_data()`/`get_menu_data()`.

#### 4. The dependency container is a 13-pointer service locator that is also a polymorphic base with a non-virtual destructor

`ArtAttack/GameData.h:13-62` — **medium** · `design`

`GameData` is a bag of 13 raw pointers (:49-61), all defaulting to `nullptr` and each populated by a separate `set_*` call scattered through `Game::initialize` (Game.cpp:32-66), `create_device_dependent_resources` (Game.cpp:230-256) and `wWinMain`. Its destructor is public, implicit and **non-virtual** — yet it is used as a base class: `MenuData : public GameData` (MenuData.h:7) adds a `MenuInput*`; `MainMenuData`, `PauseMenuData`, `ResultsMenuData`, `EndMenuData` each add more. `GameData::get_game_data()` (:46) hands out an upcast `GameData*`, so any `delete` through it is UB (avoided today only because nothing does it), and any `GameData` copy from a `MenuData*` silently slices `_input` off.

Using inheritance to bolt an extra field onto a container makes the *dependency-injection mechanism itself* polymorphic, which is backwards. And the consumers chase it unchecked: `GameLevel::draw` (:311-319) does `get_data()->get_device_resources()->get_deferred_contexts()` and `->GetD3DDeviceContext()` with no null check anywhere, so a forgotten or reordered setter is a null dereference on the render path with no diagnostic.

A state that needs a ResourceManager and a MenuInput should say so in its signature, not receive a 13-pointer bag and reach into it.

**Fix:** Mark `GameData` `final` and stop deriving from it; per-screen state (`MenuInput*`, `MenuLevelSettings*`, action flags) belongs to the State that owns it, passed as explicit constructor parameters. If it must stay a base, give it a protected non-virtual destructor so delete-through-base is a compile error. At minimum, assert the whole bag is populated at the end of `Game::initialize`.

## `ArtAttack/GameStates.h`

_7 findings: 2 high, 4 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. The state layer is bidirectionally coupled to every concrete screen; GameStates.h compiles the whole game

`ArtAttack/GameStates.h:1-12` — **high** · `design`

`GameStates.h` includes `MenuLevelSettings.h`, `GameData.h`, `LevelBuilder.h`, `PauseMenu.h`, `ResultsMenu.h`, `MainMenu.h`, `EndMenu.h`, `PlayerInput.h`. `GameData.h:4-11` in turn pulls `ResolutionManager.h`, `Save.h`, `ResourceLoader.h`, `ResourceManager.h`, `DeviceResources.h`, `ViewportManager.h`, `ThreadPool.h`, `Partitioner.h`, and `LevelBuilder.h` pulls `Level.h` → `Player.h`, `Weapon.h`, `CollisionTools.h`, plus d3d11/dxgi. Anything touching the state machine compiles the entire game.

Of the members that need those headers, every one except `MenuLevelSettings _settings` (:56) is behind a `unique_ptr` and needs only a forward declaration.

The transition graph is also hardcoded in the leaves and cyclic at the concrete-type level: `GameMenu` constructs `GameLevel` (GameStates.cpp:82) and `GameLevel` constructs `GameMenu` at five sites (:212, :253, :263, :273, :291). Each state must know its siblings' concrete types *and* their exact constructor signatures. For an engine, `State`/`StateContext` should ship alone and concrete screens should be game code.

**Fix:** Forward-declare the unique_ptr'd types, declare `~GameMenu();`/`~GameLevel();` in the header and `= default` them in the .cpp, and move heavy includes into the .cpp. Break the cycle by making transitions symbolic — states name a target by id or return a registered factory — so `GameLevel.cpp` never includes `GameMenu`. Split GameStates.h into GameMenu.h / GameLevel.h.

#### 2. GameLevel declares every menu's data object after the state that points at it, so data dies first

`ArtAttack/GameStates.h:55-70` — **high** · `lifetime` · confidence: certain

std::unique_ptr<Level> _level;                       // 57
    ...
    std::unique_ptr<StateContext> _pause_menu;           // 60
    std::unique_ptr<pause_menu_action> _pause_menu_action;// 61
    std::unique_ptr<PauseMenuData> _pause_menu_data;     // 62
    std::unique_ptr<MenuInput> _menu_input;              // 63
    std::unique_ptr<StateContext> _results_menu;         // 64
    std::unique_ptr<results_menu_action> _results_menu_action; // 65
    std::unique_ptr<ResultsMenuData> _results_menu_data; // 66
    std::unique_ptr<StateContext> _end_menu;             // 67
    std::unique_ptr<end_menu_action> _end_menu_action;   // 68
    std::unique_ptr<EndMenuData> _end_menu_data;         // 69

Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, so the order is: `_end_menu_data`, `_end_menu_action`, `_end_menu`, `_results_menu_data`, `_results_menu_action`, `_results_menu`, `_menu_input`, `_pause_menu_data`, `_pause_menu_action`, `_pause_menu`. Every pointee dies before its pointer holder:
* `_end_menu_data` dies before `_end_menu`, whose live `EndMenuInitial` holds `EndMenuData* _data` (EndMenu.h:53).
* `_menu_input` dies before both `_pause_menu_data` (which stores `MenuInput*`, MenuData.h:16) and `_pause_menu` (whose pages call `get_menu_inputs()`).

The same inversion happens *mid-life*, on the second match, and there the dangling window is two live statements long:

    // GameStates.cpp:169-181
    this->_results_menu_action = std::make_unique<...>(NONE);   // old action freed HERE
    this->_results_menu_data   = std::make_unique<ResultsMenuData>(...);  // old data freed HERE
    this->_results_menu        = std::make_unique<StateContext>();        // old page freed only HERE

Between lines 169 and 178 the still-alive `ResultsMenuInitial` from match 1 holds a `ResultsMenuData*` to freed memory, which in turn holds a freed `results_menu_action*`.

This is currently latent only because none of the destructors happen to dereference. It is one added line in `~EndMenuPage`/`~MenuPage` away from a use-after-free.

**Fix:** Declare owners before borrowers (`_menu_input`, then `*_action`, then `*_data`, then the `StateContext`), and on re-entry destroy top-down explicitly: `_results_menu.reset(); _results_menu_data.reset(); _results_menu_action.reset();` before building the new ones. Structurally the better fix is to fold the action flag and the data into one object owned by the `StateContext` (or return an action enum from `State::update()`) so the ordering cannot be got wrong.

#### 3. Member declaration order makes menu pages outlive every object they point at

`ArtAttack/GameStates.h:24-33, 55-70` — **medium** · `lifetime`

Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order. In `GameMenu` (GameStates.h:24-29): `_menu` (the `StateContext` owning the live page) is declared FIRST, so it is destroyed LAST — after `_menu_input`, `_menu_data`, `_menu_level_settings` and `_is_ready_to_load_level`, all of which the page's `MenuPage::_data` / `MainMenuPage::_data` chain points into. `GameLevel` (55-70) has the same inversion three times: `_pause_menu` (60) is destroyed after `_pause_menu_action` (61), `_pause_menu_data` (62) and `_menu_input` (63); `_results_menu` (64) after `_results_menu_data` (66); `_end_menu` (67) after `_end_menu_action` (68) and `_end_menu_data` (69). Currently survivable only because `~MainMenuPage`, `~PauseMenuPage`, `~EndMenuPage` and `~ResultsMenuPage` are all `= default` and touch nothing. One obvious line in a page destructor (`stop_effect(MUSIC)`, or writing a final value through `get_action()`) turns this into a use-after-free, and nothing records the constraint.

**Fix:** Declare the `StateContext` members LAST in both classes so pages are torn down before the data they borrow, and add a comment stating the dependency. Better: `_menu.reset();` at the top of the owning destructor so the order is stated in code.

#### 4. Member declaration order is inverted: every menu's data is destroyed before the StateContext holding raw pointers to it

`ArtAttack/GameStates.h:24-29, 55-70` — **medium** · `lifetime`

Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, and all four menu groups are declared the wrong way round.

`GameMenu` (:24-30): `_menu` (25) is declared *before* `_menu_input` (26), `_menu_data` (27), `_menu_level_settings` (28) and `_is_ready_to_load_level` (29). Destruction therefore frees `_is_ready_to_load_level`, `_menu_level_settings`, `_menu_data`, `_menu_input` — and only *last* destroys `_menu`, the `StateContext` owning a `MainMenuTitle`/`MainMenuHome`/… whose page holds a raw `MainMenuData*` to the already-freed `_menu_data`, which itself held raw pointers to the already-freed settings and flag.

`GameLevel` repeats it three times: `_pause_menu`(60) before `_pause_menu_action`(61)/`_pause_menu_data`(62); `_results_menu`(64) before `_results_menu_action`(65)/`_results_menu_data`(66); `_end_menu`(67) before `_end_menu_action`(68)/`_end_menu_data`(69). And `_menu_input`(63) is destroyed before both `_results_menu`(64) and `_end_menu`(67), whose pages reach it through `MenuData::_input`.

Nothing crashes today only because no menu page has a non-default destructor — the same "correct by luck" property as the transition_to finding. The ordering is load-bearing and undocumented.

**Fix:** Declare owned data strictly before the things that point at it, so destruction unwinds dependents first: `_menu_input`, `_menu_data`, `_menu_level_settings`, `_is_ready_to_load_level`, *then* `_menu`. Far better: have pages obtain the data through an accessor on the parent rather than storing a raw back-pointer, so there is nothing to go stale.

#### 5. Child-to-parent signalling is four heap-allocated scalars whose raw addresses are handed to sub-states

`ArtAttack/GameStates.h:29, 61, 65, 68` — **medium** · `design`

```cpp
std::unique_ptr<bool>                _is_ready_to_load_level;   // :29,  created GameStates.cpp:23
std::unique_ptr<pause_menu_action>   _pause_menu_action;        // :61,  created :150
std::unique_ptr<results_menu_action> _results_menu_action;      // :65,  created :169
std::unique_ptr<end_menu_action>     _end_menu_action;          // :68,  created :225
```
Four separate heap allocations for one `bool` and three 4-byte enums, each existing only so a raw `bool*` / `pause_menu_action*` can be handed to a child state (`_menu_data->set_is_ready_to_load_level(_is_ready_to_load_level.get())`, :68-69; `PauseMenuData(..., _pause_menu_action.get())`, :157). The child writes through the borrowed pointer (`*this->get_pause_menu_data()->get_action() = pause_menu_action::RESUME;`, PauseMenu.cpp:57) and the parent polls it next frame (`pause_menu_action action = *this->_pause_menu_action;`, :193).

A plain value member has an equally stable address, so the allocation buys nothing — while the `unique_ptr` obscures that these are just mutable out-flags, adds four null states that must be created in `init()`, and makes correctness depend on the member declaration order and the reassignment order, both of which are wrong (see the two ordering findings). `Game::_dt` being a `unique_ptr<float>` (Game.h:66) is the same anti-pattern.

**Fix:** Make them plain value members (`bool _is_ready_to_load_level = false; pause_menu_action _pause_menu_action = NONE;`) — the existing `.get()` hand-off becomes `&_flag` and everything still compiles. Better: have sub-states *return* a result from `update()` (a small tagged transition request) rather than scribbling into a borrowed cell in their owner.

#### 6. GameLevel member declaration order is the inverse of its dependency order — menu States outlive the data they point at

`ArtAttack/GameStates.h:57-69` — **medium** · `memory-safety`

Declaration order is `_pause_menu` (60), `_pause_menu_action` (61), `_pause_menu_data` (62), `_menu_input` (63), `_results_menu` (64), `_results_menu_action` (65), `_results_menu_data` (66), `_end_menu` (67), `_end_menu_action` (68), `_end_menu_data` (69).

The dependency chain runs `_pause_menu` → `PauseMenuData*` → `MenuInput*` and `pause_menu_action*`, wired at GameStates.cpp:150-162. Reverse-order destruction therefore destroys `_menu_input` (63), then `_pause_menu_data` (62), then `_pause_menu_action` (61), and only then `_pause_menu` (60) — the live `PauseMenuInitial` State is destroyed while its `PauseMenuData*` is already freed, which in turn already had a freed `MenuInput*`. Identical inversion for results (64/66) and end (67/69), which are additionally destroyed before `_menu_input` too.

No destructor currently dereferences those pointers, so it does not crash — the correctness rests entirely on an undocumented "no State destructor may touch its data" rule.

Same file, minor: GameStates.cpp:202 and :279 do `this->_level = std::move(this->_level_builder->build_level(this->_settings));` — `std::move` on a prvalue, suppressing copy elision to force a needless move-construct.

**Fix:** Reorder so owners of pointees precede their dependents: `_menu_input`, `_pause_menu_action`, `_pause_menu_data`, `_pause_menu` (and likewise for results/end), with a comment stating the rule. Better, have the data objects own what they need so order stops mattering. Drop the redundant `std::move`.

#### 7. Dead GameMenu::get_data(), redundant value-initialisers, and three include-guard end comments that name the wrong macro

`ArtAttack/GameStates.h:33, 56, 76` — **low** · `maintainability`

Three small cleanups in the module's headers.

1. `GameData* GameMenu::get_data() const` is declared at GameStates.h:33 and defined at GameStates.cpp:90-93, but nothing calls it — `GameMenu::order_level_creation` reaches for `this->_game_data` directly (:82) and `GameMenu::init` goes through `_menu_data->get_gamepad()`. Every `get_data()` call in the file (:108-120, :154, :173, :212, :229, :253, :263, :273, :291, :311-319) is inside a `GameLevel` method. `GameLevel` has a byte-identical accessor that *is* used 18 times.

2. `MenuLevelSettings _settings = MenuLevelSettings();` (GameStates.h:56) writes an explicit value-initialiser where nothing at all would do. The member is also commented `// need this to pass to GameLevel` at :24, which is an admission that the state machine has no way to carry shared services and each state smuggles the pointer through by hand.

3. Three include guards have end comments naming a different macro than the guard: `#endif // !GAMELEVEL_H` for guard `GAMESTATES_H` (GameStates.h:76); `#endif // !STATECONTEXTGENERIC_H` for guard `STATECONTEXT_H` (StateContext.h:19); `#endif // !TEAM_COLOURS_H` for guard `TEAMCOLOUR_H` (TeamColour.h:57). Stale comments from renamed files.

**Fix:** Delete the unused `GameMenu::get_data()` and the redundant `= MenuLevelSettings()`. Replace the hand-written include guards with `#pragma once` (this is an MSVC-only project and pch.h already uses it) so the comments cannot drift again. Hoist the `GameData*` into `State` or `StateContext` so states obtain services from their context rather than each re-declaring the member.

## `ArtAttack/IGameObject.h`

_6 findings: 3 high, 3 medium_

#### 1. 40 headers are not self-contained: they name DirectX/Win32 types with no include, and compile only because /Yu force-injects pch.h

`ArtAttack/IGameObject.h:1-16` — **high** · `design` · confidence: certain

IGameObject.h includes only "MattMath.h" yet its pure-virtual interface is declared as `virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch, const MattMath::Camera& camera) = 0;` (line 11). Nothing in its include closure declares DirectX::SpriteBatch - it resolves purely because MSVC's /Yu"pch.h" has already injected SpriteBatch.h into every TU. I ran the closure check across all 105 headers: 39 first-party headers (plus vendor DeviceResources.h) name a symbol whose header they do not include. Representative sites: Player.h, Projectile.h, Structure.h, StructurePaintable.h, PaintTile.h, TextureObject.h, TextObject.h, TextDropShadow.h, Visual.h, Mh.h, AnimatedSprite.h, AnimationObject.h, SpriteSheet.h, SpriteSheetObject.h, DrawObject.h, MenuPage.h, ViewportManager.h, Weapon.h + all 5 Weapon*.h + all 5 Projectile*.h (DirectX::SpriteBatch / SpriteEffects); GameData.h and Game.h (CommonStates, GamePad, HWND, SpriteBatch); ResourceManager.h (SpriteFont, Microsoft::WRL); MenuInput.h and PlayerInput.h (GamePad). For a project whose goal is a reusable engine this is fatal: a consumer cannot `#include "Player.h"` without first reproducing ArtAttack's exact pch.h.

**Fix:** Make every header compile standalone. Cheapest mechanical fix: add the missing includes (or, for pointer-only uses like `DirectX::SpriteBatch*`, forward-declare `namespace DirectX { class SpriteBatch; }` in one small fwd.h). Then add a build step or a Debug-only .cpp that includes each header first-and-alone to keep the property from regressing.

#### 2. Every game object in the engine is compiled against DirectXTK's SpriteBatch and MattMath::Camera

`ArtAttack/IGameObject.h:10-13` — **high** · `design` · confidence: certain

The engine's root object interface is:
```
virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch, const MattMath::Camera& camera) = 0;
virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch) = 0;
virtual bool is_visible_in_viewport(const MattMath::RectangleF& view) const = 0;
```
There is no renderer abstraction anywhere: `DirectX::SpriteBatch*` is threaded raw through `IGameObject`, `Mh.h:23-24,50-51`, `MenuPage.h:38-50`, `Level.h:83-85` (`std::vector<DirectX::SpriteBatch*>*`), `GameData.h:39` and `Drawer.h`. `DrawObject.h:16,24,30,40` stores `DirectX::SpriteEffects` as engine state. Culling is also each object's own responsibility (`is_visible_in_viewport`), duplicated across every concrete class rather than done once by the scene.

For a 'reusable 2D engine' this locks the whole object model to DirectXTK's immediate-mode sprite batcher. Nothing can be unit-tested without a D3D11 device, which is why `MattMathTests` covers only `MattMath` and `CollisionTools`.

**Fix:** Introduce a thin engine `IRenderer`/`SpriteDrawList` interface (`draw_sprite(texture, src_rect, dst_rect, colour, rotation, origin, depth)`) with a DirectXTK implementation, and have objects submit to that. Move culling out of objects into the scene (objects expose `get_bounds()`; the scene tests against the view rect once). This also unblocks headless tests of game logic.

#### 3. IGameObject hardwires DirectX::SpriteBatch and MattMath::Camera into the root interface of every object in the engine

`ArtAttack/IGameObject.h:11-12` — **high** · `design`

```cpp
virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch, const MattMath::Camera& camera) = 0;
virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch) = 0;
```
This is the base interface every drawable derives from — gameplay objects, projectiles, paint tiles, and the whole `Mh` UI widget tree. The rendering backend is therefore part of the type identity of every object in the engine, and `IGameObject.h:4` includes `MattMath.h` (1139 lines, itself pulling `SimpleMath.h` and `<d3d11.h>`) just to name them. Changing renderer, changing batching strategy, or introducing a render-command queue means editing all ~30 implementers.

The two-overload requirement compounds it: every implementer must write both, and the camera-less one is pure boilerplate for game objects — `Player::draw(SpriteBatch*)` (Player.cpp:91-95) just forwards with `Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA`, as do ProjectileBall/Jet/Spray/Mist/Rolling and Structure. It exists only so UI widgets, which have no camera, can be drawn. The level renderer only ever calls the camera form (Level.cpp:520, 529, 538, 550).

**Fix:** Invert the dependency: `virtual void draw(IRenderer&) const = 0;` where `IRenderer` owns the SpriteBatch and the active camera and exposes `draw_sprite(const Sprite&, const Transform&)`. Objects then never name a D3D or DirectXTK type, and the second overload disappears because "no camera" becomes an identity camera on the context — a value, not a virtual. This is the single change that makes the object layer renderer-agnostic and therefore reusable.

#### 4. IGameObject is a fat interface that hardwires DirectX types and a non-const draw into every game object

`ArtAttack/IGameObject.h:6-14` — **medium** · `design`

```cpp
class IGameObject {
    virtual void update() = 0;
    virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch*, const MattMath::Camera&) = 0;
    virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch*) = 0;
    virtual bool is_visible_in_viewport(const MattMath::RectangleF&) const = 0;
};
```
Four unrelated responsibilities in one interface, so purely static scenery has to implement all four — `Visual::update()` is literally `{ // do nothing }` (Visual.cpp:38-41).

The camera-less `draw` overload exists only so callers can skip the camera, and implementations satisfy it by forwarding with `Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA` (TextDropShadow.cpp:49-52, Player.cpp:91-95) — a default-argument problem solved with a virtual function, doubling the vtable.

Most importantly for the engine goal, `DirectX::SpriteBatch` appears in the signature, so nothing implementing `IGameObject` can be tested or rendered without DirectXTK. And `draw` being non-const is the root of the whole mutating-draw problem: the level's draw path is `const` (Level.cpp:375, :737) and reaches non-const `draw` only because `const` does not propagate through the `unique_ptr` members.

**Fix:** Split by responsibility: `IUpdatable { void update(float dt); }` and `IRenderable { void draw(Renderer&, const Camera&) const; RectangleF bounds() const; }`. Culling belongs to the renderer/scene computed from `bounds()`, not reimplemented per object. Collapse the two draw overloads into one. Replace `SpriteBatch*` with an abstract `Renderer&` so the object graph does not name a DirectX type, and make `draw` const.

#### 5. Interface mandates two draw overloads; the camera-less one is dead for every game object and non-const for all of them

`ArtAttack/IGameObject.h:11-12` — **medium** · `design`

Every implementer must supply both `draw(SpriteBatch*, const Camera&)` and `draw(SpriteBatch*)`. The one-argument form is only ever called by the `Mh` UI widget tree, `PaintTile.cpp:70` and `StructurePaintable.cpp:56/59`; the level renderer only uses the camera form (Level.cpp:520, 529, 538, 550). So `Player::draw(SpriteBatch*)` (Player.cpp:91-95), `ProjectileSpray/Jet/Ball/Mist/Rolling::draw(SpriteBatch*)` and `Structure::draw(SpriteBatch*)` are hand-written forwarders that exist only because the interface demands them — one extra dead function per new object type.

Both overloads are also **non-const**, although the primitives underneath are already const: `TextureObject::draw(...) const` (TextureObject.h:20-31) and all five `AnimationObject::draw(...) const` overloads (AnimationObject.h:34-46). The concrete overrides are pure forwarders to those const functions. The gratuitous non-const then infects the whole render path — `Level::draw_active_level(...) const` has to hold non-const object pointers just to draw them, which is a large part of why const is broken throughout Level.

**Fix:** Collapse to one `virtual void draw(...) const = 0;`. "No camera" is the identity camera — a value, not a second virtual. Do not use a virtual with a default argument, since defaults bind statically and would be a second trap. Anything that genuinely mutates during draw (animation frame advance) should do it in `update()`.

#### 6. Culling is delegated to each object, producing unimplementable stubs, one permanently-invisible object, and an infinite recursion

`ArtAttack/IGameObject.h:13` — **medium** · `design`

`virtual bool is_visible_in_viewport(const MattMath::RectangleF& view) const = 0;` forces every implementer to own frustum culling, and there is no `get_bounds()` on the interface — so the level physically cannot see where anything is, and a quadtree or grid can never be layered on without touching every derived class. `Level::draw_player_view_level` consequently makes one virtual call per object per viewport per frame across three unsorted lists (Level.cpp:516-540), and the zoom-out path gave up entirely and culls nothing (Level.cpp:629-642).

The implementations show the interface is wrong. Most are the identical one-liner `return this->_rectangle.intersects(view);` (PaintTile.cpp:151, 199; ProjectileBall.cpp:53; ProjectileJet.cpp:52; ProjectileMist.cpp:54; ProjectileSpray.cpp:54; Structure.cpp:41; Visual.cpp:52) with Player differing only by an inflate (Player.cpp:916-921). And three are broken:
- `ProjectileRolling::is_visible_in_viewport` (ProjectileRolling.cpp:44-47) is a hard `return false;` — a rolling projectile tells the renderer it is *never* on screen, so it is never drawn.
- `MText`/`MTextDropShadow` (Mh.cpp:278-282, 343-347) are `return true;` under `TODO: implement text bounding box`, because a text widget cannot cheaply compute its own bounds.
- **`MTexture::is_visible_in_viewport` (Mh.cpp:162-165) is `return this->is_visible_in_viewport(view);` — unconditional infinite recursion, i.e. a stack-overflow crash the moment it is called.** That one is outside this module group's files but is a `critical`-grade bug in its own right and should be routed to whoever owns Mh.cpp.

**Fix:** Objects expose data, the renderer decides: `virtual const MattMath::RectangleF& get_bounds() const = 0;` returning a cached AABB the object updates when it moves. The scene performs the intersection test once, over a flat array of rects with no virtual calls, and can later swap the linear scan for a spatial index without touching a single object. UI widgets simply report their layout rect. Fix ProjectileRolling and Mh.cpp:162 immediately regardless.

## `ArtAttack/InterfaceGameplay.cpp`

_5 findings: 2 high, 3 medium_

#### 1. No rule about who owns SpriteBatch Begin/End — four incompatible conventions across the rendering code

`ArtAttack/InterfaceGameplay.cpp:15-47` — **high** · `design`

Batch lifetime is decided ad hoc in four different ways, all verified:

- `InterfaceGameplay::draw_gameplay_interface` begins and ends the batch twice inside one call (`Begin(); draw_timer(); End();` at :26-28, then `Begin(SpriteSortMode_Deferred, nullptr, sampler_state); ... End();` at :30-46), and needs a caller-supplied `ID3D11SamplerState*` to do it.
- `DebugText::draw_debug_info` begins and ends its own (DebugText.cpp:109, :136).
- `Level::draw_countdown_text` wraps its one drawable in its own (Level.cpp:740-745).
- `TextureObject::draw`, `AnimationObject::draw`, `Visual::draw`, `TextObject::draw` all assume the caller has already begun one (Level.cpp begins at :513, loops, ends at :553).

So whether you may call a given `draw` depends on undocumented per-class knowledge, and the sort mode / sampler / blend state a drawable renders under is invisible at its call site. Two of the four also flush mid-frame, which is a real cost: a normal player viewport pays 3 Begin/End cycles, rising to 5 with debug text and the countdown active. (I am correcting the reviewer's flat "five per player per frame" — debug and countdown are conditional.)

**Fix:** Introduce a `Renderer`/`SpriteBatchScope` that owns `Begin`/`End` and the pipeline state. Every drawable gets `void draw(Renderer&, const Camera&) const` and only submits; nothing below the renderer calls `Begin`/`End` or sees an `ID3D11SamplerState*`. Where a different state block is genuinely needed (point-clamped UI), express it as a named pass the renderer opens.

#### 2. Health bar fill width is never clamped and player health is only clamped at the top, so a dead player renders an inverted destination RECT

`ArtAttack/InterfaceGameplay.cpp:123-142` — **high** · `correctness`

```cpp
Vector2F fill_size = Vector2F(size.x - 2.0f * border, size.y - 2.0f * border);
fill_size.x *= health;                       // :127 — no clamp
RectangleI fill_rect = RectangleI(..., static_cast<int>(fill_size.x), ...);
```
I traced the value. `health` comes straight from `Player::get_health()` at Level.cpp:563. Player health is clamped only at the top — Player.cpp:735-737 caps regen at 1.0f — while the damage path just subtracts with no floor (`_health -= SPRAY_DAMAGE/JET_DAMAGE/ROLLING_DAMAGE/BALL_DAMAGE/MIST_DAMAGE` at Player.cpp:652, 658, 664, 670, 676). A hit that takes health from 0.05 to negative is routine. `Player::update` then flags DEAD at :704 but leaves `_health` negative until `respawn()` resets it to 1.0f at :999, up to 3 seconds later — and `draw_gameplay_interface` runs unconditionally every one of those frames (Level.cpp:560-569).

With `health` negative, `fill_size.x` is negative, `RectangleI` gets a negative width, and `RectangleI::get_win_rect()` (MattMath.cpp:2043-2052) computes `right = x + width`, which is less than `left`. `SpriteBatch::Draw` receives an inverted destination rect.

`draw_ammo` (:80) has the identical missing clamp and is safe only because `Weapon` happens to pre-clamp ammo. The UI layer is the last line of defence and should not depend on that.

**Fix:** Clamp at the point of use — `const float fraction = std::clamp(health, 0.0f, 1.0f);` (needs the C++17 bump; see the LanguageStandard finding) — and separately floor `Player::_health` at 0 in the damage path so the real bug surfaces at its source. Note `draw_ammo` and `draw_health` are otherwise identical apart from the fill colour; they should be one `draw_bar(...)`.

#### 3. draw_ammo and draw_health are the same 45 lines twice, plus redundant re-lookups and double string formatting

`ArtAttack/InterfaceGameplay.cpp:49-173` — **medium** · `duplication`

`draw_ammo` (:49-96) and `draw_health` (:97-143) are identical apart from the parameter name, one local name (`empty_box_rect` vs `empty_rect`) and the final fill colour (`team_colour` vs `HEALTH_COLOUR`). Both compute `size` from `TOP_RIGHT_BOX_SIZE * resolution`, build a `RectangleI` from four `static_cast<int>`, fetch `SPRITE_SHEET`, draw `EMPTY_BOX_FRAME` in WHITE, compute `border`, build `fill_pos`/`fill_size`, scale `fill_size.x` by the fraction, and draw `FILL_FRAME`.

Both also re-fetch the identical sprite sheet pointer into the same variable for no reason — :88-89 repeats :66-67, and :135-136 repeats :113-114 — paying a second string map lookup each.

`draw_timer` builds the same string twice (`std::to_string(static_cast<int>(std::ceil(timer))).c_str()` at :158 and :167), doing two `ceil` calls per player per frame; `draw_respawn_timer` at :186 correctly hoists it into a local, so the two functions in the same class disagree. (Downgrading the reviewers' "two heap allocations" — a 2-3 character string fits MSVC's SSO, so the waste is real but small.)

**Fix:** One `draw_bar(SpriteBatch*, const Vector2F& viewport_size, float fraction, const Colour& fill, const Vector2F& position) const`, with `draw_ammo`/`draw_health` as one-line callers — then promote it out of this class into a reusable `ProgressBar` widget per the HUD finding. Delete the duplicate lookups and hoist the timer string.

#### 4. draw_ammo and draw_health are the same 47-line function twice

`ArtAttack/InterfaceGameplay.cpp:49-143` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

`InterfaceGameplay::draw_ammo` (:49-96) and `InterfaceGameplay::draw_health` (:97-143) are line-for-line identical — same `TOP_RIGHT_BOX_SIZE` computation, same `RectangleI` construction with four `static_cast<int>`, same `EMPTY_BOX_FRAME` draw, same border/fill maths, same redundant second `get_sprite_sheet(SPRITE_SHEET)` lookup — differing only in the fill fraction (`fill_size.x *= ammo;` vs `*= health;`) and the fill colour (`team_colour` vs `HEALTH_COLOUR`). ~47 duplicated lines.

`draw_timer` (:144-173) and `draw_respawn_timer` (:175-199) likewise duplicate the "DrawString at pos+shadow_offset in shadow colour, then DrawString at pos" pattern, which `TextDropShadow::draw` (TextDropShadow.cpp:24-44) already implements.

**Fix:** Collapse to one `draw_bar(SpriteBatch*, const Vector2F& resolution, const Vector2F& position, float fraction, const Colour& fill_colour) const` and call it twice. Route the two timer draws through the existing `TextDropShadow`/`Text` objects instead of calling `SpriteFont::DrawString` twice by hand.

#### 5. draw_respawn_timer ignores resolution scaling and rounds differently from draw_timer, giving a visible off-by-one on every death

`ArtAttack/InterfaceGameplay.cpp:175-199` — **medium** · `correctness`

The two timer renderers in the same class disagree on both scaling and rounding.

`draw_timer` (:144-173) computes `float scale = resolution.x / TIMER_SCALE_FACTOR;`, passes it to `DrawString`, and scales the shadow offset with it (`pos + (TIMER_SHADOW_OFFSET * scale)`).

`draw_respawn_timer` (:175-199) does neither — `DrawString(sprite_batch, text.c_str(), (pos + RESPAWN_TIMER_SHADOW_OFFSET).get_xm_vector(), ...)` passes no scale argument at all, so it defaults to 1.0. In 2-player split-screen the match timer shrinks to 0.5x while the respawn counter stays full size; at 4K the respawn counter stays tiny.

Rounding differs too: `static_cast<int>(std::ceil(timer))` at :158 versus `static_cast<int>(timer) + 1` at :186. Those agree only for non-integral positive values. `Player::_respawn_timer` is initialised to exactly `RESPAWN_DELAY = 3.0f` (Player.h:151, player_consts.h:43) and is not decremented on the frame the player dies — `Player::update` takes the ALIVE branch and sets DEAD at :704-706, and the DEAD branch that decrements (:714) only runs from the next frame. So the first respawn frame renders `int(3.0) + 1 = 4` for a 3-second delay.

**Fix:** Give `draw_respawn_timer` the same `scale` treatment and use `std::ceil`. Better, both functions are "draw a scaled number with a drop shadow" — extract one helper taking font, value, position, colours and scale, and delete the duplicate.

## `ArtAttack/InterfaceGameplay.h`

_3 findings: 1 high, 1 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. InterfaceGameplay is a Splatoon HUD welded into what is presented as an engine class

`ArtAttack/InterfaceGameplay.h:10-79` — **high** · `engine-separation`

This derives `Drawer` and sits in the rendering layer, but every part of it is game content:

- Asset identity is hardcoded in the header: `SPRITE_SHEET = "sprite_sheet_1"`, `EMPTY_BOX_FRAME = "health_box"`, `FILL_FRAME = "pixel"`, `TIMER_FONT = "gill_sans_mt_bold_48"`, `RESPAWN_TIMER_FONT = "gill_sans_mt_bold_144"` (lines 18, 26-31). Renaming an atlas is a code change and a rebuild of everything that includes this header.
- Layout is compile-time: `RIGHT_MARGIN`, `AMMO_TOP_MARGIN`, `TOP_RIGHT_BOX_SIZE`, and `TIMER_SCALE_FACTOR = 1920.0f`, which bakes in a reference resolution with no comment saying so.
- The API is nine loose game-domain parameters ending in `float respawn_timer, bool show_respawn_timer`, and it takes a raw `ID3D11SamplerState*` — the HUD knows about D3D pipeline state objects.
- Line 5 includes `player_team.h` and `InterfaceDraw` carries a `player_team` member, so "there are teams" is baked into the type.

An engine has widgets; a game has a health bar. This is the clearest instance in the module of game logic living where reusable code should be.

**Fix:** Split into (a) engine widgets — a `ProgressBar { RectangleF bounds; FrameId background, fill; Colour tint; float fraction; }` and a `Label { FontHandle; std::string; Vector2F anchor; float scale; Colour text, shadow; }`, plus anchor/margin layout in normalised units — and (b) a game-side `GameplayHud` that owns a list of those widgets built from a data file (the level JSON pipeline already exists) and updated from `Player`. The sampler state belongs to the renderer, not to a HUD signature.

#### 2. Namespace-scope `const static std::string`/`Colour`/`Vector2F` in headers give a dynamically-initialised copy per translation unit

`ArtAttack/InterfaceGameplay.h:12-34` — **medium** · `modern-cpp`

```cpp
const static MattMath::Vector2F TOP_RIGHT_BOX_SIZE = { 0.15f, 0.07f };
const static std::string TIMER_FONT = "gill_sans_mt_bold_48";
const static MattMath::Colour HEALTH_COLOUR = colour_consts::GREEN;
```
Same in `debug_text_consts` (DebugText.h:11-18).

At namespace scope `const` already implies internal linkage, so `static` is redundant (and written backwards — the idiom is `static const`). The real cost is that `std::string`, `Colour` and `Vector2F` are not literal types here, so each gets a separate object *and* a dynamic initialiser in every TU that includes the header — and both headers are pulled in via `Level.h`. The file mixes `constexpr` and `const static` for values of the same kind on adjacent lines (`TIMER_SCALE_FACTOR` vs `TIMER_SHADOW_OFFSET`), so the inconsistency is visible at a glance.

**Fix:** With the language standard bumped to C++17, use `inline constexpr` for anything literal and `inline const` for the rest, giving one object across the program. Give `Vector2F` and `Colour` constexpr constructors so they can be `inline constexpr` too. Prefer `inline constexpr std::string_view` over `std::string` for the asset names.

#### 3. `InterfaceGameplay` reverses its own method's word order and overloads the most loaded word in C++

`ArtAttack/InterfaceGameplay.h:47-52` — **low** · `naming` · confidence: likely

`class InterfaceGameplay : public Drawer` (line 47) declares `void draw_gameplay_interface(...)` (line 52) - the class says "Interface Gameplay", its own method says "gameplay interface". Its constants namespace is `interface_consts` (line 10) and its companion struct is `InterfaceDraw` (line 37), reversing the order again. Worse, "Interface" in C++ means abstract base class - this codebase uses that meaning three doors down in `IGameObject`, `ICollisionGameObject`, `IPaintableGameObject`. This class is a heads-up display.
Same reversal habit shows up elsewhere: `SpriteSheetObject.h:69` stores `_element_name` with `get_element_name()` (63) while its subclass `TextureObject.h:82` calls the identical string `frame_name`, `SpriteSheet.h:20,31` calls it `frame_name`, and `AnimationObject.h:13` calls it `animation_strip_name` - three names for the key into one map.

**Fix:** Rename the class to `GameplayHud` (file `GameplayHud.h`), the namespace to `hud_consts`, the struct to `HudDrawParams`, and the method to `draw(...)`. Separately, settle `element_name` vs `frame_name`: `SpriteSheetObject` should call it `_element_name` and so should everyone else, or all of them should say `frame_name`.

## `ArtAttack/IPaintableGameObject.h`

_2 findings: 2 high_

#### 1. An interface named `IPaintableGameObject` with a hardcoded two-team score sits alongside the engine's core interfaces

`ArtAttack/IPaintableGameObject.h:1-17` — **high** · `design` · confidence: certain

The whole file is:
```
struct PaintTotal { float team_a = 0.0f; float team_b = 0.0f; };
class IPaintableGameObject { virtual PaintTotal get_paint_total() const = 0; };
```
It sits in the same flat directory as `IGameObject.h` and `ICollisionGameObject.h`, is named to match them, and is included by `Level.h:17` — i.e. the scene type consumes it directly. Exactly two teams are baked into the interface's return type, so a 3-team or free-for-all mode cannot even be expressed. `IPaintableGameObject` is a *Splatoon territory-control scoring hook* wearing an engine interface's name.

Related: `PaintTile.h:51-84` and `PaintTile.h:10-21` (`paint_tile_consts` with `SHEET_NAME = "sprite_sheet_1"`, `SPLASH_ANIMATION_STRIP_NAME = "splash_1"`) implement the paint grid as `ICollisionGameObject`s, so paint is physically inside the collision layer.

**Fix:** Move `IPaintableGameObject.h` and `PaintTile.*` into game/paint/. Replace `PaintTotal{team_a, team_b}` with something the game owns, e.g. `std::vector<float> coverage_by_faction` or `std::map<FactionId, float>`. The engine side needs no interface at all — the game can hold its own `std::vector<PaintableSurface*>`.

#### 2. Splatoon paint scoring and a fixed two-team model are baked into an engine-level interface

`ArtAttack/IPaintableGameObject.h:4-15` — **high** · `design`

```cpp
struct PaintTotal { float team_a = 0.0f; float team_b = 0.0f; };
class IPaintableGameObject { virtual PaintTotal get_paint_total() const = 0; };
```
A core object interface that hardcodes (a) that scoring is "paint", (b) that there are exactly two teams, (c) that they are named A and B. The assumption propagates into `LevelEndInfo` (LevelEndInfo.h:10-11), `Level::get_level_end_info` (Level.cpp:706-735), and the `*_TEAM_A`/`*_TEAM_B` cross-product in `collision_object_type` (collision_object_type.h:11-24, 23 enumerators encoding class × team × weapon).
