`ArtAttack/pch.h:59-77` — **medium** · `design`

The PCH includes `BufferHelpers.h`, `Effects.h`, `GeometricPrimitive.h`, `GraphicsMemory.h`, `Keyboard.h`, `Model.h`, `Mouse.h`, `PostProcess.h`, `PrimitiveBatch.h`, `ScreenGrab.h`, `VertexTypes.h`, `WICTextureLoader.h`. I grepped every first-party .h/.cpp under ArtAttack/ for `GeometricPrimitive`, `PostProcess`, `PrimitiveBatch`, `ScreenGrab`, `GraphicsMemory`, `Keyboard`, `Mouse`, `BasicEffect`, `IEffect`, `VertexPosition`, `CreateWICTextureFromFile` and `Model` — the only hits are the `#include` lines in pch.h itself. `Model.h` and `Effects.h` are among the heaviest headers in the toolkit, and this project explicitly constructs DeviceResources with `DXGI_FORMAT_UNKNOWN` depth because it 'Renders only 2D' (Game.cpp:12-14). There is no `MultiProcessorCompilation` in the vcxproj, so the cost is serialised.

Separately, pch.h *defines* the engine's error vocabulary — `DX::com_exception` and `DX::ThrowIfFailed` (:79-106) — so any module wanting those helpers must also pull in d3d11_1.h and dxgi1_6.h. That is why pure-math code starts with `#include "pch.h"` and why MattMathTests can only reach it by #including the .cpp files.

**Fix:** Cut the PCH to what is used: CommonStates.h, DDSTextureLoader.h, DirectXHelpers.h, GamePad.h, SimpleMath.h, SpriteBatch.h, SpriteFont.h. Move `com_exception`/`ThrowIfFailed` to a small `dx_error.h`, and let platform-free modules (MattMath, EricsonMath, CollisionTools) compile with no PCH at all — a precondition for the engine ever being a linkable library. Also raise `_WIN32_WINNT` from 0x0601 (Windows 7, pch.h:10).

#### 3. The precompiled header pulls in 13 unused DirectXTK headers, including the two heaviest ones

`ArtAttack/pch.h:59-77` — **medium** · `build-hygiene` · confidence: certain

`pch.h:59-77` includes 19 DirectXTK headers. I grepped every first-party file (excluding pch.h and the vendor-supplied DeviceResources.cpp) for the identifying symbols of each. Zero hits for: `Model.h` (`Model`), `Effects.h` (`BasicEffect`/`IEffect`/`EffectFactory`), `GeometricPrimitive.h`, `PostProcess.h`, `PrimitiveBatch.h`, `ScreenGrab.h` (`SaveDDSTextureToFile`/`SaveWICTextureToFile`), `BufferHelpers.h` (`CreateStaticBuffer`/`ConstantBuffer`), `VertexTypes.h` (`VertexPosition*`), `WICTextureLoader.h` (`CreateWICTextureFromFile`), `Keyboard.h`, `Mouse.h`, `GraphicsMemory.h`, `DirectXHelpers.h` (`CreateShaderResourceView`/`SetDebugObjectName`/`MapGuard`). `Model.h` and `Effects.h` are the two largest headers in DirectXTK and they are 3D-only; this project is 2D sprite rendering. Every one of the 81 translation units pays for them.

**Fix:** Cut pch.h down to what is used: CommonStates, DDSTextureLoader, GamePad, SimpleMath, SpriteBatch, SpriteFont, Audio. Also note `MattMathTests/pch.h` is an empty stub (12 lines, no includes) while `PrecompiledHeader=Use` is set in MattMathTests.vcxproj:93,108,123,142 — a PCH that precompiles nothing.

#### 4. com_exception::what() returns a shared function-local static buffer, and its converting constructor is not explicit

`ArtAttack/pch.h:82-96` — **medium** · `robustness`

```
class com_exception : public std::exception
{
public:
    com_exception(HRESULT hr) noexcept : result(hr) {}
    const char* what() const noexcept override
    {
        static char s_str[64] = {};
        sprintf_s(s_str, "Failure with HRESULT of %08X", ...);
        return s_str;
    }
```
Every `com_exception` in the process returns a pointer to the same 64-byte static. Calling `what()` on exception A after exception B overwrites A's message, and the returned pointer's lifetime is not tied to the exception object — the opposite of what callers expect. The single-argument constructor is not `explicit`, so any HRESULT implicitly converts.

This is verbatim Microsoft template code but it lives in the project's own pch.h and is the only exception type here carrying useful information — the rest of the codebase throws `std::exception("literal")`, an MSVC-only extension.

**Fix:** Mark the constructor `explicit`, and either derive from `std::runtime_error` with the message formatted in the constructor (it owns a refcounted copy, so `what()` becomes trivially correct) or store a `char m_str[64]` member instead of a function-local static.

#### 5. com_exception::what() returns a pointer to a shared static buffer it rewrites on every call

`ArtAttack/pch.h:87-92` — **medium** · `concurrency` · confidence: certain

```cpp
const char* what() const noexcept override
{
    static char s_str[64] = {};
    sprintf_s(s_str, "Failure with HRESULT of %08X", static_cast<unsigned int>(result));
    return s_str;
}
```

A single process-wide mutable buffer written by any thread that calls `what()`, returning a pointer into it. Two concurrent failures interleave `sprintf_s` output; a caller that holds the returned pointer across another `what()` call reads a different exception's message. `ThrowIfFailed` (pch.h:99-105) is used on device-creation and resource paths, and this codebase now runs up to 16 worker threads, so "only one thread ever fails at a time" is not a safe assumption.

(This block is Microsoft template boilerplate, but it lives in first-party `pch.h` and is compiled into every TU, so it is yours to fix.)

**Fix:** Store the formatted message in a `std::string` member built in the constructor and return `_msg.c_str()` — or derive from `std::runtime_error` and pass the formatted string to its constructor, which is what the modern DirectXTK template does.

## `ArtAttack/player_consts.h`

_3 findings: 1 high, 1 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. Two divergent projectile-damage tables; the ProjectileDetails one is dead code

`ArtAttack/player_consts.h:65-69` — **high** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

Damage per projectile is specified twice, with different values:

- `player_consts.h:65-69`: `SPRAY_DAMAGE = 0.01f; JET_DAMAGE = 0.334f; ROLLING_DAMAGE = 0.015f; BALL_DAMAGE = 0.201f; MIST_DAMAGE = 0.01f;`
- `projectile_consts.h:20,33,54,67,80,101`: `player_damage` per `ProjectileDetails` = `0.0, -0.1, -0.5, -1000.0, -0.05, -0.1` (note the sign flip and the wildly different magnitudes).

`Projectile::get_player_damage()` (Projectile.h:51, Projectile.cpp:295-298) exists to read the second table — a repo-wide grep shows it is called from nowhere. Instead `Player::on_projectile_collision` (Player.cpp:645-690) hand-writes a 5-branch `if/else` over `collision_object_type` to pick a `player_consts` constant, with the same `//this->_health_regen_timer = 0.0f;` comment copy-pasted into all five branches. So the authoritative damage number depends on which table you happen to read, and (per the ProjectileMist finding) mist actually takes the SPRAY branch.

**Fix:** Delete the `*_DAMAGE` constants from `player_consts.h` and replace the whole 5-branch ladder with `this->_health -= projectile->get_player_damage();` — after `dynamic_cast`/interface-widening the collidee to `Projectile`, or by putting `get_player_damage()` on `ICollisionGameObject` with a 0 default. Fix the sign convention in `ProjectileDetails::player_damage` while doing it.

#### 2. player_consts.h is a dumping ground: per-TU dynamically-initialised strings, dead constants, and a stale duplicate of the level countdown UI block

`ArtAttack/player_consts.h:20-121` — **medium** · `design`

Merges 4 candidates. Three problems in one file.

1. **Per-TU copies.** ~13 `const std::string`s (:49-62) and six `const PlayerAnimationInfo` aggregates each holding three `std::string`s (:80-121) sit at namespace scope in a header. `const` at namespace scope gives internal linkage, so every TU that transitively includes Player.h gets its own copy — ~18 dynamically-constructed `std::string`s per TU at static-init time, before `main`, for pure compile-time data. `Player::get_animation_info` hands out references into Player.cpp's private copies; safe today, but a different address from what any other TU sees for the same logical constant. `DEFAULT_TEAM_COLOUR = colour_consts::GRAY` is worse — that is itself parsed from a hex `std::string` at static-init, a cross-header static-init-order dependency for a fixed RGB triple.

2. **Stale duplicate of level UI constants.** :71-78 declare `COUNTDOWN_TEXT`, `COUNTDOWN_FONT_NAME`, `COUNTDOWN_COLOUR`, `COUNTDOWN_SHADOW_COLOUR`, `COUNTDOWN_SCALE`, `COUNTDOWN_SHADOW_OFFSET`, `COUNTDOWN_TEXT_WIDTH/HEIGHT` — level-start UI settings with nothing to do with a Player. They duplicate `level_consts` (Level.h:35-42) with DIFFERENT values: font `gill_sans_mt_bold_72` vs `_144`, scale 1.0 vs 2.0, shadow offset {2,2} vs {5,5}. Level.cpp uses `using namespace level_consts;`, so the player copies have zero readers — and if any TU ever pulls in both using-directives, every `COUNTDOWN_*` reference becomes ambiguous.

3. **Dead constants:** `DEFAULT_COLLISION_BOUNDS` (:23), `STARTING_DX` (:24), `STARTING_VELOCITY` (:25), `JUMP_POWER` (:33) — no call sites. Spelling is also inconsistent within the file: `const std::string DEFAULT_SHEET` (:49) vs `const static std::string COUNTDOWN_TEXT` (:71); `constexpr auto DEFAULT_TEAM` hides the type for no benefit.

**Fix:** Delete the COUNTDOWN block and the four dead constants. Move to `inline constexpr std::string_view` / `inline constexpr` aggregates (C++17) so there is one object across the program with zero dynamic init. Longer term, replace the asset-name literals with a data-driven `CharacterDef { size; MovementTuning; AnimationSet; AudioCues; }` loaded from JSON, so an engine user defines a character in data rather than by editing a C++ header.

#### 3. FLT_MIN used as an 'unset' sentinel for frame_time and compared with exact != under /fp:fast

`ArtAttack/player_consts.h:14-15` — **low** · `api-design`

Merges 2 candidates.
```
// if frame_time is FLT_MIN, then the frame_time will be set to the default
float frame_time = FLT_MIN;
```
consumed at Player.cpp:66 as `if (info.frame_time != FLT_MIN) { set_frame_time(...); } else { set_frame_time_to_default(); }`.

Three problems: (1) a sentinel inside the value domain instead of an explicit optional; (2) exact float `!=` in a project built with `/fp:fast` in all four configurations, three lines of code away from `update_movement` which correctly uses `are_equal(...)` for its float comparisons; (3) `FLT_MIN` is the smallest positive NORMAL float (~1.18e-38), a perfectly legal (if absurd) frame time, and `<cfloat>` is not included by player_consts.h — it arrives transitively.

**Fix:** `std::optional<float> frame_time;` once the project moves off its implicit C++14. Until then, an explicit `bool use_default_frame_time = true;` field, or a negative default with `frame_time <= 0.0f` meaning 'use the strip default'. Add `#include <cfloat>` if the constant survives.

## `ArtAttack/Player.h`

_12 findings: 3 high, 7 medium, 2 low_

#### 1. Player inherits SpriteSheetObject/DrawObject twice (non-virtual diamond) — two divergent copies of all draw state

`ArtAttack/Player.h:63-64` — **high** · `design`

Merges 2 candidates. `class Player final : public MovingObject, public ICollisionGameObject, public AnimationObject, public TextureObject`. I confirmed `AnimationObject : public SpriteSheetObject` (AnimationObject.h:7), `TextureObject : public SpriteSheetObject` (TextureObject.h:6), `SpriteSheetObject : public DrawObject` (SpriteSheetObject.h:6), all non-virtual.

So every `Player` physically contains two `SpriteSheetObject` and two `DrawObject` subobjects: two `ResourceManager* _resource_manager`, two `_colour`, two `_draw_rotation`, two `_origin`, two `_effects`, two `_layer_depth` (DrawObject.h:36-41), two `_sheet_name`/`_element_name` (SpriteSheetObject.h:25-26). A `Player*` → `DrawObject*` conversion is ambiguous and ill-formed, so a Player can never be handled generically as a drawable — a hard blocker for the reusable-engine goal.

The two copies are deliberately initialised to different values (Player.cpp:29 passes `DEFAULT_PLAYER_COLOUR` to the AnimationObject branch, :31 passes `team_colour` to the TextureObject branch), and every access must be hand-qualified to pick a side — `TextureObject::set_effects(effects); AnimationObject::set_effects(effects);` at :83/:86 is the same value written twice or they diverge. `MovingObject` adds a third, never-rendered `_rotation` (MovingObject.h:56), which is why `respawn()`'s `MovingObject::set_rotation(0.0f)` (:996) is a visual no-op.

**Fix:** Replace inheritance with composition: `Sprite _uniform;` and `AnimatedSprite _body;` as members, each owning its own draw params, with one authoritative transform on the entity. An entity is not a sprite — it has sprites.

#### 2. Player is a god class: simulation, rendering, audio, camera, input, weapon and game rules in one type

`ArtAttack/Player.h:63-252` — **high** · `design`

Player.h declares ~90 member functions and 22 data members; Player.cpp is 1263 lines. In one type it owns: kinematics (`MovingObject` velocity/dx, `update_movement`, `do_jump`, `_air_time`), a ground/air state machine (`player_move_state`, `is_on_ground`, `is_on_ramp`, `on_no_collision`), collision response for eight directions plus ramps and jump-through platforms (`on_top_collision` … `on_structure_ramp_collision`, Player.cpp:245-639), two full sprite hierarchies plus clip selection (`calculate_animation_state`, `get_animation_info`), audio (`SoundBank* _sound_bank`, four hardcoded cue names from `player_consts`), view state that belongs to the renderer (`MattMath::Camera _camera` Player.h:140, `MattMath::Viewport _viewport` :161), input state (`PlayerInputData _input` :152), weapon ownership (`std::unique_ptr<Weapon> _primary` :142), and Splatoon rules (`_team`, `_team_colour`, `_health`, `_respawn_timer`, `_score`, per-weapon damage constants).

This is the central engine-reuse blocker for this module group: to get a moving, animated, colliding character in a different game you must take teams, respawn timers, ammo, a debug HUD flag and a splatoon damage table with it.

**Fix:** Decompose into engine parts plus a thin game script: `RigidBody2D` (position/velocity/integration), `CharacterController2D` (ground/air state machine driven by an abstract action set), `SpriteAnimator` (a state→clip table with no knowledge of 'player'), `AudioEmitter`, `CameraTarget`. `Player` then becomes ~150 lines of game glue composing them.

#### 3. Non-virtual diamond: Player physically contains two complete DrawObject subobjects

`ArtAttack/Player.h:63-64` — **high** · `design`

`class Player final : public MovingObject, public ICollisionGameObject, public AnimationObject, public TextureObject`. I traced the chain: `AnimationObject : public SpriteSheetObject` (AnimationObject.h:7), `TextureObject : public SpriteSheetObject` (TextureObject.h:6), `SpriteSheetObject : public DrawObject` (SpriteSheetObject.h:6) — all non-virtual inheritance.

So a `Player` contains **two** `DrawObject` subobjects: two `_resource_manager`, two `_colour`, two `_draw_rotation`, two `_origin`, two `_effects`, two `_layer_depth`, plus two `_sheet_name`/`_element_name` from `SpriteSheetObject`. Any unqualified `set_colour(...)` or `get_origin()` inside Player is ambiguous, and every qualified one silently mutates only half the object — which is why the code is littered with `this->AnimationObject::draw(...)` / `this->TextureObject::draw(...)` (Player.cpp:91-95, Structure.cpp:35-38, ProjectileBall.cpp:47-50).

`Player` also mixes in `MovingObject`'s `_rotation`, giving one Player three rotation floats for one concept. `Projectile.h:19-21` has the same shape.

I am flagging this from the MovingObject/interface review because it is the structural reason the object layer is unusable as engine code.

**Fix:** Stop expressing "has a sprite" and "has an animation" as base classes. Introduce one `Sprite` value type owning transform + tint + origin + effects + layer depth, with a source that is either a static frame or an animation strip, and hold it by composition (`Sprite _sprite;`). Player then has one colour, one origin, one rotation, and `draw` needs no qualification to disambiguate.

#### 4. Player.h includes CollisionTools.h for nothing and pulls the audio stack, rapidjson and D3D into every consumer

`ArtAttack/Player.h:4-14` — **medium** · `header-hygiene`

Merges 2 candidates. `#include "CollisionTools.h"` (Player.h:14) — `CollisionTools` appears nowhere in the header; the only uses are in Player.cpp. `#include "SoundBank.h"` (:13) exists solely for the raw member `SoundBank* _sound_bank = nullptr;` (:168), which a forward declaration satisfies; SoundBank.h itself drags in `<Audio.h>` and `rapidjson/document.h`. `#include "Weapon.h"` (:8) pulls `ProjectileBuilder.h`, `WeaponDetails.h`, `TextureObject.h` → `ResourceManager.h` → D3D.

`Level.h` includes `Player.h`, so every translation unit that touches a level parses the JSON library, the audio library, D3D and the whole weapon/projectile system. With all first-party sources sitting flat in one directory and no library target, there is no place where 'engine' ends and 'game' begins — Player.h is where they fuse.

**Fix:** Drop the `CollisionTools.h` include outright and forward-declare `class SoundBank;`. Structurally: split into `engine/` (math, shapes, collision world, sprites, input, audio, resources, threading) and `game/` (player, weapons, projectiles, paint, menus), build `engine` as a static library, and forbid engine headers from including anything under `game/`. That boundary is what makes 'reusable engine' checkable rather than aspirational.

#### 5. player_move_state conflates 'what surface am I on' with 'what motion am I performing'

`ArtAttack/Player.h:22-32` — **medium** · `design`

One enum mixes two orthogonal axes: contact (`ON_GROUND`, `ON_DROP_DOWN_GROUND`, `ON_RAMP_LEFT`, `ON_RAMP_RIGHT`, `ON_CEILING`) and motion (`JUMPING`, `DROPPING_DOWN`, `IN_AIR`). Consequently every 'am I grounded' test is a four-way OR, written three times: `is_on_ground()` (Player.cpp:1238-1244), `is_on_ramp()` (:1246-1250) and again inline in `on_no_collision` (:1256-1259) — which is precisely why `ON_CEILING` was forgotten in the third copy.

The surface identity is also encoded in the collision TYPE of the thing touched (`STRUCTURE_RAMP_LEFT`/`RIGHT`), which is what forces `on_structure_ramp_collision` to be a 115-line type/direction ladder with an empty branch and four copy-pasted bodies, and what forces the `RAMP_GRAVITY_MULTIPLIER = 20.0f` hack at Player.cpp:820-828 (2000 × 20 = 40,000 px/s² to keep the player stuck to a slope).

**Fix:** Split into a `GroundContact { bool grounded; Vector2F normal; const ICollisionGameObject* surface; }` produced by the collision system — the normal makes ramps fall out for free, deleting the RAMP_LEFT/RIGHT collision types, the per-ramp branch and the gravity multiplier — plus a small `motion_state { grounded, jumping, falling, dropping }`.

#### 6. Player constructor takes 16 positional parameters, with two adjacent same-typed enums that can be silently swapped

`ArtAttack/Player.h:67-83` — **medium** · `api-design`

The signature mixes geometry, animation info, a service pointer, identity (`player_num`, `team`), two `wep_type` enums PLUS an already-built `unique_ptr<Weapon>`, colour, viewport, a `const float* dt`, respawn position, and five sprite-drawing defaults. The call site (PlayerBuilder.cpp:40-60) is a 20-line unlabelled argument list.

Two specific hazards I verified: `wep_type primary` and `wep_type secondary` are separated only by the weapon pointer, so swapping them compiles silently; and `primary` is passed alongside the already-constructed `primary_weapon`, so the same fact is supplied twice and can disagree. Four parameters (`rotation`, `origin`, `effects`, `layer_depth`) are pure pass-through to the two sprite bases and are never supplied by any caller.

The body then does its own content lookup: `this->_sound_bank = resource_manager->get_sound_bank(SOUND_BANK);` where `SOUND_BANK` is the literal `"sound_bank_1"` — the entity hardcodes which asset bundle exists.

**Fix:** Take one `CharacterDef` (size, movement tuning, animation set, audio cues) plus a spawn descriptor `{position, team, player_num, viewport}` and already-resolved dependencies, with the builder doing all name→resource resolution. Drop `wep_type primary` — ask the weapon. Drop `wep_type secondary` until a secondary weapon exists.

#### 7. Player's per-frame state is only valid if the caller invokes six methods in one exact, undocumented order

`ArtAttack/Player.h:85-137` — **medium** · `design`

Merges 2 candidates. To advance one player by one frame `Level` must call, in this order: `set_player_input` (Level.cpp:192), `update` (:193), `set_camera` (:201), `update_weapon_and_get_projectiles` (:205), the whole collision pass (:222-243) including `on_no_collision` (:247), then `update_weapon_position` (:254) and `update_prev_rectangle` (:255). None of it is expressed in a type or a comment; it lives only in the caller.

The failure modes are silent, not loud:
- `on_structure_jump_through_collision` decides pass-through by `this->_prev_rectangle.get_bottom() <= other_rect.get_top()` (:372). Call `update_prev_rectangle()` before the collision pass instead of after and `_prev_rectangle == _rectangle`, so the player falls through every drop-down platform.
- `update_weapon_position()` must run after collision resolution has moved `_rectangle`, or the weapon renders at the pre-resolution position.
- `on_no_collision()` is the only thing that transitions the player out of `ON_GROUND`; omitting it leaves the player able to jump in mid-air forever. It exists purely so the caller can report 'I checked every structure and none touched you' — information the collision system already has and should not be relaying by hand.

For a reusable engine this is the opposite of an interface: the entity's invariants are the caller's responsibility.

**Fix:** Collapse the sequence into the entity: one `update(const FrameContext&)` that snapshots its own previous transform and repositions its own weapon, with grounded-ness derived from the collision system's contact set for this frame. Projectile spawning should go through a spawner/command queue rather than a return value the caller must remember to drain.

#### 8. Player has two names for its input setter and a `_primary` member whose getter returns something else entirely

`ArtAttack/Player.h:142, 217-218, 99, 230` — **medium** · `naming` · confidence: certain

Two distinct defects in one class:
  1. `std::unique_ptr<Weapon> _primary = nullptr;` (line 142) is the weapon *object*, but `wep_type get_primary() const;` (217) and `void set_primary(wep_type primary);` (218) operate on `_primary_type` (line 158). So `_primary` and `get_primary()` refer to different members of different types. A reader calling `get_primary()` expecting the Weapon gets an enum.
  2. `void set_player_input(const PlayerInputData& input);` is public at line 99 while `void set_input(const PlayerInputData& input);` is private at line 230, and the getter is `get_input()` at line 122. Three names, one concept.
Also in the same header: the ctor parameter is `const MattMath::Viewport& view_port` (line 76, and `Player.cpp:18`) while the member and setter are `_viewport` / `set_viewport` (161, 225) - the same word spelled two ways inside one class.

**Fix:** `_primary` -> `_primary_weapon`; `get_primary`/`set_primary` -> `get_primary_weapon_type`/`set_primary_weapon_type` (same for `_secondary`). Collapse `set_player_input` and `set_input` into one `set_input`. Fix `view_port` -> `viewport`.

#### 9. Frame time is a raw const float* to a heap float, stored twice per Player; team colour stored three times; viewport is a stale snapshot

`ArtAttack/Player.h:170, 160-161` — **medium** · `design`

Merges 4 candidates. Three separate duplications of the same state on one object:

1. `const float* _dt = nullptr;` (Player.h:170), dereferenced blind in `float Player::get_dt() const { return *this->_dt; }` (:692-695). The pointee is a single heap float — `Game.h` holds `std::unique_ptr<float> _dt`, `Game.cpp:244-245` does `make_unique<float>(0.f)` and hands out `.get()`, and `Game::update` writes through it at Game.cpp:90. The same pointer is ALSO stored in `AnimationObject::_dt` (AnimationObject.h:49, initialised from Player.cpp:27) and dereferenced independently there. Two non-owning copies of one pointer, both unvalidatable, in exchange for a heap allocation for one float. Nothing in Player.h documents that it is non-owning, must outlive the Player, or must be non-null.

2. `MattMath::Colour _team_colour` (Player.h:160) is the same value that is passed into `TextureObject` (stored as `DrawObject::_colour`) at Player.cpp:31 and into the `Weapon` at PlayerBuilder.cpp:50. Three copies, all write-once, none coherently updatable — `set_team_colour` touches only Player's and is itself dead.

3. `MattMath::Viewport _viewport` (Player.h:161) is a construction-time snapshot of `viewport_manager->get_player_viewport(setting.num)` (PlayerBuilder.cpp:57-58). `ViewportManager::get_player_viewport` computes it from the manager's CURRENT `_layout` and resolution (ViewportManager.cpp:84-88) — a derived value, not an identity. The layout demonstrably changes underneath it: `Level::draw_zoom_out_level_component` calls `_viewport_manager->set_layout(screen_layout::ONE_PLAYER)` (Level.cpp:619) and never restores it. `Player::set_viewport` exists but is private and never called. The only reader is `DebugText.cpp:28`, which therefore reports a stale viewport after any zoom-out or resolution change.

**Fix:** Pass dt by value — `void update(float dt)` on `IGameObject` — deleting `Player::_dt`, `AnimationObject::_dt`, `Weapon::_dt`, `Level::_dt`, the `float*` in `GameData` and the `unique_ptr<float>` in `Game`, plus a whole class of lifetime questions, and making the engine testable with a fixed dt. Store the team colour once. Delete `_viewport`/`get_viewport`/`set_viewport` and have `DebugText` ask `ViewportManager` for `player->get_player_num()`.

#### 10. Sixteen private accessors with no callers, plus two dead members and a duplicate input setter

`ArtAttack/Player.h:212-246` — **medium** · `design`

Merges 4 candidates. I grepped the whole tree for each. These `Player` members have exactly one occurrence — their own definition — and are private so unreachable from outside: `set_player_num` (Player.cpp:1167), `set_team` (:1122), `get_primary` (:1142), `set_primary` (:1147), `get_secondary` (:1152), `set_secondary` (:1157), `set_team_colour` (:1127), `set_viewport` (:1132), `set_input` (:1137), `set_health` (:1087), `alter_health` (:1092), `set_respawn_timer` (:1097), `alter_respawn_timer` (:1102), `set_score` (:1107), `alter_score` (:1112), `get_score` (:1117), `set_showing_debug` (:1162). ~90 lines of dead code.

Two members die with them: `int _score = 0;` (Player.h:148) is never read or written outside its three dead accessors — the per-player scoring the header advertises does not exist. `wep_type _secondary_type` (Player.h:159) is written once by the constructor and never read; `PlayerBuilder.cpp:55` hardcodes `wep_type::GRENADE_STD` for it, so there is no secondary-weapon feature at all.

`void set_input(const PlayerInputData&)` (Player.h:230, Player.cpp:1137-1140) is byte-identical to the public `set_player_input` (Player.h:99, Player.cpp:922-925) — `this->_input = input;` twice under two names and two access levels. Two setters for one field becomes a correctness hazard the moment one grows a side effect.

This matters beyond tidiness: a reader of the 255-line header cannot tell which dozen members actually participate in behaviour. Note the inconsistency it already creates — `on_projectile_collision` writes `this->_health -= SPRAY_DAMAGE;` directly (:652) rather than using `alter_health`.

**Fix:** Delete all sixteen accessors, `_score`, `_secondary_type` and the `wep_type secondary` constructor parameter. Reintroduce a setter only when a caller actually exists.

#### 11. Player owns a unique_ptr<Weapon> but declares no special members, and never null-checks the weapon it is handed

`ArtAttack/Player.h:63-83` — **low** · `memory-safety`

`Player` owns `std::unique_ptr<Weapon> _primary` (Player.h:142) plus three raw non-owning pointers and declares no destructor, no copy operations and no move operations. The implicit copy is deleted by the `unique_ptr` — correct, but by accident. The implicit MOVE operations are declared and not deleted (every base is at least copyable), so `Player p2 = std::move(p1);` compiles and leaves `p1` fully live with `_primary == nullptr`, while every use of `_primary` is unguarded (Player.cpp:89, 94, 643, 745, 1000, 1050, 1179).

The constructor also takes `std::unique_ptr<Weapon> primary_weapon` and stores it (:32) without checking for null, even though the class dereferences it at seven sites and nothing in the API says a weapon is mandatory.

Graded low, not medium: Players live in a `vector<unique_ptr<Player>>` and are never relocated, and `PlayerBuilder` always supplies a weapon, so neither hole is currently reachable.

**Fix:** Declare intent explicitly — `Player(const Player&) = delete; Player& operator=(const Player&) = delete; Player(Player&&) = delete; Player& operator=(Player&&) = delete;` — and throw/assert in the constructor body if `_primary == nullptr`, so the invariant is enforced once instead of assumed at seven call sites.

#### 12. get_velocity is overridden only to widen protected access to public

`ArtAttack/Player.h:104` — **low** · `design`

`const MattMath::Vector2F& get_velocity() const override;` is declared in Player's PUBLIC section and its body is a bare forward: `return MovingObject::get_velocity();` (Player.cpp:935-938). It changes no behaviour — it exists solely because `MovingObject`'s accessors are `protected` and `DebugText.cpp:25` needs to read the velocity. That is access laundering dressed as polymorphism, and it is the only override of any of the 30 `MovingObject` virtuals in the entire codebase.

**Fix:** Drop `virtual` from the `MovingObject` accessor block, make the getters public and the mutators protected, and delete `Player::get_velocity`. Then remove the `MovingObject::` qualification from every call site in Player.cpp (they suppress dispatch anyway).

## `ArtAttack/PlayerBuilder.cpp`

_7 findings: 3 high, 2 medium, 2 low_

#### 1. Spawn points chosen with the global player index into per-team spawn arrays; unchecked operator[] on JSON data

`ArtAttack/PlayerBuilder.cpp:23-37, 64` — **high** · `correctness`

Merges 5 candidates. `build_players` keeps one counter `i` incremented once per player (:64) but uses it to index two separate per-team arrays (:32, :36):

```
if (setting.team == player_team::A) { position = team_a_spawns[i]; }
else                                { position = team_b_spawns[i]; }
```

With teams ordered A,B,A,B the team-A players take `team_a_spawns[0]` and `[2]` while `[1]` and `[3]` are never used. The correct index is a per-team running counter. This is a live behavioural bug today, not just latent.

The bounds hazard is real but I verified it is NOT currently reachable: `team_a_spawns`/`team_b_spawns` come straight from level JSON via `LevelLoadedInfo::get_team_a_spawns()` with no size validation and `operator[]` is unchecked, but all three shipped levels declare exactly 4 spawns per team (I parsed close_quarters.json, king_of_the_hill.json, turbulence.json — all `{team_a: 4, team_b: 4}`) and the max player count is 4, so `i` maxes at 3. Any level authored with fewer spawns for one team is an immediate OOB read feeding `Player::_respawn_position` for the whole match.

Also verified: `MenuPlayerSettings::team` defaults to `player_team::NONE` and `num` to `-1` (MenuPlayerSettings.h:9-11); the `else` branch silently treats NONE as team B, and `team_colours.get_team_colour(NONE)` at :50/:56 then throws mid-build.

**Fix:** Track `team_a_index`/`team_b_index` separately, switch explicitly on `setting.team` with an error branch for `NONE`, and validate up front that each team's spawn list is at least as long as that team's player count — throwing a diagnostic that names the level file — rather than relying on `operator[]`.

#### 2. Per-team spawn arrays are indexed with a shared global player counter, unchecked, and team NONE falls into team B

`ArtAttack/PlayerBuilder.cpp:26-37` — **high** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

```cpp
int i = 0;
for (auto& setting : settings.get_player_settings()) {
    Vector2F position = Vector2F::ZERO;
    if (setting.team == player_team::A) position = team_a_spawns[i];
    else                                position = team_b_spawns[i];
    ...
    i++;
}
```

Three problems in seven lines:
1. `i` counts *all* players, not players on that team. With players [A, B, A, B] team A uses `team_a_spawns[0]` and `[2]` while `team_a_spawns[1]` is never used — spawn point assignment is effectively arbitrary and the level author cannot reason about it.
2. `std::vector::operator[]` with no bounds check against `.size()`. The three shipping levels each declare exactly 4 spawns per team (verified in king_of_the_hill.json, turbulence.json, close_quarters.json) and the menu caps at 4 players, so it doesn't overflow *today* — but any level authored with 2 spawns, or any future 8-player mode, is a silent out-of-bounds read with no diagnostic. The level format has no way to declare its supported player count.
3. `MenuPlayerSettings::team` defaults to `player_team::NONE` (MenuPlayerSettings.h:9). The `else` branch swallows NONE and gives it a team-B spawn rather than rejecting it.

**Fix:** Keep separate `size_t a_index`/`b_index` counters, `switch` on the team with an explicit error for `NONE`, and use `.at()` (or check `size()` up front and throw naming the level and the required spawn count).

#### 3. A player left on 'no team' in team select spawns at team B's point and then throws during level build

`ArtAttack/PlayerBuilder.cpp:26-60` — **high** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

`MenuPlayerSettings::team` defaults to `player_team::NONE` (ArtAttack/MenuPlayerSettings.h:9). The team-select screen lets a player sit on the centre icon (which *is* `player_team::NONE` — MainMenu.cpp:1258-1290) and confirm: `MainMenuTeamSelect::all_players_confirmed()` (MainMenu.cpp:1236-1246) checks only `confirmation_state`, never that a team was chosen, then `set_level_settings()` (MainMenu.cpp:1224-1235) writes NONE straight into `MenuLevelSettings`.

`PlayerBuilder::build_players` then does:

    if (setting.team == player_team::A) position = team_a_spawns[i];
    else                                position = team_b_spawns[i];

so the NONE player is silently placed at team B's spawn (king_of_the_hill.json:30-48, e.g. (5752, 4870)) — inside the enemy spawn room. Two lines later, `team_colours.get_team_colour(setting.team)` (PlayerBuilder.cpp:50 and :56) reaches `TeamColour::get_team_colour` (ArtAttack/TeamColour.cpp:13-24) whose `default: throw std::exception("Invalid team.");` fires. Uncaught → process terminates on "start match". Even if that were fixed, `Player::get_collision_object_type()` (Player.cpp) and `Projectile::is_matching_collision_object_type` (Projectile.cpp:110-118) both throw on `player_team::NONE`.

(The 1-player path is safe — MainMenu.cpp:905 explicitly does `set_player_team(0, player_team::A)` and `set_player_num(0, 0)` before skipping team select. Only 2-4 player games are affected.)

**Fix:** Either forbid confirming on NONE in `MainMenuTeamSelect` (require `team != NONE` in `all_players_confirmed`), or drop NONE from `player_team` and model 'unassigned' as a separate menu-only state. The `if (A) … else …` in PlayerBuilder should be an explicit switch that rejects NONE rather than aliasing it to team B.

#### 4. PlayerBuilder depends on menu types and hardcodes per-player configuration, so customisation is impossible by construction

`ArtAttack/PlayerBuilder.cpp:13-67` — **medium** · `design`

`PlayerBuilder.h:5` includes `MenuLevelSettings.h`, so constructing a gameplay entity depends on the menu system's state object — a UI type reaching into entity construction. In the body, the secondary weapon is the literal `wep_type::GRENADE_STD` (:55) and appearance is the literal `DEFAULT_ANIMATION_INFO` (:42), so no per-player customisation is possible even though the constructor accepts both.

The class is also called a Builder but is a one-shot factory function with six parameters and one member, and that member is pointless — see the WeaponBuilder finding.

**Fix:** Take a plain `const std::vector<PlayerSpawnRequest>&` (team, player_num, weapon, appearance) that neither the menu nor the level loader owns. Secondary weapon and appearance come from the request, not from literals in the factory.

#### 5. Global player counter indexes per-team spawn arrays with no bounds check; safe only by coincidence of the shipped data

`ArtAttack/PlayerBuilder.cpp:26-37` — **medium** · `robustness` · confidence: certain

int i = 0;
    for (auto& setting : settings.get_player_settings())
    {
        if (setting.team == player_team::A) position = team_a_spawns[i];
        else                                position = team_b_spawns[i];
        ...
        i++;
    }

`i` is a *global* player index, incremented for every player regardless of team, yet it indexes per-team arrays with unchecked `std::vector::operator[]`. Two consequences:

1. Spawn points are not used contiguously. With P0=A, P1=B, P2=A, P3=B, team A uses `team_a_spawns[0]` and `[2]` while `[1]` and `[3]` go unused, and likewise for B. The level author's intent (four adjacent spawn slots per team, x = 10/72/134/196 in king_of_the_hill.json:11-29) is not honoured.

2. Out-of-range is prevented only by an undocumented coincidence. I checked every level file on disk: all seven (levels/king_of_the_hill.json, close_quarters.json, turbulence.json and levels/unused/base.json, level_0.json, structure_test_old.json, test_1.json) declare exactly 4 entries in both `team_a` and `team_b`, and `MenuLevelSettings::set_player_count` (MenuLevelSettings.cpp:9-25) sizes `_player_settings` to the menu's max of 4 (MainMenu.cpp:903-950). So today `i` is always 0..3 and in range. Any level authored with 3 spawns per team — which nothing forbids and no code validates — is a silent out-of-bounds read on the first 4-player match.

**Fix:** Track separate per-team counters and use `.at()`, or better: assert at load time in `LevelLoadedInfo` that both spawn arrays have at least MAX_PLAYERS entries and fail the level load with a clear message.

#### 6. PlayerBuilder heap-allocates a stateless WeaponBuilder in order to make a static call

`ArtAttack/PlayerBuilder.cpp:8-11, 47` — **low** · `design`

Merges 2 candidates. `PlayerBuilder::PlayerBuilder() { this->_weapon_builder = std::make_unique<WeaponBuilder>(); }` backs `std::unique_ptr<WeaponBuilder> _weapon_builder = nullptr;` (PlayerBuilder.h:23), used as `this->_weapon_builder->build_weapon(...)` (:47).

`WeaponBuilder` has no data members at all and its single function is `static` (WeaponBuilder.h:10-22). So this is a heap allocation, an owning pointer and a pointer dereference purely to make a static call. It also silently makes `PlayerBuilder` non-copyable and leaves a nullable member that the `const` `build_players` dereferences without checking. The constructor also assigns in the body rather than in the member-init list.

**Fix:** Delete the member and the constructor, and write `WeaponBuilder::build_weapon(...)` at :47. Since `WeaponBuilder` is a stateless bag of one static function, it should be a namespace, not a class.

#### 7. Three by-value accessors deep-copy whole vectors, and a range-for binds non-const refs into the temporary

`ArtAttack/PlayerBuilder.cpp:23-27` — **low** · `performance`

Merges 2 candidates.
```
const std::vector<Vector2F> team_a_spawns = load_info->get_team_a_spawns();
const std::vector<Vector2F> team_b_spawns = load_info->get_team_b_spawns();
...
for (auto& setting : settings.get_player_settings())
```
`LevelLoadedInfo::get_team_a_spawns()`/`get_team_b_spawns()` (LevelLoadedInfo.h:17-18) and `MenuLevelSettings::get_player_settings()` (MenuLevelSettings.h:14) all return their members by value, so each call deep-copies a vector.

The range-for then binds `auto&` (non-const) into a lifetime-extended temporary. That is legal — the range-for's `auto&& __range` extends it — but it is exactly the shape that becomes a dangling-reference bug when someone hoists the call or extracts the loop body into a helper, and the non-const `auto&` falsely suggests the settings are being modified in place (any mutation would be silently discarded).

**Fix:** Make the three accessors return `const std::vector<T>&`, then write `const auto& team_a_spawns = ...;` and `for (const auto& setting : ...)`. Zero copies, and no reliance on lifetime extension.

## `ArtAttack/PlayerInput.cpp`

_7 findings: 2 high, 3 medium, 2 low_

#### 1. update_and_get_player_inputs returns a positionally compacted vector that Level indexes by player ordinal

`ArtAttack/PlayerInput.cpp:119-138` — **high** · `correctness`

Merges 5 candidates. `update_and_get_player_inputs` only pushes an entry for pads where `current[i].connected` is true (:129-134), discarding the pad index. The sole gameplay consumer indexes it by the player's slot with unchecked `operator[]`:

```
int player_index = 0;
for (const auto& object : *this->_player_objects) {
    object->set_player_input(player_inputs[player_index]);   // Level.cpp:192
    ... player_index++;
}
```

Two failures. (1) Identity shift: if pad 0 drops, pad 1 drives player 0. (2) Out-of-range read: `player_inputs.size() < _player_objects->size()` after a drop-out, so `player_inputs[player_index]` reads past the end — UB, garbage `x_movement`/`jump_pressed`/`toggle_pause_menu` copied into `Player::_input`.

The escape hatch is dead: `PlayerInputData::connection` defaults to `DISCONNECTED` (PlayerInputData.h:19) but `calculate_player_input` unconditionally sets `CONNECTED` (PlayerInput.cpp:111), and disconnected pads are never emitted, so no consumer can ever observe a drop-out. `GameLevel::check_for_pause_input` (GameStates.cpp:348-359) returns the vector index and it is used as a player number for the pause-menu owner, so that is wrong too after a drop-out (it does at least bound its own loop by `.size()`).

Secondary, also verified: on reconnect `_prev_inputs[i]` was overwritten with a default-constructed `RawPlayerInput` at :135 during the disconnected frames, so a button held across the disconnect reads as a fresh press.

**Fix:** Return a fixed-size, slot-indexed container — `std::array<PlayerInputData, MAX_PADS>` — emitting an entry for every pad slot with `connection` set correctly and axes zeroed when absent. Then index == pad index always, and `Player` can react to a drop-out (freeze / prompt to reconnect) instead of being silently reassigned.

#### 2. Input vectors are compacted by connection state, destroying the pad-slot to player mapping; the connection_state field that exists to prevent this is dead

`ArtAttack/PlayerInput.cpp:119-138` — **high** · `design` · confidence: certain

Both input pumps drop disconnected slots instead of reporting them:

```cpp
std::vector<PlayerInputData> result;
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)
{
    if (current[i].connected)
    {
        result.push_back(calculate_player_input(current[i], this->_prev_inputs[i]));  // PlayerInput.cpp:131-133
    }
    this->_prev_inputs[i] = current[i];
}
return result;
```

Identical shape in `MenuInput::update_and_get_menu_inputs`, MenuInput.cpp:138-149.

The returned index is therefore a *rank among currently-connected pads*, not a pad identity, and it silently renumbers whenever the set of connected pads changes. Meanwhile `PlayerInputData::connection` (PlayerInputData.h:19) and `ProcessedMenuInput::connection` (MenuInput.h:41) default to `DISCONNECTED` and are hardcoded to `CONNECTED` at PlayerInput.cpp:111 and MenuInput.cpp:127 - because they are only ever set on the path that already knows the pad is connected. `connection_state` (connection_state.h:4-8) is written but never read anywhere in the project (grep confirms zero consumers). The mechanism designed to solve this exact problem is present and inert.

Re-plug into a different slot: unplug the pad in slot 0 during a 2-player match and plug it into slot 2. Before: slots {0,1} -> indices {0,1}. After: slots {1,2} -> indices {0,1}. The pad that was player 1 is now index 1 and drives player 2's character; the pad that was player 2 is now index 0 and drives player 1's. Both players' controls silently swap, with no event, no message, and no way to detect it - `Player::_player_num` (Player.cpp:1077) is assigned from the menu (`set_player_num(i, i)`, MainMenu.cpp:1233) and never correlated with a hardware slot.

This is the single root cause of the Level.cpp:192 and PauseMenu.cpp:53 out-of-bounds reads and of the team-select deadlock.

**Fix:** Return `std::array<PlayerInputData, GamePad::MAX_PLAYER_COUNT>` indexed by XInput slot, with `connection` correctly set per slot and axes zeroed for disconnected pads. Add an explicit binding step ("press A to join") that records slot -> player, and surface a `pad_disconnected(slot)` event so gameplay can pause and prompt instead of reading garbage. For a reusable engine this belongs behind an `IInputDevice`/`InputSnapshot` abstraction, not an XInput-shaped `std::vector`.

#### 3. Stick deadzone applied twice and never rescaled, so x_movement jumps discontinuously from 0 to 0.5

`ArtAttack/PlayerInput.cpp:86-97` — **medium** · `correctness`

`GetState(gamepad_num, GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR)` (:20) already applies XInput's deadzone AND rescales the surviving range to 0..1. The code then applies a second, larger threshold on top without rescaling:
```
if (std::fabs(current.left_analog_stick.x) > STICK_DEADZONE)   // 0.5f
{ result.x_movement = current.left_analog_stick.x; }           // raw value, not remapped
else { result.x_movement = 0.0f; }
```
So `x_movement` snaps from 0 straight to ±0.5 — half the stick's usable travel is dead and there is no fine speed control. `X_INITIAL_VELOCITY * x_input` (Player.cpp:769) means the smallest possible starting speed is exactly half the maximum starting speed. The same untranslated 0.5 threshold gates the aim stick at :97.

**Fix:** Pick one deadzone. If you keep the manual one, request `GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_NONE` and rescale: `x = sign(x) * (|x| - DZ) / (1 - DZ)`. Also 0.5 is enormous for a movement axis — 0.15-0.25 is typical.

#### 4. Left-stick deadzone applied twice and never rescaled - horizontal movement steps discontinuously from 0 to half speed

`ArtAttack/PlayerInput.cpp:86-93` — **medium** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

Confirmed - the prior allegation is correct. Two deadzones are stacked:

1. PlayerInput.cpp:20 requests DirectXTK's own radial deadzone: `this->_gamepad->GetState(gamepad_num, GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR)`. DirectXTK's `ApplyStickDeadZone`/`ApplyLinearDeadZone` removes `XINPUT_GAMEPAD_LEFT_THUMB_DEADZONE` (7849/32767 ~= 0.24) radially and *rescales the remainder back to the full [-1,1] range*, so what comes out already starts at 0 and reaches 1 at full deflection.

2. On top of that, `calculate_player_input` applies a second, larger cut with no rescale:

```cpp
if (std::fabs(current.left_analog_stick.x) > STICK_DEADZONE)   // STICK_DEADZONE = 0.5f, PlayerInput.h:12
{
    result.x_movement = current.left_analog_stick.x;           // PlayerInput.cpp:88 - passed through raw
}
else
{
    result.x_movement = 0.0f;
}
```

Resulting response curve for `x_movement`: flat 0 for the first ~62% of physical stick travel (0.24 native + 0.5 of the remaining 0.76), then an instantaneous jump to 0.5, then linear 0.5 -> 1.0 over the last ~38%. Half the usable analogue range is thrown away and the useful range is compressed into a third of the stick's travel.

This is not cosmetic - `x_movement` is a direct velocity multiplier, so the discontinuity is felt as a lurch:

```cpp
MovingObject::set_velocity_x(X_INITIAL_VELOCITY * x_input);     // Player.cpp:769
MovingObject::alter_velocity_x(X_ACCELERATION * dt * x_input);  // Player.cpp:774, 783, 792-793, 798-799
```

A player can never walk slower than half speed; the character snaps from stationary to 0.5x the instant the threshold is crossed.

Inconsistently, the *raw* unfiltered `left_analog_stick` is also copied through at PlayerInput.cpp:113 and read directly for the drop-through-platform check (`this->_input.left_analog_stick.y > DROP_DOWN_ANALOG_THRESHOLD`, Player.cpp:762, threshold 0.8 at player_consts.h:39) - so the Y axis uses a different threshold with a different filtering path than X, in the same struct.

The right stick at PlayerInput.cpp:96-103 is defensible: it thresholds on `length()` then `normalize()`s, so the magnitude discontinuity does not matter for an aim direction. Only the left stick is broken.

**Fix:** Either drop the second deadzone entirely (DirectXTK's DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR has already done the job) or, if a larger deadzone is wanted, rescale so the response is continuous: `x = (fabs(x) - DZ) / (1.0f - DZ) * sign(x)` clamped at 0. Apply the same treatment consistently to both axes rather than leaving Y on a raw comparison in Player.cpp.

#### 5. PlayerInput and MenuInput are the same class written twice; both hardcode the pad count four times each

`ArtAttack/PlayerInput.cpp:119-137` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

`PlayerInput::update_and_get_player_inputs` (PlayerInput.cpp:119-137) and `MenuInput::update_and_get_menu_inputs` (MenuInput.cpp:131-149) are structurally identical 19-line functions — poll 4 pads into a `Raw*[4]`, for each connected pad run `calculate_*_input(current[i], _prev_inputs[i])`, push, then `_prev_inputs[i] = current[i]`. The two constructors (PlayerInput.cpp:8-15, MenuInput.cpp:7-14) are also the same loop. Both files hardcode the literal `4` four times rather than using `std::size(_prev_inputs)` or a named constant, and both classes carry their own `GamePad* _gamepad` and `_prev_inputs[4]`.

**Fix:** Extract `template <class Raw, class Processed> class GamepadPoller` holding `GamePad*`, `std::array<Raw, MAX_PADS> _prev`, and one `poll(F&& process)` that does the loop; `PlayerInput` and `MenuInput` then reduce to their `get_raw_input` and `calculate_*_input` functions. Replace the four literal `4`s per file with one `constexpr int MAX_PADS`.

#### 6. Raw C array with the literal 4 repeated five times, a redundant constructor loop, and a per-frame heap allocation

`ArtAttack/PlayerInput.cpp:11-14, 119-138` — **low** · `modern-cpp`

Merges 3 candidates. `RawPlayerInput _prev_inputs[4]` (PlayerInput.h:34), `RawPlayerInput current[4]` (:121) and two `for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` loops (:122, :127) — the magic 4 appears five times with no named constant, even though `player_input_consts` (PlayerInput.h:8-13) is the obvious home for a `MAX_PADS`.

The constructor body is dead code: `for (auto& _prev_input : this->_prev_inputs) { _prev_input = RawPlayerInput(); }` — `RawPlayerInput` has NSDMIs on every member (PlayerInput.h:17-25), so the array is already correctly initialised before the body runs; the loop default-constructs and copy-assigns four times for nothing. The loop variable is named `_prev_input`, a leading-underscore name the rest of the codebase reserves for members.

`update_and_get_player_inputs` also constructs a fresh `std::vector<PlayerInputData>` every frame (:126) with no `reserve`, so it heap-allocates and reallocates (1→2→4) on the way to at most four elements, every frame, forever — and the result is copied again into `GameLevel::update`'s local (GameStates.cpp:141-142).

**Fix:** `std::array<RawPlayerInput, player_input_consts::MAX_PADS> _prev_inputs{};`, iterate with `.size()`, and delete the constructor body entirely: `PlayerInput(DirectX::GamePad* gamepad) : _gamepad(gamepad) {}`. Returning a fixed-size `std::array` also fixes the index-mapping bug reported separately and removes the allocation.

#### 7. Pause and debug toggles fire on button RELEASE while their comments say press, and three if/else blocks that reduce to one assignment each

`ArtAttack/PlayerInput.cpp:52-84` — **low** · `correctness`

Merges 2 candidates.
```
// pause menu is on key press
bool pause_menu = !current.pause_menu && previous.pause_menu;
// show debug is on key press
bool show_debug = !current.show_debug && previous.show_debug;
```
`!current && previous` is the FALLING edge — the button was down last frame and is up now. That is release, not press. The correct rising-edge test is what the jump handling three lines above gets right: `bool jump_button_pressed = current.jump_button && !previous.jump_button;` (:45). So Start and Back are inverted relative to A: the pause menu opens when you let go of Start, and the debug toggle (consumed at Player.cpp:726-729) fires on release of Back.

Graded low rather than medium because it is functional — a one-frame-plus-hold-duration lag, arguably even deliberate for the pause menu to avoid double-triggering into the menu. But the comments explicitly claim 'key press', and being inconsistent with the jump edge detection in the same function is a maintenance trap.

The surrounding shape is also noise: three consecutive `if (x) { result.y = true; } else { result.y = false; }` blocks (:54-84) — 27 lines that say `result.y = x;` three times, in a function whose other assignments (:43-48) are already written directly. Line 82's `else` brace is indented to column 0.

**Fix:** Either fix both to `current.X && !previous.X` to match jump, or correct the comments so the intent is unambiguous. Collapse the three blocks to direct assignments.

## `ArtAttack/PlayerInput.h`

_4 findings: 1 high, 2 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. Edge-detection history is per-consumer and only advances while that consumer is the active state

`ArtAttack/PlayerInput.h:34` — **high** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

`PlayerInput::_prev_inputs[4]` (ArtAttack/PlayerInput.h:34) and `MenuInput::_prev_inputs[4]` (ArtAttack/MenuInput.h:50) are each written only by their own `update_and_get_*_inputs()` (`this->_prev_inputs[i] = current[i];` PlayerInput.cpp:135, MenuInput.cpp:147). `GameLevel` owns one of each (ArtAttack/GameStates.h:59, 63) but polls `_player_input` ONLY in the ACTIVE branch (GameStates.cpp:141-142) and `_menu_input` ONLY while a pause/results/end page is updating. So "previous" does not mean "the previous frame" — it means "the last frame this particular state happened to run", which can be minutes ago.

Concrete failure: pause the game while holding A (jump). `toggle_pause_menu` fires on Start *release* (PlayerInput.cpp:53) so the menu opens with A still down. `_menu_input._prev_inputs` was last written when the pause menu was last open (or is all-false), so the first menu poll sees `current.proceed == true, previous.proceed == false` → no action, then latches `prev.proceed = true`. The instant the player lets go of the jump button, `proceed = prev_proceed && no_press_current` fires and `PauseMenuInitial::update` activates whatever is highlighted (ArtAttack/PauseMenu.cpp:59-81) — the player is thrown straight back into the game, or into the Restart/Quit confirmation, from a button press they made *before* the menu existed.

Neither class exposes any way to clear the history, so there is no way to fix it at the call sites either. Note DirectXTK already ships exactly the right tool: `GamePad::ButtonStateTracker` with `UP/HELD/RELEASED/PRESSED` and a `Reset()` (packages/directxtk_desktop_2019.../include/GamePad.h:219-282) — both classes reimplement it, worse, and drop the `Reset()`.

**Fix:** Sample the pad once per frame into a single shared snapshot (see the polling finding) so there is exactly one authoritative `previous`. Failing that, at minimum add `PlayerInput::reset()` / `MenuInput::reset()` that re-reads the current pad state into `_prev_inputs` without emitting edges, and call it on every state entry (`GameLevel` ACTIVE↔PAUSE_MENU transitions, `PauseMenuData`/`ResultsMenuData`/`EndMenuData` construction). Or just use `GamePad::ButtonStateTracker`.

#### 2. The 'raw' input layer is hardwired to four XInput pads and already speaks game verbs

`ArtAttack/PlayerInput.h:15-39` — **medium** · `design`

Merges 2 candidates. `RawPlayerInput` — the supposedly raw layer — has fields named `jump_button`, `jump_trigger`, `primary_shoot`, `secondary_shoot`, `show_debug`, `pause_menu` (PlayerInput.h:19-24), with the binding baked in at PlayerInput.cpp:27-32 (`result.jump_button = pad.buttons.a; result.primary_shoot = pad.triggers.right; result.show_debug = pad.buttons.back; ...`).

There is no keyboard, no mouse, no rebinding, no way to add a fifth player, and no way for a different game to define different actions. For a project whose stated goal is a reusable 2D engine, this is a hard ceiling: `jump` and `shoot` should never appear in engine code.

The pad count 4 is a bare literal in four places — `RawPlayerInput _prev_inputs[4]` (PlayerInput.h:34), `RawPlayerInput current[4]` and both `for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` loops (PlayerInput.cpp:121-127) — even though a `player_input_consts` namespace (PlayerInput.h:8-13) already exists as the obvious home for a named constant. DirectXTK's real bound is `GamePad::MAX_PLAYER_COUNT`, which is 8 under GDK; nothing static-asserts the relationship.

**Fix:** Two layers: an `InputDevice` interface producing a device-neutral `DeviceState` of axes and buttons, and a data-loaded `ActionMap` producing `ActionState { axis(action), down(action), pressed(action) }`. Player count comes from device enumeration, not a literal.

#### 3. PlayerInput.h and PlayerBuilder.h are not self-contained — they compile only via the PCH and accidental transitive includes

`ArtAttack/PlayerInput.h:31-38` — **medium** · `header-hygiene`

`PlayerInput.h` uses `DirectX::GamePad` in the constructor (:31) and the member (:38) but includes only `<vector>`, `PlayerInputData.h` and `MattMath.h`. I grepped the tree: the only `#include "GamePad.h"` anywhere is `pch.h:64`. Compile this header first in any TU without the PCH and it fails.

`PlayerBuilder.h` names `LevelLoadedInfo` (:17) and `ResourceManager` (:19) without including either — it resolves only because one of `Player.h`/`ViewportManager.h` transitively reaches `ResourceManager.h`, which itself includes `LevelLoadedInfo.h`. Removing one unrelated include anywhere in that chain breaks it.

For a project whose goal is a shippable reusable engine, headers that cannot be included standalone are a hard blocker.

**Fix:** Add `#include "GamePad.h"` to PlayerInput.h; forward-declare `class LevelLoadedInfo;` and `class ResourceManager;` in PlayerBuilder.h (both are used only as pointers). Verify with a build step that compiles each header alone with the PCH disabled.

#### 4. Player slot count hardcoded as literal 4 in six places instead of GamePad::MAX_PLAYER_COUNT

`ArtAttack/PlayerInput.h:34` — **low** · `design` · confidence: certain

The magic number 4 is repeated across both input pumps with no named constant:

- `RawPlayerInput _prev_inputs[4];` (PlayerInput.h:34)
- `RawPlayerInput current[4];` and the two `for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` loops (PlayerInput.cpp:121, 122, 127)
- `RawMenuInput _prev_inputs[4];` (MenuInput.h:50)
- `RawMenuInput current[4];` and two loops (MenuInput.cpp:133, 134, 139)

DirectXTK already publishes the right value: `GamePad::MAX_PLAYER_COUNT` (GamePad.h:76-79), which is **4 for XInput but 8 when built against GameInput or Windows.Gaming.Input**. So if the engine is ever retargeted to a backend supporting 8 pads, slots 4-7 are silently ignored with no compile error - exactly the kind of hidden platform assumption that defeats the reusable-engine goal.

Also dead in the same area: `Level.h:143` declares `std::vector<PlayerInputData> _player_inputs = std::vector<PlayerInputData>();` which is never read or written anywhere in the project - a leftover of an earlier design where `Level` cached the frame's inputs, and precisely the member that would have made the Level.cpp:192 bounds bug visible.

**Fix:** Replace all six literals with `DirectX::GamePad::MAX_PLAYER_COUNT` (or a single engine-level `constexpr int MAX_PLAYERS` if you want the engine to own the number), use `std::array<RawPlayerInput, MAX_PLAYERS>` instead of C arrays, and delete the dead `Level::_player_inputs` member.

## `ArtAttack/PlayerInputData.h`

_3 findings: 1 high, 2 medium_

#### 1. The input layer emits this game's verbs directly, with a fixed XInput button map and no keyboard

`ArtAttack/PlayerInputData.h:7-23 (with PlayerInput.cpp:20-36, 119-137)` — **high** · `design` · confidence: certain

`PlayerInputData` is the engine's only input payload, and every field is a game verb: `jump_pressed`, `jump_held`, `shoot_angle`, `shoot_direction`, `primary_shoot`, `secondary_shoot`, `toggle_debug`, `toggle_pause_menu` (lines 9-19). The mapping is hardcoded in `PlayerInput::get_raw_input` (PlayerInput.cpp:27-32): `result.jump_button = pad.buttons.a; result.jump_trigger = pad.triggers.left; result.primary_shoot = pad.triggers.right; result.secondary_shoot = pad.buttons.rightShoulder; result.show_debug = pad.buttons.back; result.pause_menu = pad.buttons.start;`.

There is no action-map indirection, no rebinding, no keyboard or mouse path at all (`DirectX::Keyboard`/`Mouse` appear nowhere in the codebase), and the player count is baked in as raw `4`s: `RawPlayerInput _prev_inputs[4]` (PlayerInput.h:34) and `RawPlayerInput current[4]; for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` (PlayerInput.cpp:121-128). A second game gets 'jump' and 'shoot' whether it wants them or not, and cannot be played without a gamepad.

**Fix:** Split into engine `RawInputState` (per-device sticks/buttons/keys, N devices) plus a game-defined action enum bound through an `InputMap` the game registers (`bind(action::JUMP, gamepad_button::A)`, loadable from the save file for rebinding). `PlayerInputData` and its verbs move to game/. Add a keyboard/mouse device so the engine is not gamepad-only.

#### 2. PlayerInputData.h squats on the include guard that PlayerInput.h's own #endif comment claims

`ArtAttack/PlayerInputData.h:1-2` — **medium** · `header-hygiene`

`PlayerInputData.h:1-2` is `#ifndef PLAYER_INPUT_H / #define PLAYER_INPUT_H`. `PlayerInput.h:1-2` is `#ifndef PLAYERINPUT_H / #define PLAYERINPUT_H` but its closing line 41 reads `#endif // !PLAYER_INPUT_H` — it does not match its own `#define`.

Today this works, but `PlayerInput.h:5` includes `PlayerInputData.h`. The moment anyone 'tidies' PlayerInput.h's guard to match its trailing comment, `PlayerInputData.h` becomes a silently empty header and `PlayerInputData` vanishes with a confusing cascade of errors. The guard name also does not correspond to the file name, unlike every other header in the directory.

**Fix:** Rename PlayerInputData.h's guard to `PLAYER_INPUT_DATA_H` and fix PlayerInput.h's trailing comment. Or, since pch.h already uses `#pragma once` and the project is MSVC-only, switch all first-party headers to `#pragma once` and remove the bug class entirely.

#### 3. PlayerInputData carries derived state alongside its source, plus raw stick values that leak the device into gameplay

`ArtAttack/PlayerInputData.h:9-22` — **medium** · `api-design`

Merges 2 candidates. The struct holds `x_movement` (derived from `left_analog_stick.x`), `shoot_angle` and `shoot_direction` (both derived from `right_analog_stick`), a `shoot_direction_requested` flag guarding the direction value, and `connection` — then also ships the raw `left_analog_stick` and `right_analog_stick` it derived them from. `calculate_player_input` (PlayerInput.cpp:96-114) computes the three derived fields and then copies the raw sticks in as well. Nothing enforces that the four stay consistent, and every field is independently settable by any consumer.

`connection` is always `CONNECTED` (:111) because disconnected pads are filtered out entirely, so it carries no information (see the compaction finding).

The leak is the concrete harm: `Player::update_movement` reaches past the semantic layer — `const bool analog_stick_down = this->_input.left_analog_stick.y > DROP_DOWN_ANALOG_THRESHOLD;` (Player.cpp:762-763). 'Drop through a platform' is therefore permanently a left-thumbstick gesture that can never be a key, a button, or a rebound control. Deadzone policy is now split across three layers: `GamePad::DEAD_ZONE_CIRCULAR` (PlayerInput.cpp:20), `STICK_DEADZONE = 0.5f` (PlayerInput.cpp:86-97), and this 0.8 threshold inside the entity.

**Fix:** Reduce the struct to intent-level fields — add a `drop_down` action computed in `calculate_player_input` where the stick threshold belongs, replace the direction/angle/requested triple with an optional direction, and delete `connection` and the two raw stick fields (their only other reader is the debug dump at DebugText.cpp:33-34).

## `ArtAttack/Projectile.h`

_10 findings: 2 high, 6 medium, 2 low_

#### 1. Splatoon team rules are baked into the projectile base class, blocking the engine-reuse goal

`ArtAttack/Projectile.h:4, 24-36, 70-79` — **high** · `design`

Verified against the header. `Projectile.h:4` includes `player_team.h`; the constructor (lines 24-36) takes `player_team team, int player_num, const Colour& team_colour, projectile_type type`; the class stores all four as members (lines 72-76). `Projectile.cpp:110-118` and `:136-152` then hard-switch `case player_team::A: / case player_team::B: / default: throw`, so a two-team King-of-the-Hill ruleset is a compile-time dependency of what should be the engine's generic 'moving thing that hits stuff'. Free-for-all, 3+ teams, PvE and neutral projectiles are literally unrepresentable, and `player_team::NONE` — the default value of `_team` at Projectile.h:76 — throws on the first collision query.

Two of the four members are provably dead weight: I grepped `Projectile::get_player_num` and `Projectile::get_team_colour` repo-wide and found only the declarations (Projectile.h:60-61) and definitions (Projectile.cpp:208-215). No caller. `_team_colour` is also pure duplicated state — every leaf constructor passes the same `team_colour` argument twice, once as the `Projectile` team colour and once as the `DrawObject` `color` (e.g. ProjectileSpray.cpp:19-22), and `DrawObject` already stores it as `_colour` (DrawObject.h:37).

Merged with the near-duplicate candidate reporting the duplicated team colour and dead `_player_num`.

**Fix:** Split the class along the engine/game seam. Engine layer: a `Projectile` that knows shape, velocity, lifetime, a sprite, an opaque `owner_id`, and a `CollisionFilter { uint32_t layer; uint32_t mask; }`. Game layer: a payload struct the engine carries but never interprets — `struct PaintPayload { TeamId team; Colour colour; float damage; }`. `player_team.h` must not appear in any header the engine ships. Delete `_team_colour` and `_player_num` and their dead accessors outright.

#### 2. `enum projectile_type` is the codebase's only unscoped enum and dumps SPRAY/JET/ROLLING/MIST/BALL into the global namespace

`ArtAttack/Projectile.h:10-16` — **high** · `naming` · confidence: certain

`enum projectile_type { SPRAY, JET, ROLLING, MIST, BALL };` at Projectile.h:10-16 has no `class`. Every other enum in the repo - all 25 of them (`collision_object_type`, `shape_type`, `wep_type`, `player_team`, `level_state`, `menu_direction`, `diffusion_type`, `add_player_velocity`, ...) - is `enum class`. Because Projectile.h is pulled in transitively by Weapon.h, Player.h and Level.h, the bare identifiers `SPRAY`, `JET`, `ROLLING`, `MIST` and `BALL` are visible in most of the program. `weapon_consts.h:24` and :45 already rely on this (`projectile_type proj_type = SPRAY;`, `SPRAY, //projectile_type`), and `Projectile.h:75` does `projectile_type _type = SPRAY;`.

**Fix:** Make it `enum class projectile_type` and qualify the ~15 use sites (`projectile_type::SPRAY`). While you are there, move it into its own `projectile_type.h` to match the existing one-enum-per-snake_case-header convention used by `shape_type.h`, `wep_type.h`, `player_team.h` etc.

#### 3. Unscoped `enum projectile_type` leaks SPRAY/JET/ROLLING/MIST/BALL into the global namespace of most of the codebase

`ArtAttack/Projectile.h:10-17` — **medium** · `modern-cpp`

Verified. `enum projectile_type { SPRAY, JET, ROLLING, MIST, BALL };` at Projectile.h:10-17 is the only unscoped enum in this subsystem — every neighbour is scoped: `collision_object_type` (collision_object_type.h:4), `diffusion_type` (projectile_details.h:20), `player_team`, `rotation_origin`, `shape_type`.

Because Weapon.h:11 includes ProjectileBuilder.h which includes Projectile.h, and Player.h includes Weapon.h, and Level.h includes Player.h, five extremely generic identifiers — `BALL`, `SPRAY`, `MIST`, `JET`, `ROLLING` — become global-namespace ints across essentially the entire game, including the menu code. Exactly the kind of short common noun that will collide with a future engine or third-party header.

They also convert implicitly to `int`, so `build_projectiles(..., 3, ...)` compiles, and the switch in `get_collision_object_type` (Projectile.cpp:161-191) cannot get exhaustiveness diagnostics from /W4. It is also a weapon-taxonomy enum — a game concept — living in what should be a generic engine header.

Merged from 2 candidate reports.

**Fix:** At minimum `enum class projectile_type : std::uint8_t` and qualify the ~15 use sites (Projectile.h:74, Projectile.cpp:163-188, the five leaf constructors, ProjectileBuilder.cpp:25-93). With scoped enums and all cases handled, the `default: throw` arms can go and the compiler enforces exhaustiveness. Better: delete the enum along with the class-per-projectile design so identity is an ID in a definition registry.

#### 4. MovingObject is a polymorphic base with 30 protected virtual accessors, of which exactly one is ever overridden

`ArtAttack/Projectile.h:19-20` — **medium** · `performance`

Verified. `MovingObject` (MovingObject.h:6-58) is a pure state mixin — `_velocity`, `_dx`, `_rotation` — yet declares `virtual ~MovingObject() = default;` (line 9) and 30 protected virtual accessors (lines 17-51). I grepped the whole of ArtAttack/ for overrides: there is exactly one, `Player::get_velocity` (Player.h:104). Nothing in the projectile hierarchy overrides any of them.

`Projectile::update_movement` (Projectile.cpp:232-283) reads and writes velocity/dx entirely through those virtuals — roughly 16 non-inlinable dispatches per projectile per frame to update two floats that are members of the same object. The vtable indirection buys nothing and blocks inlining of the hottest per-object function in the game.

Structurally, `Projectile : public MovingObject, public AnimationObject, public ICollisionGameObject` (Projectile.h:19-20) therefore carries a second vptr and two independent polymorphic-base identities, so `delete static_cast<MovingObject*>(p)` and `delete static_cast<ICollisionGameObject*>(p)` are both well-formed but need different pointer adjustments — a real hazard in a codebase where every dependency travels as a raw pointer.

Merged from 2 candidate reports (one design, one performance).

**Fix:** Make the `MovingObject` accessors non-virtual and inline, and drop its virtual destructor. Better still, make it a value member (`MovingObject _motion;`) rather than a base, leaving `Projectile` with exactly one polymorphic chain, one vptr and one delete path. Restructure `Player` so it does not need to override `get_velocity`.

#### 5. Public defaulted default-constructors on Projectile, Ball, Jet and Rolling produce objects that crash on first use

`ArtAttack/Projectile.h:23` — **medium** · `robustness`

Verified. `Projectile() = default;` (Projectile.h:23), `ProjectileBall() = default;` (ProjectileBall.h:9), `ProjectileJet() = default;` (ProjectileJet.h:9) and `ProjectileRolling() = default;` (ProjectileRolling.h:9). The three leaves are `final` and override every pure virtual, so `ProjectileJet j;` compiles and yields a fully-formed `ICollisionGameObject` that is permanently broken:
- `Projectile::_dt == nullptr` (Projectile.h:79); `Projectile::get_dt()` is `return *this->_dt;` (Projectile.cpp:228-231), called unconditionally at the top of `update_movement` (line 234) — null dereference on the first update.
- `AnimationObject::_dt == nullptr` separately (AnimationObject.h:49), dereferenced at AnimationObject.cpp:88.
- `DrawObject::_resource_manager == nullptr` (DrawObject.h:36).
- `_team == player_team::NONE` (Projectile.h:76), which makes both `is_matching_collision_object_type` (Projectile.cpp:117) and `get_collision_object_type` (line 193) throw on first call.
- `_details` is the all-`-1.0f` sentinel default from projectile_details.h:9-13 — negative gravity, negative drag, empty sheet names.

The hierarchy is inconsistent about it: `ProjectileSpray() = delete;` (ProjectileSpray.h:9) and `ProjectileMist() = delete;` (ProjectileMist.h:9) get it right. Five siblings, two different answers to the same question — which is itself evidence the defaults were unintentional.

Nothing constructs them this way today, so this is a latent API hazard rather than a live crash. Merged from 4 candidate reports; two filed it as memory-safety at high severity, which I have downgraded on that basis.

**Fix:** `= delete` all four, matching Spray and Mist, then remove the `= nullptr`/`-1.0f` in-class initialisers that only exist to make those defaults compile. Better: stop threading frame time as `const float*` entirely — take `void update(float dt)` and pass it by value. That makes 'no dt' unrepresentable and removes the null-`_dt` class of bug across every class that currently stores one.

#### 6. Projectile::update() silently overrides two unrelated base virtuals; only an explicit qualification prevents infinite recursion

`ArtAttack/Projectile.h:38` — **medium** · `correctness`

Verified. `Projectile` inherits `void update()` from two independent bases with identical signatures:
- `IGameObject::update()` — public pure virtual (IGameObject.h:10), the per-frame game-object tick;
- `AnimationObject::update()` — protected virtual (AnimationObject.h:21), which only advances the sprite frame index.

The single declaration `void update() override = 0;` at Projectile.h:38, in the public section, therefore overrides **both** and promotes the protected one to public. Legal C++, compiles clean, and fuses two semantically unrelated virtuals into one slot.

The trap is live in the subclasses. `ProjectileSpray::update()` ends with `AnimationObject::update();` (ProjectileSpray.cpp:42). That only works because the call is explicitly qualified — dropping the `AnimationObject::` prefix, a completely natural edit since every other call in the file is unqualified, turns it into a virtual self-call and an immediate stack overflow. The same one-token trap sits at ProjectileJet.cpp:40, ProjectileMist.cpp:42 and ProjectileBall.cpp:40. `ProjectileRolling::update()` omits the call entirely, which is how its animation ended up frozen.

**Fix:** Rename the animation tick so the collision is impossible — `AnimationObject::advance_animation(float dt)`. That removes the accidental override and makes the four call sites self-documenting. While there, drive it from the base `Projectile::update()` so no subclass can forget it (which is exactly what ProjectileRolling did).

#### 7. Abstract classes re-declare already-pure virtuals as `= 0`, and the draw re-declaration hides the inherited overload set

`ArtAttack/Projectile.h:38-46` — **medium** · `design`

Verified. `Projectile.h:38-46` re-declares five functions that are already pure in `IGameObject`/`ICollisionGameObject` purely to write `override = 0` again, and `DiffusingProjectile` re-declares four of them a third time (Projectile.h:102-108). Four signatures maintained in three places for zero effect — removing them changes nothing, since an unimplemented pure virtual stays pure.

It is not harmless. Declaring *any* `draw` in `Projectile` hides every inherited `draw` by name lookup. Projectile.h:39-40 declares only `draw(SpriteBatch*, const Camera&)`, so `IGameObject::draw(SpriteBatch*)` (IGameObject.h:12) and the five protected `AnimationObject::draw` overloads (AnimationObject.h:34-46) are invisible in `Projectile` and below. That is why every leaf must write the explicit `this->AnimationObject::draw(sprite_batch, this->_rectangle, camera)` (ProjectileSpray.cpp:46, ProjectileMist.cpp:46, ProjectileBall.cpp:45, ProjectileJet.cpp:44) — an unqualified `draw(...)` would not compile against the leaf's own two declarations.

**Fix:** Delete the redundant `override = 0` re-declarations in both `Projectile` and `DiffusingProjectile`. Where a derived class needs the base overload set, pull it in with `using AnimationObject::draw;` rather than qualifying every call site. Note `Projectile` also has no user-declared destructor while `DiffusingProjectile` has `~DiffusingProjectile() override = default;` (Projectile.h:99) — pick one convention (the virtual destructor is already inherited from `IGameObject`, so neither is required).

#### 8. Each projectile carries a by-value copy of its immutable shared detail table plus a duplicate copy of the same two strings, and a second aliasing _dt pointer

`ArtAttack/Projectile.h:70-79` — **medium** · `performance`

Verified. `ProjectileDetails _details` (Projectile.h:70) and `DiffusionDetails _diffusion_details` (Projectile.h:112) are stored by value per instance, although the values are compile-time constants identical for every projectile of a given class and never mutated (`get_details()` is the only accessor and it is const). `ProjectileDetails` holds two `std::string`s, so that is ~100 bytes plus two string constructions per spawn — and the ctor then forwards those same two strings to `SpriteSheetObject`, which stores them **again** as `_sheet_name`/`_element_name` (SpriteSheetObject.h:25-26). Four `std::string`s per projectile to represent two string literals. The mister does this five times per shot.

Part of the copied payload is provably dead: `_details.player_damage`, `_details.rotat_origin` and `DiffusionDetails::type` are never read (see the dead-fields finding).

Merged with the candidate on the duplicated `_dt`: `Projectile` declares `const float* _dt = nullptr;` (Projectile.h:79) and initialises it at Projectile.cpp:28 from the *same* argument it already forwarded to `AnimationObject` at line 21, which stores its own `const float* _dt` (AnimationObject.h:49). Each projectile therefore carries two independent non-owning aliases to one heap `float` owned by `Game`, both dereferenced without a null check, with the lifetime contract recorded nowhere. The pointer is threaded Game -> GameData -> Level -> Player -> Weapon -> ProjectileBuilder -> Projectile purely so a float can be read once per frame.

With the delete-timer bug letting live projectile counts grow without bound, this per-instance footprint multiplies straight into cache pressure on the O(n^2) collision loop.

**Fix:** Once the detail tables have external linkage, replace both by-value members with `const ProjectileDetails* _details` (the constants outlive every projectile by construction) and have `SpriteSheetObject` take its names from that table instead of copying them. Delete both `_dt` members and change the interface to `void update(float dt)` — frame time is a value, not a resource; passing it by value removes the dangling/null exposure entirely and makes projectiles testable without a live `Game`.
