#### 2. SpriteSheet stores a borrowed ID3D11ShaderResourceView* with no AddRef that ResourceManager releases underneath it

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.h:63` — **high** · `memory-safety`

```cpp
ID3D11ShaderResourceView* _texture = nullptr;   // SpriteSheet.h:63
SpriteSheet::SpriteSheet(ID3D11ShaderResourceView* texture) : _texture(texture) {}
```
The pointer originates from `ResourceManager::get_texture()` (ResourceManager.cpp:12) as a bare `.Get()` off a `ComPtr` — no AddRef. `ResourceManager::reset_all_textures()` (ResourceManager.cpp:112-118) calls `.Reset()` on every texture, and `Game::OnDeviceLost` calls it. `_sprite_sheets` is not cleared, so every surviving `SpriteSheet` then holds a dangling COM pointer that it passes straight to `SpriteBatch::Draw` at SpriteSheet.cpp:103, 124, 145, 166.

This is the only long-lived raw COM pointer in the codebase — `ResourceManager` itself uses `ComPtr` correctly.

Secondary: `SpriteSheet` has a user-declared constructor but no destructor, so the implicit move constructor is generated and copies `_texture` without nulling the source. Currently latent (sheets live in `unique_ptr` and are never moved), so it is a hardening point, not a live bug.

**Fix:** Store `Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11ShaderResourceView> _texture;` — assignment AddRefs, so the texture cannot die while a sheet holds it. Delete the copy constructor and default the move so the borrowing story is stated rather than inferred.

#### 3. SpriteSheet caches a borrowed, non-AddRef'd ID3D11ShaderResourceView* that reset_all_textures() frees underneath it

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.h:63` — **medium** · `lifetime`

`SpriteSheet` stores `ID3D11ShaderResourceView* _texture = nullptr;` (SpriteSheet.h:63) and hands it to `SpriteBatch::Draw` in all four draw overloads (SpriteSheet.cpp:103, 124, 146, 167). The pointer comes from `ResourceManager::get_texture(...)` via `ResourceLoader::load_sprite_sheet` (ResourceLoader.cpp:119-120), and `get_texture` returns `_textures[name].Get()` — a BORROWED raw pointer with no AddRef. The only reference is the ComPtr inside `ResourceManager::_textures`.

`Game::OnDeviceLost()` (Game.cpp:277) calls `reset_all_textures()`, which does `texture.second.Reset()` for every entry, dropping the last reference and destroying the SRV — while every `SpriteSheet::_texture` still points at it. `_sprite_sheets` is NOT reset, so the sheets survive holding freed COM objects. Any draw between device-lost and device-restore passes a dead object to `SpriteBatch::Draw`.

Second vector: `add_texture` (ResourceManager.cpp:21-25) does `_textures[name] = texture`, releasing whatever was previously under that key, so reloading a texture under an existing name silently invalidates every SpriteSheet holding the old pointer.

Graded medium: the window between device-lost and the (wholesale) manager replacement on restore is narrow.

**Fix:** Store `Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr<ID3D11ShaderResourceView> _texture` in SpriteSheet, and make `add_texture`/`get_texture` take and return ComPtr so the refcount reflects the actual sharing.

#### 4. map<string, unique_ptr<AnimationStrip>> adds a heap indirection for a plain value type, next to a map that gets it right

`ArtAttack/SpriteSheet.h:62-68` — **low** · `modern-cpp`

```cpp
std::map<std::string, SpriteFrame> _sprite_frames;                       // :61 — correct
std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<AnimationStrip>> _animation_strips; // :62
```
`AnimationStrip` (AnimationStrip.h:19-23) is `vector<RECT>` + `RectangleI` + `int` + `float` + `bool` — an ordinary movable value type with no virtual functions and no derived classes. The `unique_ptr` buys nothing (`std::map` already guarantees reference stability) and costs an extra allocation per strip plus a pointer chase on every `get_frame_rect`. SpriteSheet.cpp:64-65 does `make_unique<AnimationStrip>(...)` where `emplace(name, AnimationStrip{...})` would do.

The two containers are declared one line apart and disagree about the idiom, which is the tell that it was not a deliberate choice.

**Fix:** `std::map<std::string, AnimationStrip> _animation_strips;` (or `unordered_map` — nothing depends on ordering), with `get_animation_strip` returning `const AnimationStrip*` from `.at()`. Same for the decoder's return type.

## `ArtAttack/StateContext.cpp`

_5 findings: 2 high, 3 medium_

#### 1. transition_to destroys the running state from inside its own update(); correctness rests on an unwritten 'return immediately' rule

`ArtAttack/StateContext.cpp:20-25` — **high** · `lifetime`

```cpp
void StateContext::transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state)
{
    this->_state = std::move(state);   // destroys the currently-running State
    this->_state->set_context(this);
    this->_state->init();
}
```
`unique_ptr::operator=` releases the old pointee first, so the object whose `update()` frame is on the stack is destroyed before line 22, and a new page's `init()` (allocating textures, starting music) then runs underneath a dead frame. Called from inside `update()` at MainMenu.cpp:56, 143, 152, 160, 312, 357, 657, 668, 688, 892, 910, 922, 934, 946, 954, 1167, 1218, 1452, 1458, 1505, 1797 and PauseMenu.cpp:70, 77, 225, 250. Most sites `return;` immediately; **PauseMenu.cpp:70-73 and 77-80 do not**, and neither does `MainMenuHome`'s exit branch (MainMenu.cpp:165-168, `DestroyWindow` with no return, so a second pad's BACK in the same frame runs `transition_to(MainMenuTitle)` and a full `init()` against a destroyed window). Correction to the original report: the claim that `else if (highlighted_element == "quit")` at PauseMenu.cpp:74 is "evaluated on a destroyed object" is wrong — it is an `else if`, so it is skipped once the restart branch runs. The hazard is latent, not currently firing: the code survives only because no statement after those two calls touches `this`, and `//this->_music->Stop();` sitting commented out at MainMenu.cpp:55 directly above such a call is exactly the statement that would have made it crash.

**Fix:** Make transitions deferred: have `State::update()` return a requested transition (or set a pending `unique_ptr<State>` on the context) and have `StateContext::update()` apply it after `_state->update()` returns. That removes the whole class of bug and the need for the `return;` discipline.

#### 2. transition_to destroys the State whose update() is still on the stack — `delete this` at ~30 call sites

`ArtAttack/StateContext.cpp:20-25` — **high** · `lifetime`

```cpp
void StateContext::transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state)
{
    this->_state = std::move(state);   // runs ~State() on the CURRENT state
    this->_state->set_context(this);
    this->_state->init();
}
```
`unique_ptr::operator=(unique_ptr&&)` destroys the previously-managed object. Every non-bootstrap transition in the codebase is issued by the state being destroyed, from inside its own `update()`. Grep found 45 `transition_to` occurrences across 6 files; the self-destroying ones are GameStates.cpp:81 (`GameMenu::order_level_creation`, reached from `GameMenu::update` at :76), GameStates.cpp:211, 252, 262, 272, 290 (inside `GameLevel::update`), 21 sites in MainMenu.cpp, and 4 in PauseMenu.cpp (:70, :77, :225, :250). Only Main.cpp:208 is a legitimate outside-in transition.

So the effective semantics are `delete this;` mid-member-function. Two consequences: (a) `this->_state->init()` — which for `GameLevel` builds an entire level, loads textures and sounds — runs nested inside the destroyed `GameMenu`'s still-live stack frame; (b) any statement after the call touches freed memory.

I checked every call site and none currently reads a member afterwards, so it does not crash today. That is luck, not design: adding one log line, one `this->play_wave(...)`, or one member reset after any of the ~30 calls is an immediate heap-use-after-free. GameStates.cpp:252-254 doesn't even `return` — it breaks out of two nested switches and falls off the end of `GameLevel::update`.

Severity is `high` rather than `critical` only because no live path currently dereferences the freed object.

**Fix:** Make transitions deferred: `request_transition(std::unique_ptr<State>)` parks the new state in a `_pending` member, and `StateContext::update()` applies it *after* `_state->update()` returns:
```cpp
void StateContext::update() {
    if (_state) _state->update();
    if (_pending) { _state = std::move(_pending); _state->set_context(this); _state->init(); }
}
```
No state is then ever destroyed while a frame of it is live, and call sites can fall through naturally instead of every one having to remember to return.

#### 3. transition_to publishes the new state before init(), has no null guard, and gives no exception guarantee

`ArtAttack/StateContext.cpp:20-25` — **medium** · `exception-safety`

Two further defects in the same three lines, distinct from the self-destruction issue and needing a different fix.

1. **No null guard.** `update()` and `draw()` both open with `if (this->_state == nullptr) return;` (StateContext.cpp:6-9, 14-17) and `_state` legitimately defaults to `nullptr` (StateContext.h:16) — so the class plainly contemplates a null state. But `transition_to` dereferences unconditionally at :23. `transition_to(nullptr)`, the natural way to tear a context down (and exactly the hook `~Game()` needs to fix its destruction order), is an immediate null dereference. The class is internally inconsistent about whether null is legal.

2. **New state installed before it is valid.** `_state = std::move(state)` publishes, then `_state->init()` runs. `GameLevel::init` (GameStates.cpp:105-127) calls `LevelBuilder::build_level`, which throws `std::exception` on any unexpected level JSON. If it throws, the previous state is already destroyed and `_state` is left holding a `GameLevel` whose `_level`, `_player_input` and `_menu_input` are all null — and `GameLevel::draw` dereferences `_level` unconditionally at :315.

**Fix:** Construct fully before publishing, which fixes both at once:
```cpp
if (!state) { _state.reset(); return; }
state->set_context(this);
state->init();
_state = std::move(state);
```
On throw the old state is still installed and the parameter's own unique_ptr destroys the half-built one — a strong exception guarantee. Better still, move init() work into constructors so two-phase init disappears.

#### 4. transition_to deletes the currently-running state before initialising the new one; every call site is a self-delete

`ArtAttack/StateContext.cpp:20-25` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

void StateContext::transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state)
    {
        this->_state = std::move(state);   // destroys the OLD state -- which is the caller
        this->_state->set_context(this);
        this->_state->init();
    }

Every call is made from inside the outgoing state's own `update()`: GameStates.cpp:81-84 (`GameMenu::order_level_creation`), 211-212, 252-253, 262-263, 272-273, 290-291 (all five end-menu/pause exits), PauseMenu.cpp:70-72, 77-79, 225-226, 250-252, MainMenu.cpp:1505-1506, 1797-1799. In every case `this` is freed while `this->update()` is still on the stack; execution then continues through `break;`/`return;` in the freed object's member function.

It survives only by luck — no member is touched after the call. `PauseMenuInitial::update` (PauseMenu.cpp:70-73) does not even `return` after transitioning; it relies on the subsequent `else if` chain being skipped. Adding one line of cleanup after any of these calls is an immediate use-after-free.

The secondary effect is that `GameLevel::init()` — a full level build: JSON parse, texture/sound lookup, object construction (LevelBuilder.cpp:24-83) — runs *inside* `transition_to`, i.e. inside the destroyed `GameMenu`'s stack frame, adding a multi-hundred-millisecond hitch to that frame with no loading screen.

**Fix:** Make the transition deferred and non-reentrant:

    void StateContext::transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> next) { _pending = std::move(next); }
    void StateContext::update() {
        if (_state) _state->update();
        if (_pending) { _state = std::move(_pending); _state->set_context(this); _state->init(); }
    }

That keeps the outgoing state alive for the whole of its own `update()`, makes the self-delete impossible, and gives you an obvious place to hang an async/loading-screen build later. Also note `StateContext::update()`/`draw()` are declared `const` (StateContext.h:12-13) while driving all mutation in the game — that const should go.

#### 5. transition_to destroys the running State from inside that State's own update(), leaving `this` dangling for the rest of the call chain

`ArtAttack/StateContext.cpp:20-25` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

```cpp
void StateContext::transition_to(std::unique_ptr<State> state)
{
    this->_state = std::move(state);   // :22  destroys the CURRENTLY EXECUTING state
    this->_state->set_context(this);
    this->_state->init();
}
```

Every caller reaches this from inside the outgoing state's own `update()`:
- `GameMenu::order_level_creation` (GameStates.cpp:79-84), called from `GameMenu::update` line 76;
- `GameLevel::update`, pause-menu QUIT (GameStates.cpp:211-212);
- `GameLevel::update`, end-menu CHANGE_TEAMS / CHANGE_WEAPONS / CHANGE_LEVEL / EXIT (GameStates.cpp:252, 262, 272, 290).

At line 22 the `unique_ptr` assignment deletes the old `State`, so `this` inside `GameMenu::update` / `GameLevel::update` is freed while those frames are still on the stack, as is `StateContext::update`'s `this->_state->update()` call at StateContext.cpp:10. It survives today only because every one of those six sites happens to touch no member after the call — `order_level_creation` returns immediately, and the five `GameLevel` cases fall straight through `break; break;` to the end of the function. That is one added line away from a use-after-free, in six places, with nothing marking the hazard.

It also interacts badly with the rest of this review: the transition destroys `GameLevel`, and with it the `Level` whose `this` is captured by every draw task (Level.cpp:388, 601). Today the ordering saves it — `Game::update` runs all transitions, `Game::render` runs afterwards, and each draw drains the pool before returning (Game.cpp:75-84, 91, 115) — so a transition can never land while tasks are outstanding. But that is an emergent property of three unrelated pieces of code, not a stated invariant; the moment any draw returns without draining (see the `add_task` exception finding), a transition on the next frame frees the `Level` that live callbacks are still reading.

**Fix:** Make the transition deferred: have `transition_to` stash the incoming state in a `_pending_state` member and have `StateContext::update()` perform the swap after `_state->update()` returns, at a point where no State frame is on the stack. That makes self-destruction structurally impossible and gives you one well-defined moment per frame at which it is safe to tear down a Level — which is also the right place to assert that the thread pool is idle.

## `ArtAttack/StateContext.h`

_2 findings: 1 high, 1 low_

#### 1. StateContext holds one state with no stack, forcing GameLevel to hand-roll overlay machinery three times

`ArtAttack/StateContext.h:7-17` — **high** · `design`

`StateContext` has a single `std::unique_ptr<State> _state` and one operation, `transition_to` (replace). There is no push/pop, no way to query the current state, and no notion of an overlay sitting on top of a still-live state.

But pause/results/end menus *are* overlays over a live level, so `GameLevel` re-implements the missing feature by hand three times: `_pause_menu`, `_results_menu`, `_end_menu` are three separate `unique_ptr<StateContext>` members, each with its own action enum and data object (GameStates.h:60-69), each constructed inline in the middle of `GameLevel::update` (GameStates.cpp:150-162, 169-181, 225-236), and `GameLevel::draw` (:332-345) switches over `_state` to pick which of the three to draw on top of the level. `GameMenu` does it a fourth time with its own `_menu` context (GameStates.h:25).

This is also why `game_level_state` (GameStates.h:36-44) conflates three unrelated axes: two load-warmup frames, one simulation state, and three overlay identities. PAUSE_MENU/RESULTS/END_MENU are not states of the level — the level is still drawn underneath them (:311-330 runs before the overlay switch).

**Fix:** Give the engine a state stack: `push`, `pop`, `replace`, `top()`. Add `blocks_update_below()` / `blocks_draw_below()` to `State`; `update()` walks top-down until something blocks, `draw()` walks bottom-up. PauseMenu then becomes `push(make_unique<PauseMenu>(...))` over a live GameLevel and `pop()` resumes it, and the three duplicated context/action/data triples plus half of `game_level_state` collapse to nothing.

#### 2. StateContext::update()/draw() are const yet drive the entire mutable simulation

`ArtAttack/StateContext.h:12-13` — **low** · `design`

```cpp
void update() const;
void draw() const;
```
`std::unique_ptr` does not propagate const, so inside a const member `_state` is `State* const` and `this->_state->update()` (StateContext.cpp:10) compiles happily while mutating the whole game world — `Game::update` calls it at Game.cpp:91 and through it every player, projectile and paint tile is moved.

The `const` conveys the exact opposite of the truth, so it cannot be used to reason about anything, and the pattern is propagated downward: `Level::update_level_logic(...) const` (Level.cpp:180) pushes projectiles into `_collision_objects` (:209) and erases objects (:296-305) from a const member; `Game::on_activated() const` and `Game::clear() const` inherit the same dishonesty. It also blocks the fix for the transition-during-update bug, which requires `update()` to mutate `_state`.

**Fix:** Drop `const` from both — that is honest and is a prerequisite for making `update()` perform a deferred state swap. Do the same for `Level::update_level_logic`. If const-correctness through owning pointers matters (it should, for an engine), use a `propagate_const`-style wrapper so the compiler enforces the intent rather than the annotation being decorative.

## `ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.h`

_3 findings: 1 high, 2 medium_

#### 1. StructurePaintable stores a reference member bound to a caller's local vector — dangles for the object's whole life

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.h:56` — **high** · `memory-safety`

`const std::vector<MattMath::Segment>& _paintable_edges;` (StructurePaintable.h:56), bound in the member-init list at StructurePaintable.cpp:30 to the constructor parameter.

The caller passes a function-local: `std::vector<Segment> paintable_edges;` at LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:107, filled at :110-125, passed at :140 to `std::make_unique<StructurePaintable>(...)`. `build_collision_object` then returns and the vector dies — but the StructurePaintable lives for the whole level holding a reference to that dead stack object.

The UB is latent rather than firing today because the only reads (StructurePaintable.cpp:191, :193) happen inside `generate_paint_tiles()`, called from the constructor body at :33 while the argument is still alive. It is one method away from being live.

Two side effects prove the member is wrong: `StructurePaintable() = default;` (StructurePaintable.h:28) is implicitly **deleted** because a reference member cannot be default-initialised — the declaration says the opposite of what it means — and copy/move assignment are deleted too.

**Fix:** The data is only consumed during construction, so keep no member at all: pass it as an argument to `generate_paint_tiles(const std::vector<Segment>&)`. Better still, delete the vector round-trip entirely (see the face-mapping finding) and pass a face bitmask by value. Then delete the meaningless `= default` constructor.

#### 2. StructurePaintable does not override is_colliding, so it inherits Structure's unconditional `return false` - painting works only by accident of loop order

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.h:25-50` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

`StructurePaintable` overrides `update`, both `draw`s, `on_collision` and `get_paint_total`, but not `is_colliding`, so it uses `Structure::is_colliding` which is `return false;` (ArtAttack/Structure.cpp:43-46). In `Level::update_level_logic` the object-vs-object loop tests `object->is_colliding(object_2)` and, on a hit, calls `on_collision` on both sides (ArtAttack/Level.cpp:287-291). Paint therefore fires only in the ordering where the PROJECTILE is the outer `object` - `Projectile::is_colliding` accepts `STRUCTURE_PAINTABLE` (Projectile.cpp:98-106). In the reverse ordering the structure reports false and nothing happens.
The mechanic works today, but it depends entirely on the double-sided `on_collision` dispatch at lines 289-290 and on projectiles being in the same list as structures. Anyone who changes the loop to a single-sided `object->on_collision(object_2)`, adds an early `continue` for objects that report no collisions, or moves projectiles to their own list, silently disables the entire paint system with no compile error and no runtime error. It also means `Level.cpp:268-272` (collision-object vs player) can never fire for a paintable.

**Fix:** Give StructurePaintable a real `is_colliding` (type filter for offensive projectiles + AABB against the structure rect) so the object is honest about its own collisions, and stop relying on `on_collision` being invoked on both participants. The deeper fix is to have one place decide a pair collides and one place resolve it, instead of every concrete class re-implementing the same broad+narrow phase (the identical body appears in Player.cpp:148-185, PaintTile.cpp:84-109, ProjectileSpray.cpp:56-87 and the other four projectiles).

#### 3. Reference member bound to a builder local - the reference genuinely dangles, but there is NO live use-after-free

`ArtAttack/StructurePaintable.h:56` — **medium** · `memory-safety` · confidence: certain

`const std::vector<MattMath::Segment>& _paintable_edges;` is bound in the mem-initializer list at StructurePaintable.cpp:30 to the ctor parameter, which at the sole construction site is a function-local:
```
std::vector<Segment> paintable_edges;            // LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:107
...
return std::make_unique<StructurePaintable>(..., paintable_edges, ...);  // :140
```
`build_collision_object` returns at line 132-142 and `paintable_edges` dies. The member reference is dangling for the object's entire remaining life. CONFIRMED.

But the severity as previously filed is WRONG. I traced every read of `_paintable_edges` in the whole file: there are exactly two, both inside `generate_paint_tiles()` at StructurePaintable.cpp:191 (`this->_paintable_edges.size()`) and :193 (`this->_paintable_edges[j]`). That function is called from **the constructor body**, StructurePaintable.cpp:33, while the builder's local is still alive. After construction the member is never touched again — `update` (37-43), `draw` (45-62), `on_collision` (64-102) and `get_paint_total` (300-319) do not reference it. And `_collision_objects` holds `unique_ptr`s, so the object is never copied (Level.cpp:296-305 moves pointers, not objects).

So: real defect, zero runtime symptom today. It is a landmine, not a live bug.

Two genuine secondary issues in the same header:
- `StructurePaintable() = default;` (line 28) is **implicitly deleted** by the reference member. Declaring it is legal; it just silently isn't there. Nothing uses it, which is the only reason this compiles.
- The reference member also deletes implicit copy-assignment, which is invisible from the declaration.

Contrast with how the shape is handled correctly two arguments earlier: `&rectangle` is also a pointer to a builder local (LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:136), but `Structure`'s ctor clones it — `_collision_shape(collision_shape->clone())` (Structure.cpp:22) — so that one is safe. The edges just never got the same treatment.

**Fix:** Make it a value: `std::vector<MattMath::Segment> _paintable_edges;` (or drop the member entirely, since it is only consumed during construction — pass it to `generate_paint_tiles(const std::vector<Segment>&)` as a parameter and store nothing). The latter is better: the member exists only because the loop was moved into a helper. Also delete the now-meaningless `StructurePaintable() = default;`. Reference members in classes with any lifetime beyond the enclosing scope are a rule worth banning outright in this codebase.

## `ArtAttack/TeamColour.h`

_7 findings: 1 high, 3 medium, 3 low_

#### 1. Three `#include` directives use the wrong case and only compile because of Windows' case-insensitive filesystem

`ArtAttack/TeamColour.h:5` — **high** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

`TeamColour.h:5` is `#include "colour.h"` but the file is `Colour.h`. Same bug at `InterfaceGameplay.h:7` (`#include "colour.h"`) and `Level.cpp:2` (`#include "level.h"` for `Level.h`). These are the only three case-mismatched first-party includes in the tree - I enumerated every `#include "..."` and checked it against the real filename. They resolve today purely because NTFS is case-insensitive; they are hard errors on any case-sensitive filesystem, which matters the moment this "reusable engine" is built in CI on Linux, in WSL, or under a case-sensitive Dev Drive.

**Fix:** Fix to `#include "Colour.h"` and `#include "Level.h"` (or to `colour_consts.h` if you take the rename above). Worth adding a CI check that greps includes against `ls` output, since this class of bug is invisible locally.

#### 2. Exactly-two-teams is baked into struct member names and has propagated into engine-facing interfaces

`ArtAttack/TeamColour.h:7-15` — **medium** · `design`

`struct TeamColour { MattMath::Colour team_a; MattMath::Colour team_b; }` with `player_team { A, B, NONE }` (player_team.h:4-9). Because the team count is encoded in member *names*, it cannot be varied — and it has spread well beyond this struct: `IPaintableGameObject.h` defines `struct PaintTotal { float team_a; float team_b; }` on an *interface*; `LevelEndInfo.h` carries `team_a_area`/`team_b_area` plus a set of `team_a_*`/`team_b_*`/`winning_*`/`losing_*` accessors that all assume a two-way comparison; `Level.h:136-137` has separate `_team_a_spawns`/`_team_b_spawns` vectors; and `collision_object_type` doubles every projectile enumerator by team.

Free-for-all, three teams, or solo play are all structurally impossible without touching every one of these. For a codebase whose stated goal is a reusable 2D engine, hard-coding the team count into an interface (`PaintTotal`) is the wrong side of the engine/game line.

**Fix:** `using TeamId = int;` (or a strong typedef) plus `struct TeamPalette { std::vector<MattMath::Colour> colours; const MattMath::Colour& operator[](TeamId) const; }`. `PaintTotal` becomes a small vector or map keyed by TeamId; `LevelEndInfo` becomes a sorted `std::vector<TeamScore>` with `winner() == front()`; spawns become `std::vector<std::vector<Vector2F>>` indexed by TeamId.

#### 3. MAX sentinel aliases the last enumerator, so generate_random_team_colour can never return BLUE_YELLOW

`ArtAttack/TeamColour.h:17-23` — **medium** · `correctness`

```cpp
enum class team_colour_enum { BLUE_ORANGE, PINK_GREEN, BLUE_YELLOW, MAX = BLUE_YELLOW };
```
`MAX` is 2, i.e. the last *valid* value, not a count. TeamColour.cpp:28-29 then does:
```cpp
int enum_max = static_cast<int>(team_colour_enum::MAX);   // == 2
int random = rand() % enum_max;                            // yields 0 or 1 only
```
so `case 2: return BLUE_YELLOW;` (TeamColour.cpp:36-37) is unreachable and one of the three colour schemes never appears in a match.

I checked the two other `MAX`-style sentinels several reviewers claimed had "the same off-by-one shape" and **they are correct**: `wep_type::MAX_PRIM_WEP = RANDOM_PRIMARY` is genuinely one past the last primary (BUCKET), so `rand() % MAX_PRIM_WEP` at MainMenu.cpp:1521 is right; `level_stage::MAX_STAGE = RANDOM` is one past CLOSE_QUARTERS, so MainMenu.cpp:1894 is right. `team_colour_enum` is the odd one out because `BLUE_YELLOW` is a real palette rather than a RANDOM placeholder.

**Fix:** Replace the sentinel with a one-past-the-end `COUNT` after `BLUE_YELLOW`, index a `static constexpr std::array<TeamColour, COUNT>` instead of the switch, and delete `get_team_colours`'s duplicate switch. That gives one mapping instead of two and makes the bug impossible to reintroduce.

#### 4. Namespace-scope const TeamColour objects in a header: one internally-linked, dynamically-initialised copy per translation unit

`ArtAttack/TeamColour.h:25-42` — **medium** · `performance`

```cpp
namespace team_colour_consts {
    const TeamColour BLUE_ORANGE = { colour_consts::TEAM_BLUE, colour_consts::TEAM_ORANGE };
    const TeamColour PINK_GREEN  = { ... };
    const TeamColour BLUE_YELLOW = { ... };
}
```
At namespace scope `const` implies internal linkage, so every TU including TeamColour.h gets its own private copy. TeamColour.h is included by Level.h, LevelBuilder.h, LevelEndInfo.h, PaintTile.h, PlayerBuilder.h and StructurePaintable.h — most of the simulation.

Because `MattMath::Colour` has user-provided, non-constexpr constructors (MattMath.h:593-600, including `Colour(int,int,int,int)` and `Colour(const std::string&)`), it is not a literal type, so these are **dynamically** initialised at static-init time, once per TU. It currently works only because Colour.h is included first (TeamColour.h:5), giving the right within-TU ordering; nothing enforces that.

This header drags in `Colour.h`, which is the same pattern at scale: ~150 `const MattMath::Colour` at namespace scope plus a `static MattMath::Colour colour_from_name(const std::string&)` function defined in the header (Colour.h:315+), giving every TU its own copy of both.

**Fix:** Make `Colour`'s float/int constructors `constexpr`, then declare these `inline constexpr TeamColour BLUE_ORANGE{...}` (C++17 — see the LanguageStandard finding). That gives one shared compile-time constant with no static-init ordering exposure and no per-TU duplication. Where constexpr is impossible, declare `extern const` in the header and define once in a .cpp. Same treatment for `colour_consts`.

#### 5. #include "colour.h" but the file on disk is Colour.h — compiles only because NTFS is case-insensitive

`ArtAttack/TeamColour.h:5` — **low** · `portability`

`TeamColour.h:5` is `#include "colour.h"`. `ls` confirms the file on disk is `Colour.h` (capital C) and there is no lowercase variant. This resolves on Windows/MSVC and nowhere else.

A repo-wide grep for `#include "colour.h"` returns exactly two offenders: TeamColour.h:5 and InterfaceGameplay.h:7. Every other include site spells it correctly. For a project whose stated goal is a reusable engine, a header that cannot be included on a case-sensitive filesystem is a hard portability wall and a two-character fix that MSVC will never tell you about.

**Fix:** Fix both sites to `#include "Colour.h"`, and do a one-off audit across the tree for any other mismatch between `#include "X"` spellings and the actual filenames.

#### 6. Include filename case mismatches will break any non-Windows or case-sensitive build of the engine

`ArtAttack/TeamColour.h:5 (also InterfaceGameplay.h:7)` — **low** · `robustness` · confidence: certain

The file on disk is `Colour.h`. Seven includes spell it correctly (`DrawObject.h:4`, `MenuHighlight.h:4`, `ResultsMenu.h:5`, `SpriteSheet.h:5`, `ViewportManager.h:8`, `Weapon.h:9`, `player_consts.h:6`) but two spell it `#include "colour.h"` — `TeamColour.h:5` and `InterfaceGameplay.h:7`. MSVC on NTFS does not care; clang/gcc on a case-sensitive filesystem, or a case-sensitive CI checkout, will fail to find the header.

For a codebase whose stated goal is a reusable engine this matters more than it would for a one-off Windows game: it is a one-character blocker on ever compiling the engine anywhere else, and it will be found only after the rest of the port is done.

**Fix:** Fix both includes to `"Colour.h"`. Consider a lint/CI step that compiles with clang-cl or checks include casing, so the engine stays portable-by-default as the rest of the DirectX coupling is abstracted out.

#### 7. Stateless all-static class is heap-allocated via unique_ptr to call its static functions, and two of its three functions are dead

`ArtAttack/TeamColour.h:44-55` — **low** · `design`

`class TeamColourTools` has no data members and three static functions. Yet `LevelBuilder.h:29` declares `std::unique_ptr<TeamColourTools> _team_colour = nullptr;`, `LevelBuilder.cpp:23` does `this->_team_colour = std::make_unique<TeamColourTools>();`, and `LevelBuilder.cpp:36` then calls a *static* member through the instance: `const TeamColour team_colours = _team_colour->generate_random_team_colour();`. A heap allocation, an owning smart pointer and a lifetime to reason about, all for zero bytes of state.

I grepped all first-party files: `TeamColourTools::get_team_colours` (:51) and `TeamColourTools::get_team_colour` (:53) have **zero callers**. `generate_random_team_colour` is called from exactly one place. Because `get_team_colours` is dead, `team_colour_enum` (:17-23) is never used to select anything — the player cannot choose a colour scheme, and the enum exists only to be miscounted by `generate_random_team_colour`.

The dead static `get_team_colour` also takes `TeamColour` **by value** (two non-trivially-copyable `Colour`s) and returns by value, duplicating the member function at :14 which returns `const Colour&`.

**Fix:** Delete the class. Make `generate_random_team_colour` a free function in a `team_colour` namespace, delete the two dead statics, and remove `LevelBuilder::_team_colour` and its allocation entirely. Then either wire `team_colour_enum` into the menu as a real option or delete it too. (`CollisionTools` has the identical all-static-class shape and deserves the same treatment.)

## `ArtAttack/TextDropShadow.cpp`

_1 finding: 1 high_

#### 1. TextDropShadow::draw renders by mutating and restoring its own base state, on an object shared across all render threads

`ArtAttack/TextDropShadow.cpp:28-48` — **high** · `concurrency`

```cpp
Colour original_color = this->get_colour();
Vector2F original_position = this->get_position();
float original_scale = this->get_scale();
this->TextObject::set_colour(this->_shadow_color);
this->TextObject::set_scale(this->_shadow_scale);
this->TextObject::set_position(this->get_position() + this->_shadow_offset);
this->TextObject::draw(sprite_batch, camera);
this->TextObject::set_colour(original_color);   // restore
this->TextObject::set_scale(original_scale);
this->TextObject::set_position(original_position);
this->TextObject::draw(sprite_batch, camera);
```
Save/mutate/restore at object granularity. Three consequences, all verified:

1. It is the reason `draw` is non-const, which is the direct cause of the override/hiding bug below.
2. It is a live data race. `Level::_countdown_text` is one shared `TextDropShadow`; `Level::draw_countdown_text(...) const` calls `this->_countdown_text->draw(...)` and is invoked from inside `draw_player_view_level`, which runs as one task per partition. Thread A can save `original_color` after thread B has already installed the black shadow colour; A then "restores" black permanently. Position and the `std::string` are read torn.
3. It is not exception-safe — `TextObject::draw` dereferences a `SpriteFont*` from a map lookup that can be null, and there is no scope guard, so a throw leaves the object permanently black and offset.

Note the const laundering that lets this compile: `draw_countdown_text` is a const member function, but `const` does not propagate through `unique_ptr`, so a non-const `draw` is reachable from it.

Separately, `_shadow_scale` (TextDropShadow.h:38) is independent of `_scale` and `Text::set_scale` does not touch it, so `set_scale(2.0f)` doubles the text and leaves the shadow behind. Level.cpp only avoids this by passing the same constant twice.

**Fix:** Give `TextObject` a private `draw_with(SpriteBatch*, const Camera&, const Colour&, const Vector2F& position, float scale) const` and have `TextDropShadow::draw(...) const` call it twice. No mutation, const-correct, thread-safe, exception-safe. Store the shadow scale as a multiplier of the text scale so the pair cannot desync.

## `ArtAttack/TextDropShadow.h`

_2 findings: 1 high, 1 medium_

#### 1. TextDropShadow::draw hides rather than overrides TextObject::draw — the const qualifier differs and no override keyword catches it

`ArtAttack/TextDropShadow.h:24-25` — **high** · `correctness`

```cpp
// TextObject.h:21-23
virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch, const MattMath::Camera& camera) const;
virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batch) const;

// TextDropShadow.h:24-25   -- no trailing const, no override
virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batc, const MattMath::Camera& camera);
virtual void draw(DirectX::SpriteBatch* sprite_batc);
```
Cv-qualification is part of the member-function signature, so these do not override anything. They start two new virtual slots and name-hide the base pair. Any call through a `Text*`, `TextObject*` or `const TextDropShadow&` dispatches to `TextObject::draw` and renders the text with no drop shadow at all, silently.

It only works today because every use site names the concrete type (`Level::_countdown_text` is `unique_ptr<TextDropShadow>`; the menus call `this->TextDropShadow::draw(...)` explicitly). The first person to store one in a `vector<unique_ptr<Text>>` loses the shadows with no diagnostic.

The missing `override` is exactly why the compiler is silent — `Text.h:21-24` uses `override` correctly on its four setters, `TextDropShadow.h` does not. The parameter is also misspelled `sprite_batc` in both header declarations while the definitions spell it `sprite_batch`, and the header is what shows in IntelliSense.

**Fix:** Add `const` and `override` to both and drop the redundant `virtual`. That requires making the body const, which the mutate-restore finding independently demands. Then apply `override` mechanically across the whole render hierarchy and enable `/w14263 /w14266` so MSVC flags hidden virtuals under the existing /W4.

#### 2. Constructors of 9-15 parameters with long runs of interchangeable defaulted floats, while the parameter-object struct the project already wrote sits unused

`ArtAttack/TextDropShadow.h:10-22` — **medium** · `api-design`

`TextDropShadow`'s constructor takes 13 parameters, nine defaulted, including four consecutive interchangeable floats (`scale`, `shadow_scale`, `rotation`, `layer_depth`) and two interchangeable pairs (`color`/`shadow_color`, `shadow_offset`/`origin`). Transposing any of them compiles cleanly and produces a subtly wrong render. `MTextDropShadow` (Mh.h) makes it 15 by inserting a bare `bool hidden` into the middle of the float run, so the call site reads as a naked `true`.

The same shape recurs at Visual.h:12-20 and :22-30, TextureObject.h:10-17, SpriteSheetObject.h:10-17, AnimationObject.h:11-19, TextObject.h:10-19, and four times in `SpriteSheet::draw` (SpriteSheet.h:19-59).

The project already knows the answer and did not apply it: `InterfaceGameplay.h:37-45` declares `struct InterfaceDraw` bundling exactly these fields, and a grep across all first-party sources finds it referenced at precisely one place — its own declaration. It is never constructed. Meanwhile `draw_gameplay_interface` takes nine loose positional parameters including four adjacent floats (`health, ammo, timer, ..., respawn_timer`) — swapping health and ammo silently swaps the two bars. The trailing `float respawn_timer, bool show_respawn_timer` is a textbook `std::optional<float>`. `InterfaceDraw` also disagrees with the real signature (`Vector2I resolution` vs `const Vector2F&`) and carries a `player_team` the function does not take — which is the only reason the header includes `player_team.h`.

Also: the argument actually passed as `resolution` is `player_vp.get_size()` (Level.cpp:558), a *viewport* size, so the parameter name is wrong in split-screen, which is the normal case. And `draw_gameplay_interface` is non-const while all four helpers it delegates to are const, despite mutating nothing.

**Fix:** Introduce `struct DrawStyle { Colour colour; float rotation; Vector2F origin; SpriteEffects effects; float layer_depth; }` and `struct ShadowStyle { Colour colour; Vector2F offset; float scale; }` and pass those. Either finish the `InterfaceDraw` refactor — `void draw(SpriteBatch*, ID3D11SamplerState*, const InterfaceDraw&, std::optional<float> respawn_timer) const` — or delete the struct and the `player_team.h` include. Rename `resolution` to `viewport_size` throughout. Replace `bool hidden` with `enum class visibility`.

## `ArtAttack/ThreadPool.h`

_5 findings: 2 high, 2 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. ThreadPool owns raw Win32 handles and declares a destructor but does not delete copy — the implicit copy ctor double-closes every handle

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.h:9-31` — **high** · `memory-safety`

Merged from 2 candidates. The class holds `PTP_POOL _pool`, `PTP_CLEANUP_GROUP _cleanup_group`, `TP_CALLBACK_ENVIRON _callback_environment` and `std::vector<PTP_WORK> _work_items` (ThreadPool.h:27-30), and `~ThreadPool()` (ThreadPool.cpp:30-36) closes all of them. No copy or move operation is deleted or defined, so the compiler-generated copy constructor and copy assignment are available and `ThreadPool b = a;` compiles into a double `CloseThreadpool` of the same handle. (The moves are suppressed by the user-declared destructor, so the class is copyable-but-not-movable — the worst combination.)

It cannot be correctly copied or moved even in principle: `add_task` registers work against `&_callback_environment` BY ADDRESS (ThreadPool.cpp:41) and `SetThreadpoolCallbackPool(&_callback_environment, _pool)` (line 26) was performed on the original address. The object is pinned in memory and nothing in the header says so.

Also verified: both constructor throw paths (ThreadPool.cpp:12 and :24) fire AFTER `InitializeThreadpoolEnvironment` succeeded at line 8, and neither calls `DestroyThreadpoolEnvironment` — the destructor does not run for a constructor that threw.

**Fix:** Add `ThreadPool(const ThreadPool&) = delete; ThreadPool& operator=(const ThreadPool&) = delete;` and explicitly delete the moves (or wrap each handle in its own RAII type so the destructor becomes `= default` and the ctor throw paths clean up automatically).

#### 2. ThreadPool owns raw OS handles with a user destructor but implicitly-defaulted copy/move — double-free waiting to happen

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.h:9-31` — **high** · `memory-safety` · confidence: certain

`ThreadPool` holds `PTP_POOL _pool`, `PTP_CLEANUP_GROUP _cleanup_group`, `TP_CALLBACK_ENVIRON _callback_environment`, and `std::vector<PTP_WORK> _work_items` (ThreadPool.h:27-30), declares `~ThreadPool()` which closes all of them (ThreadPool.cpp:30-36), and declares **no** copy/move operations. So copy construction and copy assignment are implicitly generated and shallow: two `ThreadPool` objects would own the same `PTP_POOL`/`PTP_CLEANUP_GROUP` and both destructors would call `CloseThreadpoolCleanupGroup`/`CloseThreadpool` on them.

Moving is worse than a plain double-free: `add_task` passes `&_callback_environment` to `CreateThreadpoolWork` (ThreadPool.cpp:41), so every outstanding work item holds the *address* of a member of the specific `ThreadPool` object. Any move (or the vector reallocation that a `std::vector<ThreadPool>` would perform) leaves live work items pointing at a dead callback environment.

Today it survives only because there is exactly one instance and it lives in a `unique_ptr` (Game.h:71) — accident, not design. For a reusable engine component this is exactly the class that must state its ownership contract.

**Fix:** `ThreadPool(const ThreadPool&) = delete; ThreadPool& operator=(const ThreadPool&) = delete;` and either delete the moves too or implement them properly (nulling the source handles). Better still, wrap each handle in a small RAII type so the destructor becomes `= default` and the rule of zero applies.

#### 3. ThreadPool.h includes <iostream> it never uses and leaks raw <windows.h> into every consumer

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.h:5-7` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

ThreadPool.h:7 includes <iostream>; ThreadPool.cpp contains no std::cout/cerr/endl (the only console output in the codebase is Save.cpp:47,51,90,93,97). <iostream> is one of the heaviest STL headers and injects a static std::ios_base::Init object into every TU that sees it. Save.h:4 does the same thing - it includes <iostream> and <chrono> for the benefit of Save.cpp, not the header. Between them 17 of 81 TUs parse <iostream> for nothing. Separately, ThreadPool.h:5 includes <windows.h> at header scope so that PTP_WORK/TP_CALLBACK_ENVIRON/PTP_POOL can appear as members (lines 27-30); every consumer of the thread pool therefore inherits the full Win32 macro soup. It only works today because pch.h defines WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN/NOMINMAX first - a header this one relies on but does not include.

**Fix:** Delete ThreadPool.h:7 and Save.h:4-5 (move <iostream>/<chrono> to the .cpp files). For ThreadPool, pimpl the Win32 handles so the header exposes only `void add_task(std::function<void()>)` and `void wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` - that also makes it swappable for a std::thread or std::jthread implementation, which is what a portable engine wants.

#### 4. ThreadPool has no batch identity and no documented thread affinity: one shared _work_items vector serves two unrelated subsystems

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.h:9-31` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

```cpp
class ThreadPool {
public:
    void add_task(std::function<void()> task);
    void wait_for_tasks_to_complete();   // drains EVERYTHING
private:
    std::vector<PTP_WORK> _work_items;   // :27  no mutex, no documentation of affinity
};
```

There is exactly one `ThreadPool` in the process (Game.cpp:236), published as a raw pointer through `GameData` (GameData.h:60) and used by two unrelated subsystems: `Level::draw_active_level`/`draw_zoom_out_level` (Level.cpp:388, 601) and `MenuPage::draw_mobjects_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:142).

I traced every caller: `add_task` appears at exactly those three sites, and none of the three task bodies (`draw_player_view_level`, `draw_zoom_out_level_component`, `draw_range_of_mobjects_in_viewports`) calls `add_task` — so today `_work_items` is only ever touched by the main thread and the unsynchronised vector is not *currently* racing. But nothing in the type says so, and two properties make that safety accidental rather than designed:

1. `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` drains and clears the entire vector. It has no idea which caller submitted what. The moment two owners have work in flight (nested draw, a task that spawns work, a second pool user added later), one owner's wait will `CloseThreadpoolWork` handles the other owner is still using — undefined behaviour with no diagnostic.
2. `GameLevel::draw` (GameStates.cpp:315-343) already interleaves the two users within one frame: `_level->draw(...)` submits and drains, then `_pause_menu->draw()` submits and drains against the *same* vector. It works only because the first drain completes before the second begins.

For a codebase whose stated goal is a reusable engine, an untyped, unowned, single-batch, thread-affine-by-accident pool is the wrong primitive to hand to arbitrary subsystems.

**Fix:** Return a handle from submission — `[[nodiscard]] TaskBatch submit(span<function<void()>>)` — and have `wait` be a member of the batch, so drains cannot cross owners. Add an assert (or a `std::thread::id` check in debug) that `add_task`/`wait_for_tasks_to_complete` are only ever called from the thread that created the pool, and say so in a comment on the class. Longer term this should be `std::async`/a `std::latch`-based parallel-for, not a hand-rolled wrapper over PTP_WORK; the Win32-specific bits are the least reusable part of the engine.

#### 5. ThreadPool.h includes <iostream> and uses no stream facility

`ArtAttack/ThreadPool.h:7` — **low** · `header-hygiene`

`#include <iostream>` at ThreadPool.h:7. I read both ThreadPool.h and ThreadPool.cpp in full — neither names `std::cout`, `std::cerr`, or any stream type. Since `GameData.h` includes `ThreadPool.h` and `GameData*` is the universal parameter, this drags the iostream machinery (and its static-initialisation cost) into nearly every translation unit in the project for nothing.

**Fix:** Delete the include.

## `ArtAttack/ViewportManager.cpp`

_9 findings: 5 high, 4 medium_

#### 1. apply_player_viewport(int) mutates the immediate context from a thread-pool worker and configures a batch belonging to a different context

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.cpp:63-70` — **high** · `correctness`

```
void ViewportManager::apply_player_viewport(int player_num) const
{
    D3D11_VIEWPORT vp = ...;
    auto context = this->_device_resources->GetD3DDeviceContext();  // IMMEDIATE context
    context->RSSetViewports(1, &vp);
    this->_sprite_batch->SetViewport(vp);                            // SpriteBatch #0, bound to DEFERRED context 0
}
```
`_sprite_batch` is wired at construction to `get_sprite_batches()->at(0)` (Game.cpp:247-249), which was built on deferred context 0 (Game.cpp:229). The two halves of one call target two different contexts, so the `RSSetViewports` is not part of the command list being recorded — the deferred context keeps whatever viewport `Game::clear()` last set.

The only live caller is `Level::draw_zoom_out_level_component` (Level.cpp:620), which runs **inside a thread-pool task** (Level.cpp:601-606). `ID3D11DeviceContext` is not free-threaded and the immediate context must never be touched from a worker while the main thread is in `clear()`/`Present()`. The same task also does `this->_viewport_manager->set_layout(screen_layout::ONE_PLAYER)` (Level.cpp:619) — mutating shared manager state from a worker and never restoring it. It only appears to work because the forced ONE_PLAYER viewport happens to equal the fullscreen one.

**Fix:** Delete this overload and the `_sprite_batch` / `_device_resources` members (ViewportManager.h:47-48) — a viewport calculator has no business owning a device or a batch. Keep only the overloads that take the context and batch explicitly, which is what the rest of the draw code already uses. Move `set_layout` out of the draw path.

#### 2. get_all_viewports() asks for viewport index 4 in a 3-player layout, so every menu draws a spurious 4th fullscreen copy

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.cpp:90-104` — **high** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

std::vector<Viewport> ViewportManager::get_all_viewports() const
    {
        std::vector<Viewport> result;
        int player_count = this->get_player_count_from_layout(this->_layout);
        for (int i = 0; i < player_count; i++)
            result.push_back(this->get_player_viewport(i));
        // Add a 4th viewport if there are 3 players
        if (player_count == 3)
            result.push_back(this->get_player_viewport(4));   // <-- should be 3
        return result;
    }

Index 4 does not exist. Tracing `calculate_viewport(THREE_PLAYER, 4, ...)`: the inner `switch (player_num)` has cases 0/1/2 only, hits `default: break;` (ViewportManager.cpp:205-206) — and because `case screen_layout::THREE_PLAYER:` has no `break` before `case screen_layout::FOUR_PLAYER:` (line 208), control falls into the FOUR_PLAYER switch, misses again (line 235-236), falls into `default: //1P screen` (line 238) and returns a **fullscreen** viewport.

`MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:99-115) loops over exactly this vector, so in any 3-player match the pause menu (PauseMenu.cpp:205), the results menu (ResultsMenu.cpp:211) and the end menu (EndMenu.cpp:241) are each drawn 3 times in quadrants plus once stretched over the whole screen.

The same missing `break` also corrupts the TWO_PLAYER case: `calculate_viewport(TWO_PLAYER, 2, ...)` falls out of lines 181-183 into the THREE_PLAYER switch and returns the three-player bottom-left rect.

**Fix:** Change `get_player_viewport(4)` to `get_player_viewport(3)`. Add the missing `break;` after each layout case in `calculate_viewport` (lines 183, 207) so a bad `player_num` reaches the intended fallback instead of silently borrowing another layout's geometry — or better, make the function a table lookup returning `optional`/throwing on an out-of-range index rather than silently returning fullscreen.

#### 3. get_all_viewports asks for player 4 to fill the empty 3-player quadrant and receives a fullscreen viewport

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.cpp:98-102` — **high** · `correctness`

```
// Add a 4th viewport if there are 3 players
if (player_count == 3)
{
    result.push_back(this->get_player_viewport(4));
}
```
Valid indices are 0..3. Traced with `_layout == THREE_PLAYER`: index 4 misses the THREE_PLAYER inner switch (`default: break` at :205), falls into FOUR_PLAYER, misses again (:235), and lands in the outer `default:` at :238 — a **fullscreen** viewport. THREE_PLAYER assigns 0=top-left, 1=bottom-right, 2=bottom-left, so the intended fill is the empty top-right quadrant.

`MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:99-115) iterates the returned vector: for `i == 3` it calls `apply_player_viewport(3, …)` — which under THREE_PLAYER falls through to FOUR_PLAYER case 3 = **bottom-right**, a duplicate of player 1's viewport — and then draws the widget positioned against `viewports[3]`, which is the **fullscreen** rect. The two disagree, so in a 3-player menu the fourth pass lays the widget out for a full screen while scissoring it to the bottom-right quadrant, and the actually-blank top-right quadrant is never drawn into.

**Fix:** The empty quadrant is index 1 of the FOUR_PLAYER layout: `result.push_back(calculate_viewport(screen_layout::FOUR_PLAYER, 1, res));`. Also reorder THREE_PLAYER so 1 = top-right and 2 = bottom-left — the current 0=TL, 1=BR, 2=BL is surprising on its own.

#### 4. calculate_viewport's layout cases fall through — an out-of-range player index silently gets another layout's geometry

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.cpp:154-245` — **high** · `correctness`

Every outer `case` ends with an inner `switch (player_num)` whose `default:` is `break`, and there is no `break`/`return` after the inner switch:

- TWO_PLAYER (:166-183) inner `default: break;` at :181-182 falls into `case THREE_PLAYER:` at :184
- THREE_PLAYER (:184-207) inner `default: break;` at :205-206 falls into `case FOUR_PLAYER:` at :208
- FOUR_PLAYER (:208-237) inner `default: break;` at :235-236 falls into `default:` at :238, which returns a fullscreen viewport

So `calculate_viewport(TWO_PLAYER, 2, …)` returns the THREE_PLAYER top-left quadrant, and `calculate_viewport(THREE_PLAYER, 3, …)` returns the FOUR_PLAYER bottom-right quadrant (a duplicate of what THREE_PLAYER already gives player 1). A bad index produces plausible-looking but wrong geometry instead of a diagnosable failure, and MSVC emits no implicit-fallthrough warning even at /W4. Callers pass unvalidated indices: `Level.cpp:503` passes `get_player_num()` straight from level data, `MenuPage.cpp:107-108` passes a `size_t` loop counter. This is also the mechanism behind the `get_player_viewport(4)` bug reported separately.

**Fix:** Replace the whole 90-line double switch with one static table of normalised rects — `static constexpr struct { float x, y, w, h; } LAYOUTS[4][4]` indexed by `[layout][player]` and multiplied by `screen_size`. That removes the fall-through by construction and makes a 6-player layout a data edit. Bounds-check `player_num` against `get_player_count_from_layout(layout)` and assert rather than returning fullscreen.

#### 5. Fall-through in calculate_viewport makes the 3-player layout draw a 4th full-screen viewport over everything

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.cpp:166-244` — **high** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

The outer `switch (layout)` has no `break` or `return` on the fall-out path of any case. `case screen_layout::TWO_PLAYER:` (line 166) contains an inner switch whose `default: break;` (line 181-182) falls straight into `case screen_layout::THREE_PLAYER:` (line 184), whose `default: break;` (205-206) falls into `case screen_layout::FOUR_PLAYER:` (208), whose `default: break;` (235-236) falls into `default: //1P screen` (238) returning a full-screen viewport.

This is not theoretical. `ViewportManager::get_all_viewports` (ViewportManager.cpp:90-104) does:

    if (player_count == 3) { result.push_back(this->get_player_viewport(4)); }

With `_layout == THREE_PLAYER` and `player_num == 4`, THREE_PLAYER's inner switch misses, falls into FOUR_PLAYER's inner switch (which only handles 0-3), misses again, and lands on the 1P default — returning `{0, 0, screen_size.x, screen_size.y}`. `MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:99-115) draws each widget once per entry of `get_all_viewports()`, so in every 3-player game the pause menu, results menu and HUD get a 4th copy stretched across the whole screen on top of the three player panels. The index is also off by one: the intended empty bottom-right quadrant is FOUR_PLAYER's `player_num == 3`, not 4.

**Fix:** Give every case an explicit `return`/`break`, use `player_num == 3` for the filler quadrant, and replace the nested switches with a small table (layout -> array of normalised rects) so a missing entry is a compile-time or assert failure rather than a silent fall-through.

#### 6. Split-screen layout is a hardcoded 1-4 player table with fall-through switches and an out-of-range lookup

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.cpp:90-104, 154-240 (with screen_layout.h:4-11)` — **medium** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

`screen_layout` (screen_layout.h:4-11) is `{ONE_PLAYER, TWO_PLAYER, THREE_PLAYER, FOUR_PLAYER}` and `calculate_viewport` (ViewportManager.cpp:154-240) is a hand-written nested switch table for each. There is no way to express 5+ views, a non-quadrant split, or a picture-in-picture minimap — an engine viewport module should compute a grid, not enumerate cases.

Worse, the outer switch has no `break`/`return` after each inner switch's `default: break;` (lines 181-184, 205-207, 235-237), so out-of-range player numbers silently fall through to the *next* layout's case and ultimately to `default: //1P screen` (:238). `get_all_viewports()` exploits this by accident: at lines 98-102, when `player_count == 3` it calls `this->get_player_viewport(4)` to add a filler 4th viewport — but valid indices are 0..3, so index 4 falls all the way through and returns a **fullscreen** viewport instead of the empty bottom-right quadrant. In 3-player mode the divider/filler viewport therefore covers the whole screen.

**Fix:** Replace the enum + switch table with `set_view_count(int n)` and a computed grid (`cols = ceil(sqrt(n))`, etc.), returning `Viewport` from arithmetic. Immediately: change line 101 to `get_player_viewport(3)`, and add `break;`/`return` after each inner switch so out-of-range indices are a hard error rather than a silent fullscreen viewport.

#### 7. get_camera_adjusted_player_viewport_rect multiplies by camera scale where it must divide

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.cpp:29-43` — **medium** · `correctness`

```
Viewport vp = this->get_player_viewport(player_num);
const float scale = camera.scale;
auto result = RectangleF(translation.x, translation.y, vp.width * scale, vp.height * scale);
```
The result is used as a WORLD-space culling rect: `Level::draw_player_view_level` feeds it into `object->is_visible_in_viewport(camera_view)` at Level.cpp:518, 527, 536.

`Camera::scale` is world→screen: `calculate_view_rectangle` computes `(world - translation) * scale` (MattMath.cpp:4119-4122) and `calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle` sets `scale = world_rectangle.width / view_rectangle.width` (MattMath.cpp:4167). The world extent covered by a `vp.width`-pixel viewport is therefore `vp.width / scale`, not `vp.width * scale`, and the error compounds to a factor of scale-squared.

Currently latent: every camera reaching this function comes from `CameraTools::calculate_camera`, which only ever adjusts `translation` and leaves `scale` at 1.0, and the zoom-out path (Level.cpp:150-159) does not use this function. Any zoom feature — or any reuse of ViewportManager in another game, which is the stated goal — makes objects get culled exactly when they should become visible.

**Fix:** `vp.width / scale, vp.height / scale`, with a guard against `scale == 0.0f` (a lerp to a degenerate camera or a zero-width `view_rectangle` in `calculate_camera_from_view_rectangle` would produce inf/NaN that then poisons every `is_visible_in_viewport` comparison). Add a test at scale 0.5 asserting the world rect doubles.

#### 8. apply_player_viewport(int) sets the viewport on the immediate context from a worker thread, for a SpriteBatch owned by deferred context 0

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.cpp:63-70` — **medium** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

void ViewportManager::apply_player_viewport(int player_num) const
    {
        D3D11_VIEWPORT vp = ...;
        auto context = this->_device_resources->GetD3DDeviceContext();   // IMMEDIATE context
        context->RSSetViewports(1, &vp);
        this->_sprite_batch->SetViewport(vp);
    }

`_sprite_batch` is `sprite_batches->at(0)` (Game.cpp:247-249), and sprite batch 0 was constructed on *deferred* context 0 (Game.cpp:229). So this overload configures the immediate context and a deferred-context SpriteBatch together — the deferred context that will actually record the draws never gets the viewport.

Its only caller is `Level::draw_zoom_out_level_component` (Level.cpp:620), which runs inside a thread-pool task submitted at Level.cpp:601, so `RSSetViewports` is issued against the immediate context from a worker thread while `Game::render` is on the main thread's stack — ID3D11DeviceContext is not thread-safe. It happens to be serialised today only because the main thread blocks in `wait_for_tasks_to_complete()` (Level.cpp:606). The recorded command list (Level.cpp:646) therefore inherits whatever viewport `Game::clear` last set on deferred context 0 (Game.cpp:146-149, the full backbuffer), which coincidentally looks right only while backbuffer size == saved resolution. Line 619 also mutates shared `ViewportManager` state (`set_layout(ONE_PLAYER)`) from a worker thread inside a `const` member function, and never restores the previous layout.

**Fix:** Delete the one-argument overload; the zoom-out path should use `apply_player_viewport(0, deferred_contexts->at(0), sprite_batches->at(0))` like the rest of the draw code. Nothing on a worker thread should ever touch the immediate context, and `set_layout` should not be called from a `const` draw function.

#### 9. Viewports are recomputed on every query, including a heap allocation per widget per frame from worker threads

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.cpp:84-104, 123-152` — **medium** · `performance`

`ViewportManager` caches nothing. `get_player_viewport` (:84-88) calls `_resolution_manager->get_resolution_vec()` — itself a switch plus a `Vector2I`→`Vector2F` construction (ResolutionManager.cpp:47-74) — and then runs the 90-line layout switch, on every call. Viewports change only when the layout or resolution changes, at most once per level load.

Call sites are per-frame or hotter: Level.cpp:82 and :198 (per player per update), Level.cpp:505, 510, 544 (per player per frame in the record path), and worst, `MenuPage::draw_mobject_in_viewports` (MenuPage.cpp:99-100) calls `get_all_viewports()` — which heap-allocates a fresh `std::vector<Viewport>` — once for **every MObject drawn**, on worker threads, every frame. `get_viewport_dividers()` (:123-152) allocates a fresh vector per call too.

**Fix:** Compute the viewport set and divider rects once in `set_layout()` (and on a resolution-change notification) into a fixed `std::array<Viewport, 4>` plus a count, and return `const Viewport&` / `const std::vector<RectangleF>&`. That also removes the per-call dependency on `_resolution_manager` from the multi-threaded draw path.

## `ArtAttack/ViewportManager.h`

_3 findings: 1 high, 1 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. The engine's split-screen viewport manager hardcodes this game's texture atlas and frame names

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.h:10-16 (consumed at LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:236-241)` — **high** · `design` · confidence: certain

`ViewportManager` is otherwise clean engine presentation code, but its header opens with:
```
namespace viewport_consts {
    constexpr float DIVIDER_THICKNESS = 2.0f;
    const std::string DIVIDER_SHEET_NAME = "sprite_sheet_1";
    const std::string DIVIDER_FRAME_NAME  = "pixel";
    const MattMath::Colour DIVIDER_COLOUR = colour_consts::BLACK;
}
```
`LevelObjectBuilder.cpp:236-241` then builds the divider `Visual`s from those constants. A viewport/window-layout module now has a hard dependency on the existence of a texture atlas literally named `sprite_sheet_1` containing a frame named `pixel`, plus a compile-time colour choice. Any second game must ship an atlas with those exact names or its split-screen dividers silently fail resource lookup.

This is the representative site of a repo-wide pattern — `"sprite_sheet_1"` appears in 34 places and the `gill_sans_*` font names in 15, including in files that should be engine: `DebugText.h:11` (`courier_new_bold_16`), `InterfaceGameplay.h:18,26,31`, and `Level.h:36`.

**Fix:** Make divider appearance a `ViewportManager` construction parameter (`DividerStyle{sheet, frame, colour, thickness}`) supplied by the game, defaulting to a 1x1 white pixel the engine itself owns. More broadly, no engine header should contain a string literal naming a content file — route all of them through a game-supplied style/theme struct or the content manifest.

#### 2. Sprite-sheet names and a colour for split-screen dividers are declared in the viewport header, as per-TU const std::strings

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.h:10-16` — **medium** · `design`

```
namespace viewport_consts
{
    constexpr float DIVIDER_THICKNESS = 2.0f;
    const std::string DIVIDER_SHEET_NAME = "sprite_sheet_1";
    const std::string DIVIDER_FRAME_NAME = "pixel";
    const MattMath::Colour DIVIDER_COLOUR = colour_consts::BLACK;
}
```
Two problems. (1) A viewport/display service has no business knowing which sprite sheet a divider is skinned from — these are consumed by `LevelObjectBuilder::build_viewport_dividers`, and they force ViewportManager.h to include Colour.h. (2) Namespace-scope `const` objects have internal linkage, so every TU that includes this header gets its own copy with its own dynamic initialiser (two heap-allocating std::strings plus a Colour constructor at static-init time). ViewportManager.h is included by GameData.h:9, which almost every file in the project includes — dozens of duplicate objects and static initialisers for three constants used at one site.

**Fix:** `ViewportManager` should return only geometry (`std::vector<RectangleF> divider_rects() const`); the sheet name, frame name and colour move to game-side UI content, ideally the level/theme JSON. Drop the Colour.h dependency from the header. If they must stay, use `inline constexpr std::string_view` (needs C++17) or `extern const` declared here and defined once in the .cpp.

#### 3. ViewportManager.h drags DeviceResources.h, MattMath.h and Colour.h into nearly every TU, and ships three near-identical overloads

`ArtAttack/ViewportManager.h:1-8, 27-32` — **low** · `design`

The header includes ResolutionManager.h, DeviceResources.h, MattMath.h and Colour.h (:4-8), yet `ResolutionManager`, `DX::DeviceResources` and `DirectX::SpriteBatch` appear only as pointer members/parameters (:21-23, 46-48) and could all be forward-declared. Because GameData.h:9 includes this header, the ~4000-line MattMath.h and the D3D-heavy DeviceResources.h are pulled into essentially the whole project.

The three `apply_player_viewport` overloads (:27, :28-30, :31-32) have bodies that are the same three lines with different sources for the context and batch (ViewportManager.cpp:45-70); the 1-arg version silently uses ambient state and is the subject of a separate finding. `get_player_count_from_layout` (:52, defined :106-121) is a `const` member that never touches `this`.

**Fix:** Forward-declare `class ResolutionManager;`, `namespace DX { class DeviceResources; }`, `namespace DirectX { class SpriteBatch; }` and move the includes to the .cpp. Delete the ambient overload and collapse the remaining two into one with a defaulted batch parameter. Make `get_player_count_from_layout` a static free function.

## `ArtAttack/weapon_consts.h`

_5 findings: 2 high, 1 medium, 2 low_

#### 1. All weapon tuning is a compile-time C++ table in a header while the rest of the content pipeline is data-driven JSON

`ArtAttack/weapon_consts.h:14-168` — **high** · `design`

weapon_consts.h holds twelve namespace-scope aggregates (`DETAILS_DEFAULT` :14, `DETAILS_RELATIVE_DEFAULT` :30, `DETAILS_SPRAYER` :36, `DETAILS_RELATIVE_SPRAYER` :52, `SPRAYER_SOUND_DETAILS` :58, `DETAILS_SNIPER` :70, `DETAILS_ROLLER` :86, `ROLLER_SOUND_DETAILS` :102, `DETAILS_MISTER` :114, `DETAILS_RELATIVE_MISTER` :130, `MISTER_SOUND_DETAILS` :136, `DETAILS_BUCKET` :148, `DETAILS_RELATIVE_BUCKET` :164) built by positional aggregate initialisation with field names only in trailing comments. Changing a fire rate recompiles the game, while levels and sound banks already load from rapidjson (`SoundBank::load_from_json`, `LevelObjectBuilder`).

The positional style has already drifted: `DETAILS_DEFAULT` (:16-20) has five unlabelled leading values, and `DETAILS_ROLLER` sets `starting_vel_length` to `0.0f` (:92) against a struct default of `1100.0f` (WeaponDetails.h:41) with no explanation. The table also couples to the projectile table at namespace scope - `nozzle_offset` is `projectile_consts::DETAILS_SPRAY.size.x / 2.0f` (:40, and likewise :74, :90, :118, :152).

Separately, every one of these is `static` at namespace scope in a header, i.e. internal linkage: one dynamically-initialised copy **per translation unit**. `WeaponDetails` has five `std::string` members (WeaponDetails.h:43-47) and `SoundEffectInstanceWeaponDetails` has eight (WeaponDetails.h:23-30), so each TU runs ~50 `std::string` constructions before `main`. weapon_consts.h reaches Weapon.h:7 -> all five Weapon*.h -> WeaponBuilder.h -> PlayerBuilder.h, and Player.h -> Level.h onwards, so this is multiplied a dozen-plus times.

**Fix:** Move weapon definitions to `weapons.json` loaded into a `WeaponRegistry`, mirroring how levels load - the engine ships the struct and the registry, the game ships the data. As an interim step, declare the tables `extern const` in the header and define them once in a `weapon_consts.cpp`; once the project moves off its default C++14 (see the vcxproj finding), `inline constexpr` with `std::string_view` removes the dynamic initialisation entirely.

#### 2. Fire rate is quantised to the tick rate (shoot_interval 0.0f / 0.0001f) and nothing caps live projectiles feeding an all-pairs collision loop

`ArtAttack/weapon_consts.h:41, 91` — **high** · `performance`

`DETAILS_SPRAYER.shoot_interval = 0.0f` (weapon_consts.h:41) and `DETAILS_ROLLER.shoot_interval = 0.0001f` (:91), against the gate `if (get_shoot_timer() > get_shoot_interval() && ...)` with `set_shoot_timer(0.0f)` on fire and `alter_shoot_timer(dt)` at the end (Weapon.cpp:202-227). With an interval below `dt`, these weapons emit exactly one projectile per update tick, so DPS and paint rate are a function of the simulation tick rate, not wall-clock time.

The volume this produces meets a brute-force collision phase. Spray projectiles live 5 s (`projectile_consts.h:32 delete_timer = 5.0f`), and `Level::update_level_logic` (Level.cpp:255-290) runs `for (object : _collision_objects) for (object_2 : _collision_objects)` - a full O(n^2) all-pairs `is_colliding` sweep with no broad phase, on top of an O(players x n) pass. Four continuously-firing sprayers put the live list into the high hundreds, i.e. ~10^5-10^6 virtual `is_colliding` calls per frame.

The roller is pure churn: `shoot_interval 0.0001f` with `DETAILS_ROLLING.delete_timer = 0.000001f` (projectile_consts.h:66) heap-allocates a full `ProjectileRolling` every tick purely to stamp paint, then destroys it the same tick.

Secondary timing defects at the same site: the reset-to-zero discards overshoot, so the real interval is always `shoot_interval + dt` (sniper's configured 1.0 s is 61 frames = 1.017 s at 60 Hz), and `>` rather than `>=` means the very first update after construction never fires.

**Fix:** Give every weapon a real non-zero interval in seconds, increment the timer at the top of the update, compare with `>=`, and on fire do `alter_shoot_timer(-get_shoot_interval())` (or a `while` loop) so leftover time carries over and the rate is tick-rate independent. Cap live projectiles per player with a recycling pool. For the roller, replace the one-tick throwaway projectile with a direct paint call.

#### 3. All game tuning and content data is compiled into C++ headers, so content changes require rebuilding

`ArtAttack/weapon_consts.h:14-56 (and projectile_consts.h:23-104, player_consts.h:20-121)` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: likely

Levels are data (`levels/*.json`) but everything else is source. `weapon_consts.h:14-56` defines `DETAILS_SPRAYER` etc. as `static const WeaponDetails` aggregates carrying sizes, velocities, ammo costs, sprite frame names (`"sprite_sheet_1"`, `"sprayer"`), sound bank and cue names; `projectile_consts.h` does the same for 6 projectile types; `player_consts.h:20-121` holds gravity, jump velocity, per-weapon damage values (`SPRAY_DAMAGE`, `JET_DAMAGE`, ...), sound cue names and 5 `PlayerAnimationInfo` records naming animation strips.

The inconsistency is the tell: the engine already has a JSON pipeline (rapidjson, `LevelLoadedInfo`, `SpriteSheet::load_from_json`, `SoundBank::load_from_json`) and uses it for levels, atlases and sound banks — but not for the entities. Balancing a weapon is a full rebuild of ~81 TUs, and a second game inherits the pattern of writing content in headers. (These are also namespace-scope non-`constexpr` `const` objects in headers: one copy plus dynamic init per including TU.)

**Fix:** Move weapon/projectile/player definitions into `content/*.json` parsed by the existing builders (`WeaponBuilder`, `ProjectileBuilder`, `PlayerBuilder` already exist and would be the natural readers). Keep only genuinely structural constants in headers, and mark those `inline constexpr`.

#### 4. Weapon asset names are string literals duplicated across three files with no load-time validation

`ArtAttack/weapon_consts.h:44-48, 58-68` — **low** · `robustness`

Each `WeaponDetails` entry hardcodes `sheet_name`/`frame_name`/`sound_bank_name`/`shoot_sound_name` as literals (e.g. weapon_consts.h:44-48 `"sprite_sheet_1", "sprayer", ..., "sound_bank_1", "WaterSprayIntoBucket"`), and the three `SoundEffectInstanceWeaponDetails` tables (:58-68, :102-112, :136-146) hardcode 24 more instance names. Every one must match an entry in `ArtAttack/sounds/sound_bank_1.json` (spot-checked: `sprayer_a0` -> wave `WaterSprayIntoBucket` at lines 33-34, currently correct) and every frame name a sprite-sheet entry. Nothing checks either. A rename on the sound side becomes an `std::out_of_range` thrown mid-frame from `handle_shoot_sound` with no catch on the path; a rename on the texture side is worse - `SpriteSheet::draw`'s `_sprite_frames[frame_name]` silently *inserts* a default frame and the weapon just goes invisible with no diagnostic at all.

**Fix:** Add a one-shot validation pass after resource loading that walks the weapon tables and asserts every referenced sheet/frame/bank/instance name resolves, failing with a message naming the offending weapon and key. Better, move the weapon table into JSON alongside the assets it references. Make `SpriteSheet::draw` use `find()` and report a missing frame rather than inserting one.

#### 5. DETAILS_ROLLER.shoot_sound_volume = 3.0f is silently clamped to 1.0 and does nothing

`ArtAttack/weapon_consts.h:99` — **low** · `robustness`

`DETAILS_ROLLER` sets `3.0f, //shoot_sound_volume`. `WeaponRoller` does not override `handle_shoot_sound`, so it goes through `SoundBank::play_effect`, whose first statement is `clamp_levels(volume, pitch, pan)` (SoundBank.cpp:32), and `clamp_levels` does `volume = clamp(volume, 0.0f, 1.0f)` (SoundBank.cpp:174-178). `play_wave` clamps identically (SoundBank.cpp:18). So 3.0 becomes 1.0 with no diagnostic - whoever wrote it wanted the roller louder and got no indication the request was discarded. Every other weapon's volume (0.2-1.0) is in range, so this is the sole outlier and the config table now carries a value that is a lie.

**Fix:** Set it to 1.0f and fix the loudness in the asset, or raise the ceiling in `clamp_levels` (XAudio2 accepts gain > 1.0) if amplification is genuinely wanted. A constant should never silently disagree with the engine that consumes it.

## `ArtAttack/Weapon.h`

_12 findings: 1 high, 6 medium, 5 low_

#### 1. Weapon is a god class welded to DirectX and to Splatoon's team/player concepts - the core obstacle to engine reuse

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:14-143` — **high** · `design`

Merging four related design reports, all verified:

1. `class Weapon : public TextureObject` (Weapon.h:14) - a weapon *is* a sprite frame. Weapon.h therefore transitively pulls in SpriteSheetObject.h -> DrawObject.h -> ResourceManager.h -> D3D/SpriteBatch, so the whole weapon module compiles against DirectX. A weapon with two sprites, no sprite, or particle-only presentation cannot exist.
2. One type owns six responsibilities: rendering (`draw`, Weapon.cpp:36-82), input interpretation (`update_movement_and_rotation` reads `input.shoot_direction_requested` / `input.shoot_angle`, Weapon.cpp:283-285), ammo economy (`_ammo`/`_ammo_timer`, :217-227), fire timing (`_shoot_timer` vs `_details.shoot_interval`, :202), audio (owns a `SoundBank*`, names per-team instances, :236-277), and object spawning (owns a `ProjectileBuilder`, returns owned `ICollisionGameObject`s, :313-328). None of the pure arithmetic (ammo regen, fire rate) can be unit-tested without a live `ResourceManager` with loaded sheets and sound banks.
3. The base constructor takes `player_team team, int player_num, const Colour& team_colour, wep_type type` and stores all four (Weapon.h:135-138). `player_team` is a closed A/B/NONE enum; `_player_num` exists only to index eight hardcoded sound names; `_team_colour` is a paint rule. All four are forwarded verbatim into `ProjectileBuilder::build_projectiles` (Weapon.cpp:319-327) - the weapon is a conduit for game rules it never uses.
4. Both update entry points take the game's gamepad struct `PlayerInputData` by value (Weapon.h:36, 106, 110) and read exactly three of its thirteen fields. An AI turret or replay system would have to fabricate a `PlayerInputData` including a `connection_state` (PlayerInputData.h:7-23) to pull a trigger.

**Fix:** Decompose: an immutable `WeaponDefinition` (already almost `WeaponDetails`), a `FireControl { bool try_fire(dt); }`, an `AmmoPool`, a data-driven audio policy, and a separate render component that consumes an emitted `WeaponRenderState`. Replace `PlayerInputData` with a tiny engine-level `WeaponIntent { bool fire; bool aim_requested; float aim_angle; }` that the game maps onto in one place.
