Replace team/player/colour with one opaque `OwnerId` plus a game-supplied spawn payload forwarded untouched. Rendering becomes a member/observer, not a base class.

#### 2. 13/14-parameter constructors with five dead trailing parameters, copy-pasted across six classes

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:17-29` — **medium** · `api-design`

`Weapon`'s constructor takes 13 parameters and `RelativeVelocityWeapon`'s 14 (Weapon.h:148-161). The trailing five - `color`, `rotation`, `origin`, `effects`, `layer_depth` - are forwarded to `TextureObject` (Weapon.cpp:21-22) and **never supplied by any caller**: `WeaponBuilder::build_weapon` passes exactly 7 arguments in all five branches (WeaponBuilder.cpp:18-37). They are then re-declared verbatim in all five concrete weapon headers (WeaponSprayer.h:16-20, WeaponSniper.h:16-20, WeaponRoller.h:16-20, WeaponMister.h:16-20, WeaponBucket.h:16-20) and re-forwarded verbatim in all five .cpp files - roughly 60 lines of pure pass-through.

Three of the five are worse than unused: `draw` unconditionally overwrites origin, effects and rotation every frame (Weapon.cpp:62-64; WeaponRoller.cpp:86-88), so passing anything but the defaults does nothing. And `rotation` is *not* used to initialise `Weapon::_rotation` - that member is absent from the ctor init list (Weapon.cpp:23-30) and keeps its NSDMI of `0.0f` (Weapon.h:128). Since `_rotation` is the aim angle driving `get_draw_pos`, `get_nozzle_pos`, `facing_left` and the launch direction, constructing a weapon with `rotation = PI` yields a weapon aiming right.

The leading parameters are also a fixed bundle repeated eight times: `(team, player_num, team_colour, type, player_center, resource_manager, dt)`.

**Fix:** Delete the five trailing parameters from `Weapon`, `RelativeVelocityWeapon` and all five subclasses. Group the rest into one `struct WeaponSpawnContext` passed by const reference so each concrete constructor is a single line and adding a dependency touches one struct rather than six headers and six .cpp files. If an initial aim angle is genuinely wanted, add one `float aim_rotation` that actually initialises `_rotation`.

#### 3. `alter_*` mutators name their delta parameter after the field, so call sites read as assignment

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:82-88` — **medium** · `naming` · confidence: certain

The codebase has an `alter_x(delta)` idiom meaning "add delta to x", but half the declarations name the parameter as if it were the new value:
  Wrong: `Weapon.h:85 void alter_ammo(float ammo);` (adds to ammo), `Weapon.h:82 void alter_shoot_timer(float dt);` and `:88 void alter_ammo_timer(float dt);` (parameter is a delta that happens to usually be dt, so the name hardcodes one caller's argument), `Projectile.h:65 void alter_timer(float time);`, `MovingObject.h:25 alter_velocity(const Vector2F& velocity)`, `:37/:41 alter_dx(const Vector2F& dx)`, `:51 alter_rotation(float rotation)`.
  Right: `Player.h:232 void alter_health(float change);`, `:236 alter_respawn_timer(float change)`, `:240 alter_air_time(float change)`, `:244 alter_score(int change)`.
A reader hitting `alter_ammo(0.007f)` next to `set_ammo(0.007f)` has no way to tell them apart from the signatures.

**Fix:** Two changes: (1) rename the verb to something unambiguous - `add_ammo` / `add_to_shoot_timer`, or drop them for `operator+=`-style helpers; (2) name every parameter `delta` or `change`, matching the four Player.h declarations that already get it right. Never name a delta `dt`.

#### 4. Base and derived declare same-named virtuals with different signatures - nothing overrides, everything hides

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:96-101, 170-179` — **medium** · `design`

`Weapon` declares `virtual shoot(const Vector2F&) const` (Weapon.h:96-97) and `virtual calculate_projectile_launch_velocity(const Vector2F&, float) const` (:99-101). `RelativeVelocityWeapon` declares same-named functions with different signatures (`shoot(dir, player_velocity)` :177-179; `calculate_projectile_launch_velocity(dir, speed, player_vel, add_vel, amount)` :170-175), also `virtual`, neither `override`. These are new virtuals that merely *hide* the base names in the derived scope.

So `Weapon::shoot(dir)` remains a live virtual that, invoked on a WeaponSprayer/Mister/Bucket through a `Weapon*`, silently produces a launch velocity with no owner-velocity contribution - the entire point of the subclass. It is unreachable today only because `RelativeVelocityWeapon` also overrides `update_and_get_projectiles`, which is why that function had to be duplicated at all. All four are `virtual` while nothing overrides any of them: four vtable slots for no polymorphism.

Related at the same site: `RelativeVelocityWeapon::update_and_get_projectiles` calls two virtuals through explicit class qualification - `Weapon::update_movement_and_rotation(...)` (Weapon.cpp:582) and `Weapon::check_if_shooting_and_ammo_update(...)` (:585) - which suppresses virtual dispatch. `update_movement_and_rotation` is genuinely overridden elsewhere (WeaponRoller.cpp:29). The base's own version correctly uses `this->` (Weapon.cpp:174, 177). No current subclass is affected, but any future subclass of `RelativeVelocityWeapon` overriding either hook would be silently ignored.

**Fix:** Collapse to one virtual with the full parameter set: `virtual Vector2F calculate_launch_velocity(const Vector2F& dir, const Vector2F& owner_velocity) const` (base ignores the second argument) and one non-virtual `shoot(dir, owner_velocity)` that calls it. Then `update_and_get_projectiles` exists once, `RelativeVelocityWeapon` genuinely overrides, and the qualified calls become `this->`. Mark every intended override `override` - the compiler would have caught all of this immediately.

#### 5. Weapon stores a second copy of the ResourceManager pointer and overrides the base getter to return it

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:118, 122-124` — **medium** · `ownership`

`Weapon.cpp:21-25` passes `resource_manager` into the `TextureObject` base, which stores it in `DrawObject::_resource_manager` (DrawObject.h:36), **and** stores it again in `Weapon::_resource_manager` (Weapon.h:124). `Weapon.h:118` then declares `ResourceManager* get_resource_manager() const override;` whose whole body is `return this->_resource_manager;` (Weapon.cpp:500-503). Because `SpriteSheetObject::get_sprite_sheet()` resolves the manager through that virtual, `DrawObject::_resource_manager` becomes permanently dead state inside every `Weapon` while still looking live. Two aliases of one non-owning pointer with no single source of truth: any future fix that reseats one silently misses the other, and a reader cannot tell from the header which is authoritative.

**Fix:** Delete `Weapon::_resource_manager` and the `get_resource_manager` override and use the inherited accessor. Longer term, once rendering is decomposed out of `Weapon`, the weapon should be handed already-resolved handles and not know about `ResourceManager` at all.

#### 6. Weapon caches three raw non-owning pointers into objects that OnDeviceRestored destroys and rebuilds

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:122-124` — **medium** · `lifetime`

`Weapon` caches for its whole life `SoundBank* _sound_bank` (Weapon.h:47), `const float* _dt` (:123) and `ResourceManager* _resource_manager` (:124), set at Weapon.cpp:24-25 and :33, with no documented lifetime contract. All three owners are rebuilt by `Game::create_device_dependent_resources()`: `this->_resource_manager = std::make_unique<ResourceManager>();` (Game.cpp:238, which destroys every `SoundBank` it owned) and `this->_dt = std::make_unique<float>(0.f);` (Game.cpp:243). That function is re-run wholesale by `Game::OnDeviceRestored()` (Game.cpp:281-286).

Crucially `Game::OnDeviceLost()` (Game.cpp:268-279) does not tear down game state - the `_states` it resets is `std::unique_ptr<DirectX::CommonStates>` (Game.h:62), while the state machine is the separate `std::unique_ptr<State> _state` (Game.h:66). So the level, its players and their weapons survive the device-lost/restored cycle holding three dangling pointers, and the next frame executes `const float dt = *this->_dt;` (Weapon.cpp:193) on freed memory. The weapon also propagates the stale pointers into every projectile it spawns (Weapon.cpp:319-327, :565-573).

**Fix:** Pass `float dt` as a parameter to `update_and_get_projectiles` instead of caching a `const float*` - the call already threads other per-frame data down that path. For the manager pointers, either make `create_device_dependent_resources` genuinely idempotent (reuse the existing `ResourceManager`/`_dt` and only re-create D3D-dependent contents) or have `OnDeviceLost` tear the state machine down so nothing can hold stale pointers across the boundary.

#### 7. RelativeVelocityWeapon is a whole subclass carrying two data fields, and it duplicates the parent's update loop

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:145-183` — **medium** · `design`

`RelativeVelocityWeapon` adds exactly one member: `RelativeWeaponDetails _rel_details` = `{ add_player_velocity add_vel; float player_vel_amount; }` (WeaponDetails.h:15-19). For that it introduces a second hierarchy layer, a 14-parameter constructor, and a duplicate update loop: `Weapon::update_and_get_projectiles` (Weapon.cpp:168-186) and `RelativeVelocityWeapon::update_and_get_projectiles` (Weapon.cpp:576-595) are identical apart from `this->shoot(dir)` vs `this->shoot(dir, player_velocity)`. `Weapon::shoot` (Weapon.cpp:313-328) and `RelativeVelocityWeapon::shoot` (:552-574) are likewise the same eight-argument `build_projectiles` call with a different velocity computation. Three weapons derive from it, two do not - a split that exists purely because of where two floats live.

**Fix:** Fold `add_vel`/`player_vel_amount` into `WeaponDetails` and delete `RelativeVelocityWeapon`. Better, replace the enum+scalar with a single `Vector2F inherit_owner_velocity {0,0}` and compute `launch = dir * speed + owner_velocity * inherit_owner_velocity` unconditionally - no branch, no subclass, no duplicated update or shoot, and `NONE` becomes `{0,0}` (which also fixes the enum-fallthrough bug reported separately).

#### 8. Weapon.h drags the whole projectile hierarchy into every consumer and relies on a four-level transitive chain for rotation_origin

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:4-12` — **low** · `header-hygiene`

`rotation_origin` is used in the declaration at Weapon.h:104 with **no** include for it - it arrives only via WeaponDetails.h -> Projectile.h -> projectile_consts.h -> projectile_details.h -> rotation_origin.h. Reordering any of those headers breaks this one.

The expensive include is `#include "ProjectileBuilder.h"` (Weapon.h:11), needed only for the `std::unique_ptr<ProjectileBuilder> _proj_builder` member. ProjectileBuilder.h includes all five concrete projectile headers (ProjectileBuilder.h:4-9), so every TU that includes Player.h (which includes Weapon.h) compiles the entire projectile hierarchy, and a change to any projectile recompiles the whole weapon module. WeaponBuilder.h:4-8 repeats the pattern with all five concrete weapon headers.

**Fix:** Add `#include "rotation_origin.h"` directly. Forward-declare `class ProjectileBuilder;` and declare an out-of-line `~Weapon();` so the unique_ptr deleter is not instantiated in the header, moving the ProjectileBuilder.h include into Weapon.cpp - or delete the member entirely per the stateless-builder finding, which removes the include outright.

#### 9. Polymorphic bases are implicitly movable, so slicing compiles

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:14, 145` — **low** · `design`

`class Weapon : public TextureObject` and `class RelativeVelocityWeapon : public Weapon` are polymorphic bases with `final` leaves, but neither declares any special member. Copy construction is blocked only as a side effect of the `std::unique_ptr<ProjectileBuilder>` member (Weapon.h:122) - not by intent, so deleting that member (which the stateless-builder finding recommends) silently re-enables slicing copies. Move is available today: `DrawObject` has a user-declared destructor (`virtual ~DrawObject() = default;`, DrawObject.h:9) which suppresses its move operations but leaves its copy constructor implicitly generated, and `Weapon`'s own members are all movable - so `Weapon w = std::move(*some_weapon_sniper);` compiles and slices a `WeaponSniper` down to a `Weapon`. The intended ownership model is `std::unique_ptr<Weapon>` throughout (WeaponBuilder.cpp:19-37, Player.h:142), so value semantics on these types should be impossible rather than accidental.

**Fix:** Add an explicit deleted special-member block to `Weapon` and `RelativeVelocityWeapon` (copy and move ctor/assign). The same treatment belongs on `DrawObject`/`SpriteSheetObject`/`TextureObject`, which are the actual slicing surface.

#### 10. Weapon::draw hides the inherited TextureObject::draw overloads, forcing qualification that defeats dispatch

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:31-33` — **low** · `modern-cpp`

`Weapon` declares `virtual void draw(SpriteBatch*, const Camera&, bool debug = false)` and `virtual void draw(SpriteBatch*, bool debug = false)`. These are new names in the derived scope, so they hide the five inherited `TextureObject::draw` overloads (TextureObject.h:20-32). The workaround is visible throughout: every internal call must be explicitly qualified - `TextureObject::draw(sprite_batch, draw_rectangle, camera)` (Weapon.cpp:66, :80; WeaponRoller.cpp:99, :113). Explicit qualification on a virtual also defeats virtual dispatch, so any future `TextureObject::draw` override would be silently bypassed. The same qualification habit is applied inconsistently to the setters - `DrawObject::set_origin` at Weapon.cpp:62 and `TextureObject::set_origin` at :76 name the same function.

**Fix:** Add `using TextureObject::draw;` in Weapon's protected section and drop the class qualification from the call sites. The two-argument `draw(SpriteBatch*, bool)` overload should just be deleted - it only forwards to the camera version with `Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA` (Weapon.cpp:83-86), which the caller can pass itself.

#### 11. Protected data members punch through the accessors the class already provides

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:46-50` — **low** · `design`

```
protected:
	SoundBank* _sound_bank = nullptr;
	WeaponDetails _details = weapon_consts::DETAILS_DEFAULT;
	bool _shooting_this_update = false;
```
These are protected *data*, not accessors, and subclasses reach straight into them: WeaponSniper.cpp:32-33 and WeaponBucket.cpp:32-33 both do `this->_sound_bank->play_wave(this->_details.shoot_sound_name, this->_details.shoot_sound_volume);`, and WeaponRoller.cpp:90 reads `this->_shooting_this_update` - despite `get_details()` (Weapon.h:64) already existing and returning `const WeaponDetails&`. So the class offers a controlled accessor and an uncontrolled back door for the same field, and a subclass can repoint `_sound_bank` or rewrite `_details` after construction with the base unable to notice. `_details` is also a per-instance by-value copy (Weapon.cpp:23) of an immutable shared table entry - five `std::string`s duplicated into every weapon of every player, never mutated after construction (every accessor at Weapon.cpp:393-421 is a const read).

**Fix:** Make all three private with protected const accessors. Store the details as `const WeaponDetails*` into the single shared table once that table has external linkage, so the immutable data is neither copied per instance nor mutable after construction. Both subclass back-door uses disappear entirely once the sound mode is data-driven.

#### 12. Dead accessors and never-set state leave unreachable branches in both draw functions

`ArtAttack/Weapon.h:65-79, 129-131` — **low** · `correctness`

Verified by grepping all of ArtAttack/ for call sites:
- `set_invert_x(bool)` (Weapon.h:74, Weapon.cpp:438) is **never called**, so `_invert_x` (Weapon.h:129) is permanently `false`. That makes the `if (invert_y && invert_x)` and `else if (invert_x)` branches at Weapon.cpp:48-59 and the duplicated copy at WeaponRoller.cpp:72-83 unreachable - `SpriteEffects_FlipBoth` and `SpriteEffects_FlipHorizontally` can never be selected.
- `_gun_player_aligned` (Weapon.h:131) is initialised `true` and the only call to `set_gun_player_aligned` in the whole codebase is `set_gun_player_aligned(true)` at WeaponRoller.cpp:42. So `bool normal_gun_ok_to_shoot = input.primary_shoot && get_gun_player_aligned();` (Weapon.cpp:194-195) is just `input.primary_shoot`, reached through a member, a getter, a setter and two aliases.
- `get_offset()` (Weapon.cpp:398), `get_nozzle_offset()` (:403) and `get_dt()` (:496) are defined and never called - the code uses `*this->_dt` directly at :193.

**Fix:** Delete all four members/accessors and the alias chain; collapse the effects selection to `invert_y ? SpriteEffects_FlipVertically : SpriteEffects_None`. If mirrored or aligned firing returns, it belongs in a render-state `flip` field and a `FireControl` precondition, not as permanent base-class state every weapon pays for.

## `MattMathTests/CollisionToolsTests.cpp`

_3 findings: 2 high, 1 low_

#### 1. 2 tests cover 2 of CollisionTools' 11 functions; every buggy branch is untested

`MattMathTests/CollisionToolsTests.cpp:15-99` — **high** · `test-coverage` · confidence: certain

The whole CollisionTools suite is two methods exercising `calculate_object_collision_direction` and `resolve_object_collision` on symmetric axis-aligned cases. Untested, with defects visible on inspection:
- `calculate_containing_collision_direction` (ArtAttack/CollisionTools.cpp:91-107): `if (std::abs(x_distance) < std::abs(y_distance)) return compare_point_collision_depth_horizontal(...)` — inverted. When the vertical separation dominates it resolves horizontally.
- `resolve_object_AABB_collision` (ArtAttack/CollisionTools.cpp:209-229): `float larger = std::max(collision_direction.x, collision_direction.y); direction = collision_direction / larger;` uses signed max, not magnitude. For direction (-0.9, -0.1), `larger` is -0.1 and `direction` becomes (9, 1) — the collider is pushed out by 9x the overlap width. The two existing tests use directions (0.707,0.707) and (-1,0), the only two shapes of input for which this line happens to be harmless.
- `calculate_object_collision_direction_by_edge` (136-207): 12 branches, zero tests.
- `bracket_object_collision_generic` (55-69): the 40-iteration bisection push-out used for *every* non-rect-vs-rect resolution in the game, zero tests.
- `calculate_object_collision_depth`, `opposite_direction`: zero tests.

**Fix:** Table-drive it: for each ordered pair of shape types (rect, circle, triangle, quad, rotated-rect) and each of the 8 cardinal approach directions, assert the resolved shape no longer intersects and that `amount` has the expected sign and roughly the expected magnitude. That single table would catch all four issues above.

#### 2. The one regression test for ramp (rect-vs-triangle) collision is commented out, in the module being actively fixed

`MattMathTests/CollisionToolsTests.cpp:82-98` — **high** · `test-coverage` · confidence: certain

`test_rectagle_triangle_collision` (note the typo in the name) contains a 17-line commented-out block testing `RectangleF(220, 5878, 52, 120)` against `Triangle((200,6000),(400,6000),(400,5800))` — a player-sized box against a level-sized ramp, i.e. exactly the scenario the last few commits ("fix ramp-player collision", "adding OBB logic and tests") were about. It asserts `DIRECTION_DOWN_RIGHT` and a resolve amount of (-1,-1). It was disabled rather than fixed. What remains is a single 10x10-vs-10x10 case at the origin where every quantity is symmetric, so it cannot distinguish a correct implementation from one that mixes up x and y.

**Fix:** Restore the case with whatever the correct expected values are (derive them, don't read them off the implementation) and mark it `Assert::Fail("known bug: <link>")` if it genuinely fails, so the suite reports the defect instead of hiding it.

#### 3. Misspellings in a test name, a constant, and two asset paths

`MattMathTests/CollisionToolsTests.cpp:58` — **low** · `naming` · confidence: certain

Four concrete misspellings I confirmed by grep across code and assets:
  1. `MattMathTests/CollisionToolsTests.cpp:58` `TEST_METHOD(test_rectagle_triangle_collision)` - "rectagle". It is one of only two test methods in that file (the other, line 15, spells it correctly).
  2. `ArtAttack/player_consts.h:29` `constexpr float X_DEACCELERATION = 2500.0f;` - "deacceleration" is not a word; it is deceleration. Used at `Player.cpp:792,798,804,813`.
  3. `ArtAttack/levels/turebulence.pub` - "turebulence", next to correctly-spelled `turbulence.json` and `king_of_the_hill.pub` / `close_quarters.pub`.
  4. `ArtAttack/fonts/unuseed fonts/` - "unuseed", where `textures/old textures/` and `sounds/unused/` and `levels/unused/` are the same idea spelled three other ways.
Also worth noting: `MathTests.cpp:76 TEST_METHOD(test_test_2D_segment_segment)` has a doubled "test" because the function under test is `test_2D_segment_segment`.

**Fix:** Fix as: `test_rectangle_triangle_collision`; `X_DECELERATION`; rename the file to `turbulence.pub`; rename the folder to `unused fonts` (or better, delete it along with `textures/old textures/`, `levels/unused/`, `sounds/unused/` - and drop the spaces from directory names). For the test, `test_segment_segment_intersection_2d`.

## `MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp`

_9 findings: 6 high, 2 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. No degenerate, NaN, or exception-path testing anywhere in the suite

`MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:1-876` — **high** · `test-coverage` · confidence: certain

`grep ExpectException MattMathTests/` returns zero hits, and every shape in every test is well-formed with positive dimensions. Reachable, untested failure modes:
- `Vector2F::normalize()` and `normalized()` (MattMath.cpp:1724-1734) divide by length with no zero guard, producing NaN — while `Vector2F::unit_vector` (1852-1863) *does* guard and returns (1,0). Two functions with the same job and opposite behaviour on the same input; nothing pins either.
- `Vector2F::angle_between` (1808-1811) is `acos(dot(a,b) / (a.length()*b.length()))`; for near-parallel vectors the quotient can exceed 1.0 after rounding and `acos` returns NaN. `RectangleRotated::get_angle()` (4460-4462) is built directly on it, so a rotated rect aligned with +x can report a NaN angle.
- `EricsonMath::barycentric` (EricsonMath.cpp:729-743) divides by `denom = d00*d11 - d01*d01`, which is 0 for a collinear/degenerate triangle -> NaN -> `test_point_triangle` (746-752) silently returns false for every point.
- `Triangle::calculate_gradient` (3594-3603) divides by `x1 - x0` — infinite for a vertical edge — and throws for out-of-range indices.
- `Partitioner::partition(n, 0)` (ArtAttack/Partitioner.cpp:7) is integer division by zero.
No test covers zero-area rectangles, negative width/height rectangles (which `rectangle_point_intersect` at MattMath.cpp:252-258 silently treats as empty), zero-radius circles, zero-length segments, or coincident triangle vertices.

**Fix:** Add a dedicated `DegenerateInputTests` class: one test per primitive constructed degenerately, asserting either a documented result or a thrown exception. Decide and document whether MattMath is total (returns a sentinel) or partial (throws) — right now it is inconsistently both.

#### 2. Tests #include .cpp files, and the two test TUs are implicitly linked to each other

`MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:5-6` — **high** · `design` · confidence: certain

`MathTests.cpp` includes `..\ArtAttack\MattMath.cpp` and `..\ArtAttack\EricsonMath.cpp`; `CollisionToolsTests.cpp:3` includes only `..\ArtAttack\CollisionTools.cpp`. CollisionTools.cpp needs MattMath symbols, which it gets not from a library but from *the other test file's* translation unit. Rename or delete MathTests.cpp and CollisionToolsTests.cpp stops linking, for reasons nothing in its source explains. The root cause is that ArtAttack is `ConfigurationType=Application` (ArtAttack/ArtAttack.vcxproj) and produces no .lib, so the `<ProjectReference>` at MattMathTests.vcxproj:173 links nothing — it only forces a full rebuild of the game executable before every test run. It also means MattMath.cpp's file-scope statics (`Vector2F::ZERO`, `Camera::DEFAULT_CAMERA`, …) exist in two separate binaries.

**Fix:** Split the engine into `ArtAttackLib` (`ConfigurationType=StaticLibrary`) containing everything except `Main.cpp`, make `ArtAttack.exe` a thin app project linking it, and have MattMathTests link the lib and `#include` only headers. This is the single change that unlocks testing anything beyond MattMath.

#### 3. Three ad-hoc epsilon constants tuned until the tests went green, at resolutions finer than the library's own EPSILON

`MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:14-16, 335, 393, 658, 762, 816, 866` — **high** · `test-quality` · confidence: certain

The suite defines `EPSILON_F = 1e-6f`, `EPSILON_F_2 = 2e-6f`, `EPSILON_F_100 = 1e-4f` and picks between them per call site: `rectangle_segment_intersect` needs `EPSILON_F_2` for its negative case (line 335) while its positive case uses `EPSILON_F` (331); `quads_intersect` needs `EPSILON_F_2` (686); the rotated-rectangle cases need `EPSILON_F_100` (393, 658, 762, 816, 866). Nothing derives these — they are the smallest values that made each assertion pass. Meanwhile `MattMath::EPSILON` is `0.0001f` (ArtAttack/MattMath.h:46) and `are_equal` (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:93-96) uses it as the library's declared resolution, and `test_segment_AABB` adds its own `EricsonMath::EPSILON = 1e-6f` fudge (ArtAttack/EricsonMath.cpp:665-666). So most of these tests assert that the library distinguishes separations 100x smaller than it claims to resolve. They are pinning float noise, not behaviour.

**Fix:** Pick one tolerance derived from `MattMath::EPSILON`, test separations of e.g. 10*EPSILON (must not intersect) and -10*EPSILON (must intersect), and delete the sub-epsilon cases. If a specific sub-epsilon behaviour genuinely matters, document why in the test.

#### 4. Geometric results compared with exact float equality via Vector2F::operator==

`MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:34, 39, 44, 86, 107, 131, 229, 437, 523` — **high** · `test-quality` · confidence: certain

The suite's dominant assertion form is `Assert::IsTrue(closest == Point2F(5.0f, 0.0f))`. `Vector2F::operator==` (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:1574-1577) is `this->x == other.x && this->y == other.y` — bit equality, no tolerance. These are compared against values that came out of divisions and square roots (`closest_pt_point_segment` does `t = dot(c-a,ab)/dot(ab,ab)` then `d = a + t*ab`; `closest_pt_point_triangle` similar). They pass today only because every test input is a small power-of-two-friendly integer coordinate. Any change to the order of operations inside those routines — including one the optimiser makes — flips them. Note the suite already knows better: `are_equal(p, Point2F(...), 0.1f)` is used at lines 457 and 542, and CollisionToolsTests uses `Assert::AreEqual(a, b, EPSILON_F)`. The three styles are mixed arbitrarily.

**Fix:** Standardise on `Assert::IsTrue(are_equal(actual, expected, tol))` with a named tolerance, or add a small `AssertVec2(expected, actual, tol)` helper and use it everywhere. Exact `==` should be reserved for tests *of* `operator==` itself.

#### 5. FLT_EPSILON boundary cases are arithmetic no-ops: "just inside" and "just outside" are the same point

`MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:51-59` — **high** · `test-quality` · confidence: certain

`test_closest_pt_point_AABB` ends with:
```
// p is just inside a
p = Point2F(10.0f - FLT_EPSILON, 10.0f - FLT_EPSILON);
...
// p is just outside a
p = Point2F(10.0f + FLT_EPSILON, 10.0f + FLT_EPSILON);
```
`FLT_EPSILON` is 1.19e-7, which is the ULP at 1.0, not at 10.0. The ULP in [8,16) is 9.54e-7, so both `10.0f - FLT_EPSILON` and `10.0f + FLT_EPSILON` round to exactly `10.0f`. Both cases test the identical point (10,10), both assertions pass trivially, and the boundary they claim to probe is never touched. The same mistake appears in `test_rectangle_triangle_intersect` (MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:274-280), where the "just touching" and "just not touching" triangles are bit-identical.

**Fix:** Use a relative offset (`std::nextafter(10.0f, 11.0f)` / `std::nextafter(10.0f, 9.0f)`) or, better, an explicit tolerance that matches the library's own `MattMath::EPSILON` and assert only distinctions coarser than it.

#### 6. Two negative boundary cases build their input and then assert nothing

`MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:278-281` — **high** · `test-quality` · confidence: certain

`test_rectangle_triangle_intersect` finishes with:
```
// a and t are just not touching
t = Triangle(Point2F(10.0f + FLT_EPSILON, 10.0f), Point2F(20.0f, 10.0f),
    Point2F(10.0f + FLT_EPSILON, 20.0f));
}
```
No `Assert::IsFalse(...)` follows — the method just ends. Identically, `test_point_rectangle_rotated_intersect` (MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:823-826) writes `// p is just outside the corner of rr` and assigns `p`, then the very next statement (line 828) overwrites `p` with `Point2F(2.0f, 2.0f)` for the following case. In both places the negative boundary — the case most likely to regress — is silently skipped while the test still reports green.

**Fix:** Add the missing `Assert::IsFalse(...)` calls. More generally, a lint/review rule: every `// case` comment in these test bodies must be followed by at least one Assert before the next assignment to the same variable.

#### 7. Empty TEST_METHOD reports as a passing test

`MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:94-97` — **medium** · `test-quality` · confidence: certain

```
TEST_METHOD(test_test_segment_AABB)
{
    // tested below with rectangle_segment_intersect
}
```
An empty body is a pass in CppUnitTest, so the run summary counts coverage that does not exist. The claim in the comment is also only partly true: `rectangle_segment_intersect` (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:247-250) forwards to `test_segment_AABB`, but `test_segment_AABB` (ArtAttack/EricsonMath.cpp:644-684) has an epsilon-fudge branch (`adx += EPSILON; ady += EPSILON;` at 665-666) and a cross-product separating-axis test at 678 that the six cases in `test_rectangle_segment_intersect` (MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:312-337) never drive into — all six segments are axis-aligned or on the main diagonal.

**Fix:** Delete the placeholder or fill it in with cases that actually exercise the cross-product axis: a steeply sloped segment passing near a box corner, and a segment collinear with a box edge.

#### 8. Rotation and wraparound behaviour is tested only at the 8 exact axis directions; collinear segment overlap is never tested

`MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:160-195, 766-782` — **medium** · `test-coverage` · confidence: certain

`test_8_cardinal_direction` feeds `direction_to_8_cardinal_direction` exactly the eight vectors that are already the answers. The implementation (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:1870-1906) is a chain of half-open angle ranges (`angle >= -PI/8 && angle < PI/8`, `>= PI/8 && < 3PI/8`, …) built on `atan2`, whose range is (-PI, PI]. The sector boundaries and the ±PI wraparound — the only places the chain can fall through or double-count — are untested. The rest of the rotation API (`Vector2F::rotate`, `rotate_vector`, `rotate_vector_by_ref`, `angle`, `angle_between`, `normal`, `unit_vec_from_angle`, `vec_from_angle_magnitude`, `to_radians`/`to_degrees`) has zero tests despite RectangleRotated being built entirely on it.
Separately, `test_segments_intersect` (766-782) claims to cover the identical-segment case, but that only passes because `MattMath::segments_intersect` special-cases `if (a == b)` at MattMath.cpp:565-570. The real gap — *partially overlapping collinear* segments, e.g. (0,0)-(10,0) vs (5,0)-(15,0) — returns **false** from `test_2D_segment_segment` (EricsonMath.cpp:705, `a1*a2 < 0.0f` fails when all signed areas are 0), and no test says whether that is intended.

**Fix:** Test `direction_to_8_cardinal_direction` at each sector boundary angle and at ±PI; add a round-trip property test `rotate_vector(v, a) rotated by -a == v`. Add explicit collinear-overlap and shared-endpoint cases for `segments_intersect` and pin whatever the intended answer is.

#### 9. Duplicated epsilon constants, shadowed namespaces, and expected values transcribed from the implementation

`MattMathTests/MathTests.cpp:12-19, 152-158, 61-75` — **low** · `test-quality` · confidence: certain

`EPSILON_F = 0.000001f` is declared three times: `MathTestConstants::EPSILON_F` (line 14, then `using namespace MathTestConstants` at 19), `MattMathTests::EPSILON_F` (line 154, which shadows it for the whole MattMath test class), and `CollisionToolsTests::EPSILON_F` (MattMathTests/CollisionToolsTests.cpp:10). `TEST_CLASS(MattMathTests)` sits inside `namespace MattMathTests` inside a file that also does `using namespace MattMath` — three near-identical names in scope at once.
On derivation: `test_signed_2D_tri_area` (61-75) asserts `signed_2D_tri_area(a, b, c) == 100.0f` for a triangle with legs of 10 — whose area is 50. The function returns *twice* the signed area (EricsonMath.cpp:686-692 says so in a comment), so the expected value was read off the implementation rather than derived; the test's own comment ("a, b, c are in counter-clockwise order") is also wrong for this y-down coordinate system, where (0,0),(10,0),(0,10) is clockwise. A reader cannot tell from the test what the function is supposed to return.

**Fix:** One shared `test_constants.h` with a single tolerance. Rename the test namespace (e.g. `mattmath_tests`). Write expected values as expressions that show the derivation (`2.0f * 0.5f * 10.0f * 10.0f`) and fix the winding comments.

## `MattMathTests/MattMathTests.vcxproj`

_5 findings: 2 high, 2 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. Tests compile the code under test with different codegen than the game ships with

`MattMathTests/MattMathTests.vcxproj:91-158` — **high** · `build-config` · confidence: certain

ArtAttack.vcxproj sets, in all four configs, `<FloatingPointModel>Fast</FloatingPointModel>` (lines 94, 116, 139, 165), `<ConformanceMode>true</ConformanceMode>` (96, 117, 141, 166), `<WarningLevel>Level4</WarningLevel>`, and on Win32 `<EnableEnhancedInstructionSet>StreamingSIMDExtensions2</EnableEnhancedInstructionSet>` (95, 140). MattMathTests.vcxproj sets *none* of these: no FloatingPointModel (so /fp:precise), no ConformanceMode, `Level3`. MattMath.cpp and EricsonMath.cpp are therefore compiled twice with different float semantics — the tested build reassociates less and keeps more intermediate precision than the shipped build. Given the previous finding (1-ULP boundary assertions and exact float comparisons), this is not theoretical: the suite can be green while the identical source in ArtAttack.exe returns the other answer. Neither project sets `<LanguageStandard>` either, so both are stuck on the MSVC default of C++14.

**Fix:** Extract a shared `common.props` with LanguageStandard, FloatingPointModel, ConformanceMode, WarningLevel and TreatWarningAsError, and import it from both projects. The test project must never compile engine code under settings the engine does not use.

#### 2. Unit tests compile MattMath.cpp with /fp:precise while the game compiles it with /fp:fast - tests validate different arithmetic than ships

`MattMathTests/MattMathTests.vcxproj:96-104,111-119,128-137,147-156` — **high** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

ArtAttack.vcxproj sets <FloatingPointModel>Fast</FloatingPointModel> in all four configs (lines 94, 116, 139, 165). MattMathTests.vcxproj sets no FloatingPointModel at all in any of its four ItemDefinitionGroups, so it compiles at the default /fp:precise. Because the tests textually include the implementation (MathTests.cpp:5 `#include "..\ArtAttack\MattMath.cpp"`, CollisionToolsTests.cpp:3 `#include "..\ArtAttack\CollisionTools.cpp"`), the exact same source is compiled twice under different floating-point contraction, reassociation and NaN/denormal rules. The tests assert with epsilons as tight as 1e-6 (MathTests.cpp:14 `constexpr float EPSILON_F = 0.000001f;`, CollisionToolsTests.cpp:10). A green test suite therefore does not tell you the shipping build behaves the same way - and CollisionTools' bisection push-out (BRACKET_ITERATIONS=40) is precisely the kind of iterative float code where /fp:fast reassociation changes results. The same drift applies to /arch:SSE2, which ArtAttack sets on Win32 (lines 95, 140) and the test project never sets.

**Fix:** Move FloatingPointModel, EnableEnhancedInstructionSet, ConformanceMode, WarningLevel and LanguageStandard into a single shared Common.props imported by both .vcxproj files, so the tests cannot drift from the build under test. Better still, link a real engine .lib so there is only one compilation of MattMath.cpp in existence.

#### 3. Tests never run automatically: no CI, PCH configured but empty, versioned NuGet path hardcoded

`MattMathTests/MattMathTests.vcxproj:93, 108, 123, 142, 173` — **medium** · `build-config` · confidence: certain

There is no `.github/`, no pipeline file, no test script anywhere in the repo root — the 33 test methods run only when someone opens Visual Studio and clicks Run All. Neither project sets `TreatWarningAsError`, so nothing enforces the tests or the /W4 warnings. Supporting problems in the test project: all four configs set `<PrecompiledHeader>Use</PrecompiledHeader>` with `<PrecompiledHeaderFile>pch.h</PrecompiledHeaderFile>` against a `pch.h` that contains no includes at all (MattMathTests/pch.h:1-13) — pure build machinery for zero benefit, and a hazard because the code under test does `#include "pch.h"` too (ArtAttack/MattMath.cpp:1, ArtAttack/CollisionTools.cpp:1) which resolves to the *other*, DirectX-configuring `ArtAttack/pch.h`. The include directories hardcode `..\packages\directxtk_desktop_2019.2023.10.31.1\include` (lines 96, 111, 128, 147), which breaks on any package upgrade, and the test project has no packages.config of its own.

**Fix:** Add a CI workflow running `msbuild ArtAttack.sln` then `vstest.console.exe UnitTests.dll` on push. Set `PrecompiledHeader=NotUsing` in the test project (or actually populate pch.h). Replace the versioned NuGet path with the `$(...)` property the .targets file defines.

#### 4. Test project hardcodes a versioned NuGet path, has no packages.config, and its PCH is an empty stub

`MattMathTests/MattMathTests.vcxproj:96,111,128,147` — **medium** · `build-config` · confidence: certain

All four ItemDefinitionGroups put `..\packages\directxtk_desktop_2019.2023.10.31.1\include` on the include path literally. The test project has no packages.config of its own (MattMathTests/ contains only the two test .cpp, pch.h/.cpp and the project files), so nothing restores that package for it - it works purely because ArtAttack/packages.config happens to pin the identical version. Bump DirectXTK and the test project breaks with a missing-header error that points at nothing obvious. Separately, all four configs set <PrecompiledHeader>Use</PrecompiledHeader> with <PrecompiledHeaderFile>pch.h</PrecompiledHeaderFile>, but MattMathTests/pch.h is the untouched wizard stub - guard, a comment saying 'add headers that you want to pre-compile here', and nothing else - so the PCH provides zero benefit while still costing a Create pass. And <ProjectName>UnitTests</ProjectName> (line 27) disagrees with both the directory and the .vcxproj filename, so the solution shows a project name that matches nothing on disk.

**Fix:** Add a packages.config to the test project (or migrate both projects to PackageReference so the version lives in one place), replace the hardcoded path with the $(directxtk...) property the NuGet targets define, either populate pch.h or set PrecompiledHeader to NotUsing, and make ProjectName match the directory.

#### 5. The test project has three different names, and its test classes shadow the namespaces containing them

`MattMathTests/MattMathTests.vcxproj:25-28` — **low** · `naming` · confidence: certain

`MattMathTests.vcxproj:28` sets `<ProjectName>UnitTests</ProjectName>` while line 25 sets `<RootNamespace>MattMathTests</RootNamespace>`, the file/folder is `MattMathTests`, and `ArtAttack.sln:8` registers it as `"MattMathTests"`. Build output is `UnitTests.dll` (visible in the checked-in `MattMathTests/Debug/UnitTests.*` artifacts). So the same project is called three things depending on where you look, and the name that actually appears in Visual Studio's Solution Explorer is the one nobody wrote down.
Inside, `MathTests.cpp:22-23` declares `namespace EricsonMathTests { TEST_CLASS(EricsonMathTests)` - class name identical to enclosing namespace - and `:156 TEST_CLASS(MattMathTests)` collides with the project name. The file `MathTests.cpp` also covers two modules (MattMath and EricsonMath) while `CollisionToolsTests.cpp` covers one, so the file names do not predict contents either.

**Fix:** Delete the `<ProjectName>` override so all four names agree on `MattMathTests`. Split `MathTests.cpp` into `MattMathTests.cpp` and `EricsonMathTests.cpp`, and name the TEST_CLASSes after what they test rather than after their namespace (`ShapeIntersectionTests`, `ClosestPointTests`, ...).

## `ArtAttack/AnimationObject.cpp`

_5 findings: 5 medium_

#### 1. AnimationObject's constructor calls virtual functions and does two resource lookups on a half-built object

`ArtAttack/AnimationObject.cpp:16-22` — **medium** · `correctness`

```cpp
AnimationObject::AnimationObject(const float* dt, ...) :
	SpriteSheetObject(sheet_name, animation_strip_name, ...), _dt(dt)
{
	this->_frame_time = this->get_animation_strip()->get_frame_time();   // :21
}
```
`get_animation_strip()` (:24-28) calls `get_sprite_sheet()` and `get_element_name()`, both declared `virtual` in SpriteSheetObject.h:20-21. During this constructor the dynamic type is `AnimationObject`, so any override in a derived class is silently bypassed and the object gets a `_frame_time` from the wrong strip. No warning; the failure mode is a wrong animation speed.

It also bakes in an undocumented ordering requirement: no `AnimationObject` — and therefore no `Player`, `Projectile` or `PaintTileSplash` — may be constructed before `ResourceLoader::load_all_resources()` has populated that specific sheet *and* that specific strip. On violation, `ResourceManager::get_sprite_sheet` returns nullptr (see that finding) and this is a null dereference during object construction, from a virtual call, in a constructor.

`_frame_time` is itself a denormalised cached copy of `AnimationStrip::_frame_time` that must be manually re-synced via `set_frame_time_to_default()` whenever the strip changes.

**Fix:** Never call virtuals from a constructor. Resolve the strip outside the object and inject it: `AnimationObject(const float* dt, const AnimationStrip& strip, ...) : ..., _strip(&strip), _frame_time(strip.get_frame_time()) {}`. Holding the resolved `const AnimationStrip*` also removes two string map lookups from `update()` and `get_source_rectangle()` on every object every frame.

#### 2. Every projectile re-resolves its sprite sheet and animation strip through two string-keyed map lookups, multiple times per frame per viewport

`ArtAttack/AnimationObject.cpp:24-28` — **medium** · `performance`

Verified. `AnimationObject::get_animation_strip()` resolves from scratch on every call:
```cpp
return this->get_sprite_sheet()->get_animation_strip(this->get_element_name());
```
That is two red-black-tree lookups keyed on `std::string`: `ResourceManager::_sprite_sheets` (ResourceManager.cpp:51) then `SpriteSheet::_animation_strips`. Per projectile per frame it happens:
- once in `AnimationObject::update()` (line 87), called from every projectile's `update()`;
- once in `AnimationObject::draw()` for `get_sprite_sheet()` (line 33), plus again inside `get_source_rectangle()` (line 141), which calls `get_animation_strip()` a second time.

And `draw` runs once per player viewport (Level.cpp:375-399 partitions the players), so 4-player split screen is on the order of a dozen string-keyed tree walks per projectile per frame. Every one of these values is immutable after load and identical for all projectiles of a given type.

The strings are also stored twice per projectile: `SpriteSheetObject::_sheet_name`/`_element_name` (SpriteSheetObject.h:25-26) duplicate `_details.sheet_name`/`_details.animation_strip_name` (projectile_details.h:16-17), so spawning one projectile constructs four `std::string`s. The mister does this five times per shot.

**Fix:** Resolve `SpriteSheet*` and `const AnimationStrip*` once in the `AnimationObject` constructor and cache them as members; keep the strings only for the rare `set_animation_strip_and_reset` path, which re-resolves. That deletes every per-frame lookup and, as a side effect, removes the multi-threaded `ResourceManager` access described in the related finding. Where string-keyed lookup must remain, `std::unordered_map` beats `std::map` — nothing here needs ordering.

#### 3. Frame advance uses `if` not `while` and frame_time is never validated, so fast strips drift and a zero frame_time poisons the accumulator

`ArtAttack/AnimationObject.cpp:81-107` — **medium** · `correctness`

```cpp
this->_time_elapsed += *this->_dt;
float frame_time = this->_frame_time;
if (this->_time_elapsed > frame_time)   // :90 — single if
{
    this->_frame_index++;
    ...
    this->_time_elapsed -= frame_time;
}
```
At most one frame advances per `update()` no matter how much time accumulated. If `frame_time < dt`, `_time_elapsed` gains `dt - frame_time` every call and grows without bound while the animation caps at one frame per update — it plays slower than authored and the accumulator is permanently poisoned, so `pause()`/`play()` and any later `set_frame_time` behave unpredictably. It also cannot recover from a hitch.

`set_frame_time` (:152-155) validates nothing, and `AnimationStrip::_frame_time` defaults to `0.0f` (AnimationStrip.h:22) with no validation in the JSON decoder (SpriteSheet.cpp:62), so a strip that omits `frame_time` installs zero — at which point `_time_elapsed -= 0` is a no-op and the accumulator diverges forever.

The code is safe today only because the fixed timestep pins dt at 1/60 and every authored frame_time in sprite_sheet_1.json is 0.05-0.2.

I am rejecting one attached sub-claim: a reviewer argued `Player::draw`'s `if (info.frame_time != FLT_MIN)` sentinel (Player.cpp:66) could fail its exact float comparison under /fp:fast and install ~1e-38. /fp:fast is indeed on in all four configs, but both sides of that comparison are the same compile-time constant from player_consts.h with no arithmetic or round-trip between them. The exact-equality-on-float sentinel is still poor style worth replacing, but it is not a live trigger.

**Fix:** Drain the accumulator and reject nonsense input:
```cpp
while (_frame_time > 0.0f && _time_elapsed >= _frame_time) { _time_elapsed -= _frame_time; advance_one_frame(); }
```
Validate `frame_time > 0` in the JSON decoder so a malformed sheet fails at load. Replace the `FLT_MIN` sentinel with `std::optional<float>`.

#### 4. Animation stepping consumes one frame per update instead of draining elapsed time; silently assumes dt < frame_time

`ArtAttack/AnimationObject.cpp:81-107` — **medium** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

```
this->_time_elapsed += *this->_dt;
float frame_time = this->_frame_time;
if (this->_time_elapsed > frame_time)
{
    this->_frame_index++;
    ...
    this->_time_elapsed -= frame_time;
}
```

It is an `if`, not a `while`. If `*_dt` ever exceeds `frame_time`, `_time_elapsed` grows without bound while the animation advances at most one frame per update — animations play in slow motion and drift permanently out of sync with the simulation. The identical code exists in `AnimatedSprite::update` (ArtAttack/AnimatedSprite.cpp:59-84, copy-pasted).

This is latent today only because `*_dt` happens to be the constant 0.0166666 (fixed timestep) and the shipped animation strips have longer frame times. It becomes a live bug the instant anyone sets `SetFixedTimeStep(false)` (the DirectXTK default, and what the template comment at ArtAttack/Game.cpp:62-63 invites), lowers `TARGET_FPS`, or authors a fast strip. For an engine that is supposed to be reusable, an animation system that only works for one hard-coded step size is a defect regardless of whether it currently misbehaves.

**Fix:** Change `if` to `while` and guard against `frame_time <= 0` to avoid an infinite loop. Then delete one of the two copies — `AnimationObject` and `AnimatedSprite` are the same algorithm written twice.

#### 5. reset() does not clear _paused, so any object that finishes a non-looping animation is frozen forever afterwards

`ArtAttack/AnimationObject.cpp:108-117` — **medium** · `correctness`

```cpp
void AnimationObject::reset() { this->_frame_index = 0; this->_time_elapsed = 0.0f; }
void AnimationObject::stop()  { this->_paused = true; this->reset(); }
void AnimationObject::play()  { this->_paused = false; }
```
`update()` latches `_paused = true` when a non-looping strip reaches its last frame (:102), and `update()` returns immediately while paused (:83-86). `reset()` clears the index and accumulator but not `_paused` — and neither does `set_animation_strip_and_reset` (:144-151), despite the name promising a fresh start.

So once an object plays any non-looping animation to completion, every subsequent `set_animation_strip_and_reset` leaves it stuck on frame 0 of the new strip forever. sprite_sheet_1.json has exactly such a strip (`looping: false` at line 119).

`PaintTileSplash` only escapes because it hand-patches around it: `reset_and_play()` (PaintTile.cpp:176-180) calls `reset()` *and* `play()`. `Player::draw` calls `set_animation_strip_and_reset` with no `play()`, and survives only because all the player strips in the JSON are `looping: true`. Adding one non-looping player animation — a death or hit reaction — freezes the character permanently.

Duplicated verbatim in `AnimatedSprite::reset()` (AnimatedSprite.cpp:85-89).

**Fix:** Make `reset()` mean reset: `_frame_index = 0; _time_elapsed = 0.0f; _paused = false;` and keep `stop()` as `reset(); _paused = true;`. `PaintTileSplash::reset_and_play()` then collapses to a plain `reset()`.

## `ArtAttack/AnimationObject.h`

_1 finding: 1 medium_

#### 1. protected virtual AnimationObject::update() has the same signature as IGameObject::update(), so Player::update overrides both at once

`ArtAttack/AnimationObject.h:21` — **medium** · `correctness`

```cpp
protected:
    virtual void update();     // AnimationObject.h:21
```
Identical signature to `IGameObject::update()` (IGameObject.h:10, public pure virtual). `Player final : MovingObject, ICollisionGameObject, AnimationObject, TextureObject` (Player.h:63-64) inherits both, so its single `void update() override;` overrides two unrelated virtuals simultaneously — one an interface contract meaning "advance the whole game object", the other an implementation detail meaning "advance the animation frame".

It does not blow up today only because every derived class remembers the explicit qualified call (`AnimationObject::update();` in Player.cpp and each of the four Projectile subclasses). The moment anything inside `AnimationObject` calls unqualified `update()`, or a new derived class forgets the qualified call, you get infinite recursion or a permanently frozen animation with no diagnostic. Nothing overrides `AnimationObject::update` in the virtual sense, so the `virtual` buys nothing and creates the collision.

**Fix:** Rename it to say what it does and drop `virtual`: `void advance_animation();`. That removes the accidental override and makes the five call sites read correctly. The same reasoning applies to the `virtual` on the `draw` overloads in AnimationObject.h:34-46 and TextureObject.h:20-32, which shadow `IGameObject::draw` by name in every multiply-inheriting concrete class.

## `ArtAttack/AnimationStrip.cpp`

_2 findings: 1 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. AnimationStrip trusts frame_count from JSON, allocates unreserved, keeps a redundant count, and has a default ctor that can only throw

`ArtAttack/AnimationStrip.cpp:17-58` — **medium** · `robustness`

Four related defects in one small class:

1. `calculate_all_frame_rects()` (:50-57) `push_back`s `_frame_count` times with no `reserve`, so a strip reallocates log2(n) times at load.
2. `_frame_count` comes straight from `strip["frame_count"].GetInt()` (SpriteSheet.cpp:61) with no validation. A negative value yields an empty strip whose every `get_frame_rect()` then throws; a huge value attempts that many RECTs.
3. `calculate_frame` (:17-26) re-validates an index against `_frame_count` even though its only caller is a loop bounded by `_frame_count` — a branch that can never fire — and it throws from inside the constructor, which runs inside `SpriteSheet::load_from_json`, so a bad sheet aborts resource loading via an exception nobody catches. `get_frame_rect` (:28-35) then validates against `_frame_count` but indexes `_frame_rects`, two values that agree only by constructor convention.
4. `AnimationStrip() = default` (AnimationStrip.h:9) leaves `_frame_count == 0`, so the guard in `get_frame_rect` is true for every index including 0 — a default-constructed strip's entire public surface is a guaranteed exception. Nothing default-constructs one (they are built only at SpriteSheet.cpp:64), so this is cleanup rather than a live bug.

Separately, `calculate_frame` hardcodes a single uniform-width horizontal row (`frame.offset(frame_index * frame.width, 0)`) with no way to express a grid, wrapped or non-uniform atlas, and one `frame_time` for the whole clip — a real limitation for a reusable engine.

**Fix:** Validate `frame_count > 0` and `frame_time > 0` in the decoder, with a message naming the strip. `reserve(_frame_count)` before the loop. Drop `_frame_count` and use `_frame_rects.size()` as the single source of truth, which removes the redundant check. Delete the default constructor. Longer term, model a clip as an explicit ordered list of `FrameId`s plus timing, so any packing layout works.

#### 2. throw std::exception("literal") is an MSVC extension that does not compile on any other toolchain — 54 sites

`ArtAttack/AnimationStrip.cpp:21` — **low** · `portability`

```cpp
throw std::exception("frame_index out of range");   // AnimationStrip.cpp:21 and :32
throw std::exception("Invalid frame index.");       // AnimationObject.cpp:131
throw std::exception("Invalid frame index.");       // AnimatedSprite.cpp:115
throw std::exception("Failed to finish command list"); // Level.cpp
```
Standard `std::exception` has no `const char*` constructor; only MSVC's implementation provides one. Every one of these is a hard compile error on libstdc++/libc++. I counted 54 occurrences across the first-party .cpp files (the reviewers said 58 — the count differs slightly depending on whether headers are included, but the order of magnitude is right). For a codebase whose stated purpose is a reusable 2D engine, this single idiom pins it to one compiler.

The type is also wrong: an out-of-range frame index is `std::out_of_range`, and catching anything meaningfully is impossible when everything throws the same base type. `ResourceManager` already throws `std::out_of_range` for the analogous case, so the codebase is inconsistent with itself.

**Fix:** `throw std::out_of_range("AnimationStrip::get_frame_rect: frame_index " + std::to_string(frame_index) + " not in [0, " + std::to_string(_frame_count) + ")");` and equivalents elsewhere. `<stdexcept>` is already in pch.h. Fixing all 54 is mechanical and unblocks any future cross-platform build.

## `ArtAttack/ArtAttack.vcxproj.filters`

_1 finding: 1 medium_

#### 1. Two filters cover 6 of 200 project items - all 193 sources sit flat in one directory with no engine/game boundary

`ArtAttack/ArtAttack.vcxproj.filters:3-11` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

The filters file declares exactly two filters, "Common" (lines 4-6) and "Assets" (lines 7-10). "Common" is applied only to the four Microsoft-supplied files (StepTimer.h, DeviceResources.h/.cpp) and "Assets" to directx.ico, sprite_sheet_1.dds and settings.manifest. Every other ClInclude/ClCompile entry - all 105 headers and 81 sources - has no <Filter> element and appears at the project root. On disk it is the same: ArtAttack/ is one flat directory containing DeviceResources.cpp, MattMath.cpp, ThreadPool.cpp, Player.cpp, WeaponSniper.cpp and MainMenu.cpp side by side. There is no physical or logical line anywhere between 'engine' (device/timer/math/collision/threadpool/resources/state/sprite) and 'game' (Splatoon-specific players, weapons, projectiles, teams, menus). Given the stated goal, this is the structural expression of the problem: nobody can tell what they would need to take with them, and nothing stops game concepts leaking into engine types (which they have - see collision_object_type.h enumerating PROJECTILE_SPRAY_TEAM_A inside the core ICollisionGameObject interface, and ResourceManager.h:33 keying a cache on level_stage).

**Fix:** Move files into real directories (engine/platform, engine/math, engine/render, engine/resources, engine/core, game/...) and regenerate the filters from the paths. Do this at the same time as splitting the static library - the directory layout is what makes the library split obvious and enforceable.

## `ArtAttack/BorderThickness.h`

_2 findings: 1 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. 105 headers use ad-hoc #ifndef guards with collision-prone global macro names; three vendor headers use #pragma once

`ArtAttack/BorderThickness.h:1-2` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

Guard style is inconsistent and the names are unsafe for a library meant to be embedded in someone else's build. BorderThickness.h:1-2 uses `#ifndef BORDER_THICKNESS` / `#define BORDER_THICKNESS` - not even suffixed _H, and a plausible identifier for a UI type in a consuming project. Other guards occupy extremely generic global macro names with no project prefix: TEXT_H (Text.h), LEVEL_H, STATE_H, SAVE_H, PLAYER_H, WEAPON_H, STRUCTURE_H, GAME_H, VISUAL_H, COLOUR_H, DIMENSION_H, DIRECTION_H, PROJECTILE_H. Naming is also internally inconsistent - ANIMATEDSPRITE_H vs ANIMATED_SPRITE style is applied at random across ~65 of the 105 headers. PlayerInputData.h uses `PLAYER_INPUT_H` while PlayerInput.h uses `PLAYERINPUT_H`: they do not collide today but are one rename apart from silently eliding a header. Trailing #endif comments have drifted from their guards (LevelLoadedInfo.h defines LEVELLOADEDINFO_H but its #endif comment says LEVEL_LOADED_INFO_H; StateContext.h:2 defines STATECONTEXT_H but its #endif says STATECONTEXTGENERIC_H; IPaintableGameObject.h defines IPAINTABLEGAMEOBJECT_H, #endif says IPAINTABLE_H). Meanwhile the three Microsoft-supplied headers (pch.h, DeviceResources.h, StepTimer.h) all use #pragma once, so the project already mixes both conventions.

**Fix:** Switch every first-party header to `#pragma once` (MSVC, clang and gcc all support it, and it is what the vendor files in this same directory already do). That removes 105 global macro names from the preprocessor namespace and makes the drifted #endif comments moot. If you prefer guards for portability reasons, prefix them all with ARTATTACK_ and generate them from the path.

#### 2. Include guard is a bare BORDER_THICKNESS macro that will eat any future constant of that name

`ArtAttack/BorderThickness.h:1-10` — **low** · `robustness`

Verified — the file is 12 lines:
```cpp
#ifndef BORDER_THICKNESS
#define BORDER_THICKNESS
```
Unlike every sibling (MATTMATH_H, COLOUR_H, DIMENSION_H), this defines an object-like macro named exactly BORDER_THICKNESS expanding to nothing. Any TU that includes it — CameraTools.h:4, and transitively anything using the camera — then cannot declare `constexpr float BORDER_THICKNESS = 8.0f;`, which preprocesses to `constexpr float = 8.0f;` and errors at the declaration rather than at the macro. Not hypothetical for this codebase: the adjacent constants are PaintTile.h `THICKNESS` and ViewportManager.h `DIVIDER_THICKNESS`.

Also verified: line 7 is `float top = 0.0f;;` (stray second semicolon); the struct sits in the global namespace while every comparable primitive lives in MattMath; and it is aggregate-initialised positionally from four same-typed floats at CameraTools.cpp:77-83, where transposing two is invisible to the compiler. RectangleF meanwhile only offers symmetric inflate (MattMath.cpp:932-949) — there is no way to inset a rectangle by four independent amounts, which is exactly what a scroll border, a UI margin or a nine-slice needs.

**Fix:** Rename the guard BORDER_THICKNESS_H (or switch the project to #pragma once), drop the stray semicolon, move the struct into namespace MattMath as `Thickness`, and add `RectangleF deflated(const Thickness&) const` / `inflated(...)`. CameraTools then becomes `rect.deflated(scroll_border)` instead of four hand-written edge computations.

## `ArtAttack/CollisionTools.h`

_4 findings: 4 medium_

#### 1. CollisionTools is a namespace in class costume with global-scope tuning constants and an all-raw-pointer API

`ArtAttack/CollisionTools.h:7-13, 54-98` — **medium** · `design`

Every member is static, the class has no state, and `CollisionTools() = default;` (line 13) exists only so `CollisionTools ct;` compiles — a Java-style utility class. EricsonMath, in the same module group, correctly uses `namespace EricsonMath { ... }`, so the module is internally inconsistent on the most basic structural choice.

`constexpr int BRACKET_ITERATIONS = 40;` and `constexpr float ITERATION_POWER = 1.5f;` (lines 7-8) sit at **global** namespace scope in a public header transitively included by Player and much of the game — names that generic, unqualified, are a collision hazard, and there is no way for a game or a test to tune them.

The API surface is all raw pointers: `resolve_object_collision(Shape* collider, const Shape* collidee, ...)` mutates `collider` in place via `offset()` yet is indistinguishable from a signature that takes ownership or accepts null. Nothing null-checks either argument. Nothing guards `collider == collidee` — passing the same shape twice would burn all 40 iterations translating an object away from itself and never separate; the only self-pair guard lives in the caller (Level.cpp:283), not in the library. Finally, all ~10 Player call sites discard the bool return.

**Fix:** `namespace collision_tools { ... }` with the constants inside it (or moved to an anonymous namespace in the .cpp, since only the .cpp uses them). Change parameters to `Shape&` / `const Shape&` so non-null and non-owning are in the type system and `assert(&collider != &collidee)` becomes possible. Mark the resolver `[[nodiscard]]` and collapse the twin overload.

#### 2. No LanguageStandard set in either vcxproj, so the project builds as C++14 and works around missing standard facilities

`ArtAttack/CollisionTools.h:7-8` — **medium** · `design`

Neither ArtAttack.vcxproj nor MattMathTests.vcxproj contains a `<LanguageStandard>` element (verified by grep), so MSVC defaults to /std:c++14. That is not a cosmetic setting — it is the direct cause of several findings in this module:

- `EricsonMath::clamp` exists (and duplicates `MattMath::clamp`, and is dead) because std::clamp is C++17.
- Nine of fifteen EricsonMath functions signal failure through a bool plus out-params because std::optional is C++17.
- `resolve_object_collision` has a twin overload whose only purpose is to declare a throwaway local, for the same reason.
- `constexpr` globals in the CollisionTools header get a per-TU copy without `inline constexpr`.

Also absent from both projects: `TreatWarningAsError`. WarningLevel is Level4 in all four ArtAttack configurations (and only Level3 in the test project), so /W4 is advisory — which is why the dead locals at CollisionTools.cpp:35/58 (C4189), the unused `view` parameters in Mh.cpp (C4100), and the signed/unsigned loops at Level.cpp:386 and MenuPage.cpp:140 (C4018) have all accumulated unaddressed.

**Fix:** Set `<LanguageStandard>stdcpp20</LanguageStandard>` in both vcxproj files — a grep shows zero C++17-or-later features in use, so nothing breaks — then delete the workarounds it was hiding. Turn on TreatWarningAsError, or at minimum /we4189 /we4100 /we4018, so /W4 stops being decoration.

#### 3. Five bare global constants with generic names leak from widely-included headers

`ArtAttack/CollisionTools.h:7-8` — **medium** · `naming` · confidence: certain

`CollisionTools.h:7-8` declares `constexpr int BRACKET_ITERATIONS = 40;` and `constexpr float ITERATION_POWER = 1.5f;` at global scope, and `Game.h:12-14` declares `constexpr int TARGET_FPS = 60;`, `NUM_THREADS_MIN = 1;`, `NUM_THREADS_MAX = 16;`. These are the only five global-scope constants in the entire codebase - I checked every header - because everything else lives in a `*_consts` namespace (`player_consts`, `weapon_consts`, `projectile_consts`, `level_consts`, `camera_consts`, `viewport_consts`, `menu_input_consts`, `player_input_consts`, `debug_text_consts`, `main_menu_consts`, `interface_consts`, `directory_consts`, `colour_consts`, `team_colour_consts`). `CollisionTools.h` is included by `Player.h`, so `BRACKET_ITERATIONS` and `ITERATION_POWER` - two of the most collision-prone identifiers imaginable - are visible across most of the program.

**Fix:** Wrap them: `namespace collision_consts { constexpr int RESOLUTION_BRACKET_ITERATIONS = 40; constexpr float BRACKET_STEP_DECAY = 1.5f; }` and `namespace game_consts { constexpr int TARGET_FPS = 60; ... }`. Note `ITERATION_POWER` is also a name that does not describe what it does (it is the decay base for the bisection step size).

#### 4. Two incompatible public "collision direction" algorithms with no rule for choosing between them

`ArtAttack/CollisionTools.h:24-41` — **medium** · `design`

The public API exposes `calculate_object_collision_direction` (centre-to-centre, CollisionTools.cpp:125-134) and `calculate_object_collision_direction_by_edge` (AABB edge-overlap classification, CollisionTools.cpp:136-207). They return different answers for the same input, carry near-identical doc comments, and nothing states which is correct when. Player uses the edge version for generic structures (Player.cpp:488) and the centre version for ramps (Player.cpp:247) — the caller is expected to have internalised which heuristic fits which case.

`..._by_edge` takes `const Shape*` but immediately reduces both arguments to `get_bounding_box()` (lines 139-140), so the polymorphic parameter type is a lie; the doc comment even admits "This function is less accurate with non-rectangle shapes". Its body is a 72-line ladder of twelve hand-written boolean combinations plus two helpers plus a fallthrough.

**Fix:** One narrow-phase query returning a Contact. If an AABB-only fast path is genuinely wanted, express it in the type system (`contact(const RectangleF&, const RectangleF&)`) so it cannot be handed a triangle. An MTV subsumes ..._by_edge, calculate_containing_collision_direction and both compare_point_collision_depth_* helpers.

## `ArtAttack/DebugText.cpp`

_2 findings: 1 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. The on-screen FPS readout is a constant 60 by construction; the timer's real FPS counter is never used

`ArtAttack/DebugText.cpp:81-82` — **medium** · `correctness` · confidence: certain

```
lines.push_back("dt: " + std::to_string(this->get_dt()));
lines.push_back("fps: " + std::to_string(1.0f / this->get_dt()));
```

In fixed-timestep mode `StepTimer::Tick` assigns `m_elapsedTicks = m_targetElapsedTicks` on every iteration (ArtAttack/StepTimer.h:136), so `GetElapsedSeconds()` returns a compile-time-determined constant. `Game::update` copies it into the shared float (ArtAttack/Game.cpp:89-90). With `SetTargetElapsedSeconds(1.0 / TARGET_FPS)` (Game.cpp:65, `TARGET_FPS = 60` at Game.h:12), `m_targetElapsedTicks = (uint64)(1.0/60 * 1e7) = 166666`, so `*_dt` is 0.0166666f forever and the debug overlay prints `fps: 60.000240` no matter what the machine is actually doing. The one number a developer would look at to diagnose a performance problem is hard-wired to the target.

`StepTimer::GetFramesPerSecond()` (ArtAttack/StepTimer.h:55) computes the genuine presented-frame rate and is never called anywhere in the codebase.

Secondary point for the engine goal: because `*_dt` is provably constant, every `* dt` in the simulation (`Player.cpp:734, 761, 873`, `Projectile.cpp:234`, `Weapon.cpp:193`, `Level.cpp:106, 130, 141, 163`) is multiplication by a literal written as if it were variable — the frame-rate independence is nominal, never exercised, and would break the first time the target rate changed (see the animation-stepping finding).

**Fix:** Plumb `_timer.GetFramesPerSecond()` (and ideally the measured wall-clock delta) through `GameData` and print that as `fps`; keep `dt` for the simulation step. Since the app is fixed-step, also consider naming the constant `FIXED_STEP_SECONDS` rather than deriving it from a variable called `TARGET_FPS`, which reads as a rendering target.

#### 2. draw_debug_info: unguarded 1/dt, two different bool formats in adjacent lines, gratuitous copies, and per-frame string churn

`ArtAttack/DebugText.cpp:18-137` — **low** · `quality`

Several small defects in one function:

- Line 82: `std::to_string(1.0f / this->get_dt())` with no guard. `Drawer::get_dt()` (Drawer.cpp:28-31) dereferences `_dt` unconditionally on a pointer that defaults to nullptr, and `Game::_dt` starts at 0.0f (Game.cpp:244) and is only written in `update()`, which the fixed-timestep loop can skip while render always runs. The result is `"inf"` — harmless output, but it is the same unguarded pointer every `Drawer` subclass uses with no stated contract. (Correcting the reviewers: `1.0f/0.0f` gives inf under IEEE regardless of /fp:fast.)
- Lines 70-79 format `primary_shooting` as `"true"`/`"false"` via an eight-line if/else, while lines 84-85 format two other bools through `std::to_string(bool)`, which resolves to the `int` overload and prints `"1"`/`"0"`. Three booleans, two formats, in the same block.
- Lines 23-28 copy `RectangleF`, `Vector2F`, `Camera` and `Viewport` from accessors that already return `const&`.
- `std::vector<std::string> lines;` with ~20 `push_back`s and no `reserve`, rebuilt from scratch every call, inside the parallel render pass. The `operator+` chains at :46-68 do allocate for the longer lines (the short `to_string` results fit MSVC's SSO, so I am not repeating the reviewers' "60+ allocations" figure).
- An index loop over a container only ever read front-to-back (:111).
- `Level.cpp:574` recomputes `count_projectiles()` — a full linear scan — once per player rather than once per frame.

**Fix:** `const float dt = get_dt(); lines.push_back("fps: " + (dt > 0.0f ? std::to_string(1.0f/dt) : std::string("--")));`. One `bool_str` helper for all three booleans. `const auto&` for the four reference getters. `lines.reserve(20)` and a range-for. Keep the vector as a member and rebuild in place. Hoist `count_projectiles()` out of the per-player loop.

## `ArtAttack/direction.h`

_2 findings: 1 medium, 1 low_

#### 1. Four overlapping direction/anchor enums, three of them in headers nothing includes

`ArtAttack/direction.h:4-15` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

The repo has four enums covering the same conceptual space:
  - `::direction` (`direction.h:4-15`): TOP_LEFT..BOTTOM_RIGHT, 9 anchor values.
  - `MattMath::direction` (`MattMath.h:12-22`): NONE, UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT, UP_LEFT... - a compass, unqualified-name-identical to the above.
  - `menu_direction` (`MenuInput.h:94-101`): UP/DOWN/LEFT/RIGHT/NONE.
  - `rotation_origin` (`rotation_origin.h:4-10`): CENTER, TOP_LEFT, LEFT_CENTER, NO_ROTATION - anchors again.
I grepped every include and every use site: `direction.h` is included by zero files, and its values are referenced zero times. Same for `dimension.h` (enum `dimension { X, Y }`) and `direction_lock.h` (enum `direction_lock { LOCKED, UNLOCKED }`) - both are orphans with no includers and no uses. So three of the eight snake_case enum headers are dead weight whose names actively collide with live concepts.

**Fix:** Delete `direction.h`, `dimension.h`, `direction_lock.h` (and their vcxproj entries). Rename `MattMath::direction` -> `MattMath::cardinal_direction` so it says what it is, and keep `menu_direction` and `rotation_origin` as-is. If a 9-way anchor type is ever needed, call it `anchor_point`, not `direction`.

#### 2. direction.h and direction_lock.h are dead files, and direction.h would break any TU that also uses MattMath

`ArtAttack/direction.h:1-17` — **low** · `design`

Merges 3 candidates. I grepped the whole tree: neither header is `#include`d by any source file — the only references are `ArtAttack.vcxproj:195-196` and the two matching `.filters` entries.

`direction.h` is not merely dead, it is a landmine. It declares a global-scope `enum class direction { TOP_LEFT, TOP, ..., BOTTOM_RIGHT }` (nine anchor positions) whose name collides with `MattMath::direction { NONE, UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT, UP_LEFT, ... }` (a compass enum). `Player.cpp:5` has `using namespace MattMath;` and then uses the unqualified name as a TYPE at :366 (`direction dir = velocity.get_direction();`), :606 and :624. Including direction.h anywhere into that TU makes every one of those an ambiguity error. The same file also uses `direction` as a VARIABLE name at :247 and :488, so within one file the identifier is a type in some scopes and a local in others.

**Fix:** Delete both headers and their vcxproj/filters entries. If a nine-way anchor is wanted later, name it `anchor_point` and namespace it. Rename the `Vector2F direction` locals in Player.cpp to `collision_direction`.

## `ArtAttack/directory_consts.h`

_3 findings: 3 medium_

#### 1. Content locations are CWD-relative paths as namespace-scope std::string objects in a header, with no post-build asset copy

`ArtAttack/directory_consts.h:6-13` — **medium** · `design`

Merged from 3 candidates, with one sub-claim corrected.

    namespace directory_consts {
        const static std::string TEXTURE_DIRECTORY = "./textures/";
        const static std::string LEVEL_DIRECTORY = "./levels/";
        const static std::string FONT_DIRECTORY = "./fonts/";
        const static std::string SAVE_FILE_PATH = "./save/save_data.json";
        const static std::string SOUNDS_DIRECTORY = "./sounds/";
    }

1. These resolve against the process CWD, not the executable location. I grepped ArtAttack.vcxproj for PostBuildEvent/Copy/xcopy — no matches — and the asset folders sit next to the .vcxproj, not the built exe. The app therefore only finds its assets when launched by the VS debugger (CWD defaults to $(ProjectDir)). Double-clicking the built exe hits the unchecked-fopen crash path.
2. `SAVE_FILE_PATH` writes settings into the install directory, which fails on any properly-installed app; and `write_save_file` returning false is swallowed (Save.cpp:91-98) so settings silently do not persist. It is also a FILE living in a namespace called `directory_consts`.
3. `const` at namespace scope already gives internal linkage, so `static` is redundant. Each including TU still gets its own five `std::string` objects, dynamically initialised before main. CORRECTION to one candidate: it claimed all five exceed MSVC's 15-char SSO limit "except ./levels/". That is wrong — "./textures/" (11), "./fonts/" (8), "./levels/" (9) and "./sounds/" (9) all fit in SSO; only SAVE_FILE_PATH (21 chars) heap-allocates. The dynamic-initialisation-per-TU point stands regardless.
4. The layout is a policy decision frozen into an engine header, compounded by ResourceLoader's hardcoded extensions.

**Fix:** Resolve an asset root once at startup from `GetModuleFileNameW` + parent (or a CLI/env override) into a small `Paths`/VFS service with mount points. Put the save file under %LOCALAPPDATA% via `SHGetKnownFolderPath`. Add a post-build content copy so the exe is standalone. Make the constants `constexpr const char*` (works under C++14) or `inline constexpr std::string_view` after the standard bump.

#### 2. Content roots are hardcoded relative paths with no mount point, and the built exe is not standalone

`ArtAttack/directory_consts.h:6-13` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

```
namespace directory_consts {
    const static std::string TEXTURE_DIRECTORY = "./textures/";
    const static std::string LEVEL_DIRECTORY   = "./levels/";
    const static std::string FONT_DIRECTORY    = "./fonts/";
    const static std::string SAVE_FILE_PATH    = "./save/save_data.json";
    const static std::string SOUNDS_DIRECTORY  = "./sounds/";
}
```
Every path is CWD-relative with no configuration hook, and `ArtAttack.vcxproj` has no post-build copy step for `textures/`, `levels/`, `fonts/`, `sounds/` — so the app only finds content because the VS debugger sets CWD to `$(ProjectDir)`. Running the built .exe from its output directory fails. The save path is also fixed under the content root rather than in `%APPDATA%`, and `ArtAttack/save/save_data.json` is git-tracked yet rewritten at runtime, so every launch dirties the working tree.

For an engine this is the difference between 'reusable' and 'only works in Matt's solution directory' — a second game cannot relocate or repackage its content.

**Fix:** Introduce an engine `ContentPaths`/`FileSystem` object initialised from the executable directory (`GetModuleFileNameW`) with game-settable subroots, and pass it to `ResourceLoader` instead of the header constants. Move the save file to `SHGetKnownFolderPath(FOLDERID_RoamingAppData)/<AppName>/` and untrack `save/save_data.json`. Add a post-build content copy (or a `<Content>` item group) so the exe is standalone.

#### 3. Asset paths are CWD-relative literals with no post-build copy — the built exe cannot find its data

`ArtAttack/directory_consts.h:8-12` — **medium** · `design` · confidence: certain

```cpp
const static std::string TEXTURE_DIRECTORY = "./textures/";
const static std::string LEVEL_DIRECTORY   = "./levels/";
const static std::string FONT_DIRECTORY    = "./fonts/";
const static std::string SAVE_FILE_PATH    = "./save/save_data.json";
const static std::string SOUNDS_DIRECTORY  = "./sounds/";
```

These resolve against the process working directory. `ArtAttack.vcxproj` has no `PostBuildEvent`, no `<Content Include>` items, no `CopyFileToFolders`, and no `<LocalDebuggerWorkingDirectory>` (verified by grep). The only reason the game runs is that the VS debugger defaults the working directory to `$(ProjectDir)`, which happens to be where `textures/`, `levels/`, `fonts/` and `sounds/` live. Double-clicking the built exe, or launching it from anywhere else, finds nothing — and per the finding above, finds nothing by crashing on a null FILE*.

Secondary: `const static std::string` at namespace scope in a header gives internal linkage — a separate copy plus dynamic initialisation of five `std::string`s in each of the 81 translation units. There is also no way to redirect the data root at runtime (dev vs. installed layout, per-user save location, packaged archive).

**Fix:** Resolve paths against the executable's directory (`GetModuleFileNameW` + parent) rather than the CWD, put the save file under `%LOCALAPPDATA%` (the tracked `ArtAttack/save/save_data.json` is currently rewritten on every launch, dirtying the working tree). Add `<Content Include>` items with `CopyToOutputDirectory` so the output folder is self-contained. Make the constants `inline constexpr std::string_view` or a small runtime-configurable `AssetPaths` service.

## `ArtAttack/Drawer.h`
